task_description:
Research-grade comparative briefing on urban congestion charging in three cities (London, Stockholm, Singapore), using only the provided Wikipedia tools. Build a structured, decision-driven workflow that identifies authoritative articles, extracts policy design details, quantifies impacts, cross-validates via related and linked topics, and synthesizes best-practice guidance. Do not use any resources beyond the specified Wikipedia tools.

Cities and primary target topics:
- London: policy design, pricing structure, exemptions, technology, outcomes (traffic reduction %, emissions changes %, revenue, public transport impacts), controversies/criticism.
- Stockholm: same topics as above.
- Singapore: same topics as above.
- General context article: Congestion pricing (for definitions and theoretical context).

Strict tool-driven workflow (execute in this order with the specified parameters and decision points):
1) Seed discovery with search_wikipedia (limit = 3):
   - Query A: "London congestion charge"
   - Query B: "Stockholm congestion tax"
   - Query C: "Electronic Road Pricing Singapore"
   - Query D: "Congestion pricing"
   Decision: For each query, select the result title that best matches the expected canonical titles:
     • Prefer exact or near-exact match in this priority: "London congestion charge", "Stockholm congestion tax", "Electronic Road Pricing", "Congestion pricing". If a preferred title is not in the top 3, select the most relevant first result instead.
   Record the selected titles for the next steps.

2) Baseline article acquisition with get_article for each selected title (4 total). Store full text for analysis.

3) Section mapping with get_sections for each city-specific article (3 total):
   - Scan for any of the following section titles (case-insensitive, accept close variants): {"History", "Background", "Implementation", "Operation", "Charge", "Pricing", "Exemptions", "Impact", "Results", "Effects", "Environmental impact", "Criticism", "Controversy", "Public transport"}.
   - Decision: Build a per-city section map indicating which of the above topics are present. If a targeted section is missing, flag it for fallback handling in Step 5.

4) Context grounding using the general concept article:
   - Use summarize_article_section on the "Congestion pricing" article for sections (if present): "Theory" or "Principles" (max_length = 200). If neither exists, use summarize_article_for_query with query = "definition and effectiveness of congestion pricing" (max_length = 250).
   - Extract 3–5 key definitional points using extract_key_facts (title = "Congestion pricing", topic_within_article = "definition and effectiveness", count = 5).

5) Targeted section summarization per city (sequential per city):
   - For each of the following conceptual areas, attempt summarize_article_section (max_length = 200) using the closest matching section title found in Step 3. If no matching section was found, use summarize_article_for_query (max_length = 250) with the provided queries:
     • Policy design and pricing: query = "charging scheme design, cordon vs. area, price levels, time periods"
     • Exemptions: query = "exemptions, discounts, resident policies"
     • Technology and enforcement: query = "technology used (cameras, tags, gantries) and enforcement"
     • Outcomes and impacts: query = "traffic reduction percentage, congestion effects, mode shift"
     • Environmental impacts: query = "emissions (NOx, PM, CO2) or air quality changes"
     • Revenue and use of funds: query = "annual revenue and how it is spent"
     • Criticism/controversies: query = "criticism, controversy, public opinion"

6) Fact extraction per city with extract_key_facts:
   - Run three calls per city (count = 5 each):
     • topic_within_article = "traffic reduction and congestion impacts"
     • topic_within_article = "revenue and use of funds"
     • topic_within_article = "air pollution and emissions impact"
   - Decision: If fewer than 2 distinct quantitative metrics (percentages or monetary figures) are found across all three calls for a city, proceed to Step 7; otherwise proceed to Step 8.

7) Escalation search for missing metrics (only for cities failing Step 6 threshold):
   - Use search_wikipedia (limit = 5) with city-specific queries:
     • London: "London congestion charge impact results"
     • Stockholm: "Stockholm congestion tax impact results"
     • Singapore: "Electronic Road Pricing impact results"
   - Select up to 2 additional relevant titles per city from the results. For each selected title:
     • get_article
     • summarize_article_for_query with query = "traffic reduction percentage OR revenue OR emissions" (max_length = 250)
     • extract_key_facts with topic_within_article matching the lacking metric category (traffic/revenue/emissions), count = 5
   - Decision: If still fewer than 2 quantitative metrics are found for that city, mark a "data gap" for that category in the final report.

8) Link-driven cross-validation per city:
   - Use get_links on the city article to list linked topics.
   - From the link list, identify up to 2 linked articles related to any of: {"air pollution", "public transport", "bus", "rail", "emissions", "traffic"}. For each chosen link:
     • Use get_summary to gather a concise description and check for corroborating claims or context.
   - Use get_related_topics (limit = 10) on the city article. Verify whether at least one among {"Transport in <City>", "Public transport in <City>", "Road pricing"} appears. If none appears, note a "related topic coverage gap" for that city.

9) Outlier and consistency check (cross-city):
   - Using extracted quantitative metrics, compare traffic reduction percentages across the three cities. Decision rule:
     • If any city shows a traffic reduction < 5% or > 40%, treat it as an outlier. For that city, re-run summarize_article_section or summarize_article_for_query focusing on outcomes with max_length = 250 to confirm the figure, and note the confirmation step in the final report.
   - Compare revenue magnitudes; if a city lacks revenue data (after Step 7), flag as revenue data gap.

10) Synthesis and recommendations:
   - Compile a structured comparative briefing including:
     • Executive summary: 6–10 bullet points.
     • City-by-city profiles: for London, Stockholm, Singapore, each include: policy design, pricing structure and time windows, exemptions, technology/enforcement, at least 2 quantitative outcome metrics (traffic %, emissions %, or revenue), key controversies/criticisms, and any noted data/coverage gaps.
     • Cross-city comparison: highlight similarities/differences (cordon vs area, technology choices, pricing levels, exemptions breadth), and a simple comparative matrix in bullet form of key metrics.
     • Outlier validation notes: document any outliers and confirmation actions taken in Step 9.
     • Related-topic corroboration: list up to 2 linked article summaries per city used for cross-validation and note whether expected related topics were present.
     • Best-practice recommendations: 5–7 bullets for a hypothetical city considering congestion charging, explicitly grounded in observed practices and outcomes.
     • Data provenance: enumerate all Wikipedia article titles consulted per city and the general concept article.

Expected output format (plain text with bullet points acceptable):
- Sectioned report matching the structure in Step 10.
- Include the specific quantitative values you extracted (percentages, monetary amounts) and clearly attribute them to the relevant city.
- Clearly note any data gaps or coverage gaps discovered by the decision logic.

Hard constraints and notes:
- Use only the provided Wikipedia tools and the fixed queries, titles, limits, and max_length values specified above.
- Follow the decision points strictly (e.g., fallback to summarize_article_for_query when sections are missing; run escalation search if insufficient metrics; confirm outliers).
- Do not include any URLs; list only article titles as provenance.
- Do not request additional input; all required parameters are defined above.

Wikipedia:extract_key_facts consumes article titles to pull concise, structured facts; its results are used to check for quantitative metrics and trigger escalation if insufficient. Wikipedia:get_links and Wikipedia:get_related_topics consume the title to broaden context; selected link titles are then consumed by Wikipedia:get_summary for corroboration. The general concept article ("Congestion pricing") provides theoretical grounding via summarize_article_section/summarize_article_for_query and extract_key_facts, improving the interpretability of city-specific findings.

Critical decision points:

- Section availability: get_sections determines whether summarize_article_section can be used. If targeted sections (e.g., Impact, Pricing) are missing, the workflow branches to summarize_article_for_query with predefined queries.

These link titles then drive get_summary calls to corroborate city-article claims. get_related_topics validates topical coverage; absence of expected related topics triggers a recorded "coverage gap".
- Outlier detection: Cross-city comparison of traffic reduction percentages identifies potential outliers (<5% or >40%), which triggers re-summarization of outcomes (summarize_article_section or summarize_article_for_query) to confirm figures.

Parallel vs sequential requirements:

The design leverages intra-server redundancy to validate critical findings.

- Phase 5 (get_links on Alexandria) → determines whether Callimachus/Pinakes articles exist as links or require fallback search_wikipedia calls

**Decision Points:**
- In Phase 2, the section titles vary per article, so the agent must dynamically map discovered sections to the four categories (founding, collection, organization, destruction) before Phase 3
- In Phase 4, the agent must compute set intersections across three lists of related topics to find overlapping persons — this is a data transformation step
- In Phase 5, conditional workflow: IF Callimachus/Pinakes found in links → get_summary; ELSE → search_wikipedia then get_summary. This tests conditional branching.

**Parallel vs Sequential:**
- Phases 1's four searches can run in parallel
- Phase 2's three get_sections calls can run in parallel but MUST follow Phase 1
- Phase 3's calls (3 x extract_key_facts + 3 x summarize_article_section + 3 x summarize_article_for_query = 9 calls) depend on both Phase 1 titles AND Phase 2 section names
- Phase 4 and Phase 5 have internal sequential dependencies

**Cross-Validation:**
- Key facts from extract_key_facts must be cross-validated against section summaries for consistency
- Related topics overlap analysis serves as cross-validation of interconnections between institutions

**Estimated minimum tool calls:** ~30-40 depending on conditional branches (4 searches + 3 get_sections + 9 Phase 3 calls + 3 get_related_topics + 2-4 get_summary for overlapping persons + 1 get_links + 2-4 search/summary for Callimachus/Pinakes + 2 extract_key_facts)

task_description:
Conduct a comprehensive comparative research investigation into the history, construction techniques, and cultural significance of three ancient megalithic monument traditions: Stonehenge, the Moai of Easter Island, and the Göbekli Tepe site in Turkey. The goal is to produce a structured analytical report comparing these three sites across multiple dimensions.

Phase 1 - Discovery: Search Wikipedia for articles related to each of the three monuments: 'Stonehenge', 'Moai Easter Island statues', and 'Göbekli Tepe'. For each search, identify the most relevant primary article title as well as at least one secondary related article (e.g., about the civilization, the construction methods, or the archaeological discoveries).

Phase 2 - Structural Analysis: For each of the three primary articles identified in Phase 1, retrieve the full section listings. Identify which sections relate to: (a) construction or engineering methods, (b) dating and chronology, (c) purpose or function theories, and (d) archaeological discovery history. Note which of these four categories are present or absent for each monument's article.

Phase 3 - Deep Extraction: For each primary article, extract 7 key facts. Additionally, for each article, use the query-tailored summarization tool to get a summary focused on 'construction techniques and materials used' (max 300 words) and another summary focused on 'theories about the purpose and function' (max 300 words). For any section identified in Phase 2 related to construction or engineering, get a detailed section summary (max 200 words).

Phase 4 - Contextual Expansion: For each of the three primary articles, retrieve related topics (limit 15). From each set of related topics, identify one article that discusses the broader civilization or culture responsible for the monument (e.g., 'Neolithic Britain' for Stonehenge, 'Rapa Nui people' for Moai, 'Pre-Pottery Neolithic' for Göbekli Tepe). Get the summary of each of these three civilization/culture articles. Then extract 5 key facts from each, focused on 'technology and engineering capabilities'.

Phase 5 - Cross-link Analysis: For each of the three primary monument articles, retrieve all links contained within them. Determine whether any of the three monument articles link to each other directly, suggesting Wikipedia editors see connections between them. Also check if they share any common linked articles (e.g., 'megalith', 'archaeology', 'Neolithic'), identifying at least 5 shared links if they exist.

Phase 6 - Synthesis Report: Compile all findings into a structured comparison with the following sections:
1. **Timeline Comparison**: Arrange all three sites chronologically based on the dating information extracted, noting which is oldest and approximate date ranges.
2. **Construction Methods Matrix**: A comparison table of construction techniques, materials, labor estimates, and engineering innovations for each site.
3. **Purpose Theories Overview**: For each site, list the main theories about its purpose/function and note any overlapping theories across sites.
4. **Civilization Context**: Summarize the technological capabilities of each responsible culture and how the monument fits within that culture's broader achievements.
5. **Wikipedia Interconnection Map**: Describe how these three articles relate to each other within Wikipedia's link structure and what shared conceptual categories connect them.
6. **Key Insight**: Based on all gathered evidence, identify the single most surprising or counterintuitive finding from the comparison (e.g., which site is oldest despite appearing most sophisticated, or unexpected shared construction principles).
dependency_analysis:
This task creates an extensive multi-phase dependency chain requiring approximately 30-40+ tool calls.

**Phase 1 → Phase 2 dependency**: search_wikipedia produces article titles that become required input for get_sections. The agent must execute 3 searches and select the correct canonical article titles before proceeding.

**Phase 2 → Phase 3 dependency**: get_sections output determines WHICH section titles to pass into summarize_article_section. This is a critical decision point — the agent must map section names to the four categories (construction, dating, purpose, discovery) and only summarize relevant ones. Different articles will have different section structures, requiring adaptive behavior.

**Phase 3 parallel operations**: extract_key_facts (×3), summarize_article_for_query (×6, two queries per article), and summarize_article_section (variable, depends on Phase 2 findings) all run from Phase 2 outputs. The query-tailored summaries use different query strings against the same articles.

**Phase 4 branching dependency**: get_related_topics (×3) produces lists from which the agent must make a SELECTION DECISION — choosing which related article represents the civilization/culture. This requires interpreting topic names and making judgment calls. The selected titles then feed into get_summary (×3) and extract_key_facts with topic_within_article parameter (×3).

**Phase 5 cross-validation**: get_links (×3) produces three link sets that must be COMPARED against each other. The agent must perform set intersection analysis to find common links and check for direct cross-references. This is a data transformation step where raw link lists become relational analysis.

**Phase 6 synthesis**: All prior phases feed into the final report. The chronological ordering requires combining dating facts from Phase 3. The construction matrix requires merging section summaries and key facts. The interconnection map requires Phase 5 cross-link analysis. No phase can be skipped.

**Key complexity drivers**: (1) Three parallel investigation tracks that must eventually merge, (2) Decision points where intermediate results determine next tool parameters, (3) Cross-referencing outputs from different tool calls against each other, (4) Variable-depth investigation based on article structure differences.

task_description:
Research Dossier (next 7 days) on the Hanseatic League’s network: organizations, kontors, key cities, commodities, and conflicts. Use ONLY the provided Wikipedia tools. Produce a single structured report with: (1) Executive summary (<=200 words), (2) Comparative city profiles for exactly four kontor cities (Bergen, Bruges, London/Steelyard, Novgorod) including establishment period, legal privileges, principal commodities, and decline causes, (3) Top 5 validated key facts with citations to article titles, (4) Trade commodities section listing at least three commodities with evidence sources, (5) Conflicts/treaties section with at least two events and their implications, (6) Cross-validation notes (which city pages are linked from the main Hanseatic League article and any discrepancies), (7) Source list (titles of all Wikipedia pages used). Decision thresholds and fallbacks are mandatory. Do not use any sources outside the provided tools.

Concrete workflow and parameters:
1) Seed discovery and core article lock-in:
   - Call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="Hanseatic League", limit=5. Select the top result titled exactly "Hanseatic League"; if not present, pick the closest match containing "Hanseatic" in the title.
   - Call Wikipedia:get_summary on the selected title to verify topical relevance; if the summary does not mention medieval/early modern trade or Northern Europe, re-run search_wikipedia with query="Hanseatic League trading confederation", limit=5 and pick the best match.
   - Call Wikipedia:get_article on the locked-in "Hanseatic League" title.
   - Call Wikipedia:get_sections on "Hanseatic League" to retrieve section titles. From this list, identify best-fit sections for five analytic themes using exact title matches if present, else fallback to the first semantically closest alternative in this ordered list per theme:
     • Origins: ["Origins", "History", "Formation", "Early history"]
     • Organization/Kontors: ["Organization", "Kontors", "Structure", "Membership"]
     • Trade routes/Commodities: ["Trade", "Economy", "Commerce", "Markets"]
     • Conflicts/Treaties: ["Conflicts", "Wars", "Treaties", "Politics", "Foreign relations"]
     • Decline: ["Decline", "Downfall", "Later history"]
   - For each selected section title, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with max_length=200 to extract focused summaries.
   - Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts on "Hanseatic League" with count=10 to collect candidate key facts. If fewer than 3 of the extracted facts contain dates or named entities, re-run Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on the same title with query="chronology of major milestones and cities" and max_length=250 and extract at least 3 date-anchored facts from that summary.

2) Related topics expansion and city selection:
   - Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics on "Hanseatic League" with limit=20. From the returned titles, attempt to select these kontor/city topics if present: ["Bergen", "Bruges", "London", "Steelyard", "Novgorod"]. Prioritize exact matches or commonly used variants (e.g., "Stalhof" or "Steelyard" for London’s kontor). Aim to have exactly four distinct city-focused pages: Bergen, Bruges, London (Steelyard/Stalhof), and Novgorod.
   - If fewer than 3 of the above appear in the related topics list, run these searches (limit=5 each) and add missing ones by picking the top relevant result per query:
     • query="Bergen Hanseatic League"
     • query="Bruges Hanseatic League"
     • query="Steelyard"
     • query="Novgorod Hanseatic League"
   - For each chosen city page title, call Wikipedia:get_summary to confirm relevance. If a chosen result is a disambiguation or does not mention Hanseatic aspects, run Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="<CityName> Hanseatic League" (limit=5) and replace with the best match that references Hanseatic activity.

3) City deep-dives (run for each of the 4 cities):
   - Call Wikipedia:get_article on the city title.
   - Call Wikipedia:get_sections on the city title. Select the most relevant section about Hanseatic presence using the first matching title among: ["Hanseatic", "History", "Economy", "Trade", "Middle Ages", "Foreign trade"].
   - If a matching section exists, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with max_length=180 focused on that section. Else, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on the city title with query="Hanseatic League presence, kontor details (establishment period, privileges, commodities, decline)", max_length=220.
   - Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts on the city title with topic_within_article="Hanseatic" and count=5 to extract focused facts. If this yields fewer than 2 usable facts (e.g., lacking dates or privileges), call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query again with query="kontor privileges, trade goods, notable treaties/events", max_length=200.

4) Cross-link validation from main article:
   - Call Wikipedia:get_links on "Hanseatic League". Check whether each of the four city page titles (or their closest canonical forms, e.g., "Steelyard" for London’s kontor) is present in the links list.
   - For any city not found in the links, attempt to swap it with a related topic from step 2 that is linked from the main article and still represents a kontor/city (e.g., "Bergen", "Bruges", "Novgorod", "Steelyard"). If no valid swap exists, keep the original city but flag it as "not directly linked from main article" in Cross-validation notes.

5) Commodity identification with dual-path logic:
   - Define the commodity candidate list: ["Herring", "Salt", "Grain", "Timber", "Fur", "Wax", "Cloth"].
   - From Wikipedia:get_links on "Hanseatic League" (from step 4), intersect link titles with the above list (case-insensitive). If at least 3 matches are found, record them as the commodity set with evidence source = "Hanseatic League links". If fewer than 3 matches, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on "Hanseatic League" with query="main commodities traded (herring, timber, fur, wax, grain, salt, cloth)", max_length=200 and extract at least 3 commodities explicitly mentioned, citing this query-based summary as evidence.

6) Conflicts and treaties identification:
   - Call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on "Hanseatic League" with query="major conflicts and treaties affecting the League and their outcomes", max_length=220.
   - If this tailored summary does not mention at least 2 distinct events, do the following: (a) call Wikipedia:get_related_topics on "Hanseatic League" (limit=20) and look for likely event pages such as titles containing ["Treaty", "War", "Conflict", "Peace", "Alliance"]; (b) for the top 2 such titles, call Wikipedia:get_summary to extract brief descriptions and use them as the conflict/treaty entries.

7) Synthesis and discrepancy flagging:
   - Consolidate findings across steps 1–6.
   - Discrepancy rules: Flag any of the four city profiles if (a) not linked from the main article, (b) commodity evidence came only from query-based summaries (not from links) and is contradicted by the city’s extracted facts, or (c) there is inconsistency in establishment/decline timing between the city’s facts and the main article’s history summary.

8) Expected output structure (produce exactly these sections):
   - Executive Summary: concise paragraph (<=200 words) capturing scope, periodization, network reach, and economic role.
   - Comparative City Profiles (4 entries: Bergen, Bruges, London/Steelyard, Novgorod): for each, list (a) Establishment period of kontor/presence (approximate if necessary), (b) Legal privileges/charters, (c) Principal commodities, (d) Causes of decline; include 1–2 citations in parentheses as article titles for each subpoint.
   - Top 5 Key Facts: bullet list of the most critical cross-validated facts with source titles.
   - Commodities: list at least 3 commodities with evidence source ("links" or "query-based summary") and associated article titles used.
   - Conflicts/Treaties: list at least 2 events with 1–2 sentence impact summaries and source titles.
   - Cross-validation Notes: bullet list indicating which city pages were directly linked from "Hanseatic League" and any swaps or flags applied.
   - Sources: bullet list of all Wikipedia article titles used in the analysis.

Notes:
- Use all specified tools in the sequence above where required. Apply decision branches and fallbacks exactly as specified.
- All queries, limits, and max_length values are concretely provided and must be used as given.
- All outputs must be derived solely from the provided Wikipedia tools.
dependency_analysis:
Available server: Wikipedia (single server). All tools must be used; no cross-server dependencies are possible here. Inherent dependencies: search → summary → article → sections → targeted section summaries → key facts → related topics and links for network expansion and validation. Scenario-based dependencies and data flow:
- Chain A (Core topic anchoring): Wikipedia:search_wikipedia outputs a candidate title that feeds into Wikipedia:get_summary for topical confirmation, then Wikipedia:get_article and Wikipedia:get_sections to enumerate actual section titles. These section titles are required as exact inputs to Wikipedia:summarize_article_section, ensuring precise, section-aware summarization. If extract_key_facts lacks date-rich facts, summarize_article_for_query provides a tailored fallback.
- Chain B (City selection via related topics): Wikipedia:get_related_topics produces a title set that determines which city pages to select. If results are insufficient, search_wikipedia is re-invoked with concrete city+Hanseatic queries to fill gaps. get_summary validates each city page’s relevance; if invalid (e.g., disambiguation), search_wikipedia is called again to replace it. This creates a controlled decision branch where related_topics sufficiency determines the next step.
- Chain C (City deep-dives): For each selected city, get_article → get_sections determines which exact section title to pass to summarize_article_section. If no relevant section is present, summarize_article_for_query is invoked as a fallback to extract kontor-focused details. extract_key_facts with topic_within_article="Hanseatic" offers a targeted fact set; if too sparse, another summarize_article_for_query call fills the gap. This chain uses iterative refinement and fallback logic triggered by the presence/absence of relevant sections/facts.
- Chain D (Cross-validation via links): Wikipedia:get_links on the main "Hanseatic League" article yields a definitive outbound link list. City titles are checked against this list. If a city is not linked, the dependency triggers a conditional swap with an alternative from get_related_topics that is linked; otherwise, the city is retained and flagged. This cross-check ensures that selection is validated against the main article’s link graph.
- Chain E (Commodity identification with dual evidence paths): get_links output is intersected with a predefined commodity list. If ≥3 commodities are present, links serve as the primary evidence source; else, summarize_article_for_query is used to extract commodities, establishing a fallback branch based on link coverage insufficiency. The choice of evidence source is recorded in the final output.
- Chain F (Conflicts/Treaties via targeted summary and topic expansion): summarize_article_for_query first attempts to produce at least two events. If it fails, get_related_topics (on the main article) supplies candidate event pages; then get_summary on these event titles yields compact descriptions. This provides a two-tiered identification mechanism controlled by the content sufficiency of the tailored summary.
- Parallel vs. sequential: The initial anchoring (Chain A) is sequential and must complete before Chains B–F. After city selection, the four city deep-dives (Chain C) can proceed in parallel, but each still follows its own sequential subchain (article → sections → summarize/extract → fallback if needed). Commodity and conflicts identification (Chains E and F) can run in parallel after Chain A, but they both depend on the main article (and links/related topics) outputs.
- Critical decision points: (1) If initial summary lacks topical relevance, re-search with refined query; (2) Section selection uses ordered fallbacks based on actual section titles from get_sections; (3) If key facts lack dates/entities, use summarize_article_for_query; (4) If related topics produce <3 target cities, supplement via search; (5) If a city is not linked from the main article, attempt a linked swap; (6) If <3 commodities found via links, rely on tailored summary; (7) If <2 conflicts/treaties in tailored summary, switch to related topics + summaries of event pages. Each decision point explicitly routes the workflow to the appropriate tool.
- Tool coverage: The task compels the use of every Wikipedia tool. search_wikipedia discovers entries; get_summary validates; get_article provides full content; get_sections guides exact section targeting; summarize_article_section extracts precise section content; summarize_article_for_query tailors content for specific analytical needs and serves as fallback; extract_key_facts derives concise facts; get_related_topics expands the network; get_links validates cross-references. The inter-tool dependencies ensure the task cannot be completed without understanding how outputs feed subsequent inputs and when to branch or fallback.

task_description:
Investigate the history and global impact of the Green Revolution in agriculture. Perform the following multi-step research:

1. Search Wikipedia for 'Green Revolution' and identify the main article. Retrieve the full list of sections of that article.

2. From the sections list, summarize the following sections (if they exist): the section covering the history/origins of the Green Revolution, the section on criticism or environmental impact, and the section on key figures or leaders.

3. Extract 7 key facts from the main Green Revolution article, focused specifically on the topic of 'crop yield improvements'.

4. Get the related topics for the Green Revolution article (limit 15). From the related topics, identify at least 3 that are specific people (scientists, politicians, or activists associated with the Green Revolution — for example, Norman Borlaug or M.S. Swaminathan). For each identified person:
   a. Get a summary of their Wikipedia article.
   b. Use the summarize_article_for_query tool on their article with the query 'contributions to the Green Revolution' (max_length 300).
   c. Extract 4 key facts from their article focused on 'awards and recognition'.

5. From the related topics, also identify at least 2 that are specific crops or agricultural technologies (e.g., dwarf wheat, IR8 rice, or similar). For each:
   a. Get the full article content.
   b. Summarize the article for the query 'development and adoption history' (max_length 250).
   c. Get the links from each crop/technology article and note any links that also appear in the main Green Revolution article's links (cross-reference check).

6. Search Wikipedia for 'Indian Green Revolution' and 'Mexican Green Revolution' separately. For each result:
   a. Retrieve the summary of the top result article.
   b. Summarize a section related to 'outcomes' or 'results' from each article (if the section exists; if not, summarize the article for the query 'outcomes and food production results', max_length 200).

7. Finally, compile a structured research brief that includes:
   - A timeline of the Green Revolution's origins and spread (based on section summaries and key facts)
   - A profile of each key person identified, including their specific contributions and recognitions
   - A profile of each crop/technology, including development history and cross-links to the main article
   - A comparison of the Green Revolution's impact in India vs. Mexico based on the country-specific research
   - A section on criticisms and environmental concerns drawn from the relevant section summary
   - A list of all cross-referenced links found between the crop/technology articles and the main Green Revolution article

Present the final output as a well-organized report with clearly labeled sections.

task_description:
Objective: Produce a structured research brief on the rise, standardization, and economic impact of maritime containerization, focusing on ISO standards, TEU metrics, key figures, and major port case studies. Use only the provided Wikipedia tools, and follow the dependency-driven workflow below. Required tools: Wikipedia:search_wikipedia, Wikipedia:get_article, Wikipedia:get_summary, Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query, Wikipedia:summarize_article_section, Wikipedia:extract_key_facts, Wikipedia:get_related_topics, Wikipedia:get_sections, Wikipedia:get_links. Anchor topic: containerization in shipping (distinct from banned topics).

Primary deliverables:
- Executive summary (max 250 words) synthesizing origins, standardization milestones, TEU definitions, and economic impacts.
- ISO standards overview: capture what ISO 668 and ISO 1496-1 define (dimensions, categories), and any standardization timelines.
- TEU metrics: concise definition and context; note equivalencies and limitations.
- Timeline: 7 to 10 major events in containerization development (company innovations, standards adoption, infrastructure changes).
- Key figures: 3 to 5 individuals with roles (e.g., innovators, policymakers); include 1–2 sentences per figure.
- Port case studies: 3 major container ports with short summaries of their role in containerization (historical adoption, scale, or notable developments).
- Cross-validation notes: identify at least 3 points where multiple articles agree or diverge (dates, standards, definitions).
- Discrepancies: list up to 3 conflicting or ambiguous facts to flag for further review.
- Bibliography: list all Wikipedia article titles used.

Workflow with concrete parameters and decision branches:
1) Seed search (sequential start):
   - Call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="Containerization history logistics ISO 668 intermodal shipping" and limit=10.
   - Decision: If an article titled "Containerization" appears in the results, set ANCHOR_TITLE="Containerization"; else set ANCHOR_TITLE to the first result title.

2) Anchor article acquisition and structure mapping:
   - Call Wikipedia:get_article with title=ANCHOR_TITLE to obtain full text (for deep context if needed later).
   - Call Wikipedia:get_summary with title=ANCHOR_TITLE to obtain a high-level overview.
   - Call Wikipedia:get_sections with title=ANCHOR_TITLE to enumerate sections.
   - Decision A: If a section with title containing "History" exists, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with title=ANCHOR_TITLE, section_title="History", max_length=200. Else call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with title=ANCHOR_TITLE, query="Historical development of maritime containerization", max_length=250.
   - Decision B: If any section title contains "ISO" or "Standard", call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with that section_title and max_length=200; else call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with title=ANCHOR_TITLE, query="ISO standards relevant to intermodal containers (ISO 668, ISO 1496-1)", max_length=250.

3) Extract key facts from the anchor article:
   - Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with title=ANCHOR_TITLE, topic_within_article="ISO dimensions and TEU definition", count=7.
   - Decision: If fewer than 5 key facts are returned (agent must inspect the tool output), pivot by targeting more specific articles:
     a) Call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="Intermodal container ISO 668 ISO 1496-1" limit=10. If "Intermodal container" appears, set INTERMODAL_TITLE="Intermodal container"; else set INTERMODAL_TITLE to the first result title.
     b) Call Wikipedia:get_summary with title=INTERMODAL_TITLE.
     c) Call Wikipedia:get_sections with title=INTERMODAL_TITLE; if a section contains "Standards" or "ISO", call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section (title=INTERMODAL_TITLE, section_title=the matched title, max_length=200). Also call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts (title=INTERMODAL_TITLE, topic_within_article="ISO standards and dimensions", count=7).

4) Identify TEU concept article:
   - Call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="Twenty-foot equivalent unit TEU" limit=10.
   - Decision: If an article titled "Twenty-foot equivalent unit" appears, set TEU_TITLE="Twenty-foot equivalent unit"; else set TEU_TITLE to the first result title.
   - Call Wikipedia:get_summary with title=TEU_TITLE.
   - Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with title=TEU_TITLE, topic_within_article="Definition and equivalencies", count=5.
   - Call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with title=TEU_TITLE, query="Limitations and interpretation of TEU as a capacity measure", max_length=200.

5) Key figure identification via anchor links and related topics:
   - Call Wikipedia:get_links with title=ANCHOR_TITLE.
   - Decision: If the links include a title containing "Malcolm McLean", set FIGURE1_TITLE="Malcolm McLean"; else fall back to search by calling Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="Malcolm McLean containerization" limit=5 and set FIGURE1_TITLE to the top result.
   - Call Wikipedia:get_summary with title=FIGURE1_TITLE.
   - Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with title=FIGURE1_TITLE, topic_within_article="Role in containerization", count=3.
   - Expand figures set using related topics:
     a) Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics with title=ANCHOR_TITLE, limit=10.
     b) Decision: From related topics, select up to 2 additional biographies (agent chooses titles that appear to be people associated with containerization or intermodal logistics). For each selected figure title FIGUREX_TITLE:
        - Call Wikipedia:get_summary with title=FIGUREX_TITLE.
        - Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with title=FIGUREX_TITLE, topic_within_article="Contributions to containerization and logistics", count=3.

6) Port case studies collection:
   - From step 5b related topics, select up to 3 titles that appear to be major container ports or port-related topics (e.g., "Port of Singapore", "Port of Shanghai", "Port of Rotterdam"). For each selected PORT_TITLE:
     - Call Wikipedia:get_summary with title=PORT_TITLE.
     - Call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with title=PORT_TITLE, query="Role in adoption and scaling of containerization, historical milestones", max_length=200.
   - Decision: If fewer than 2 port topics are available from related topics, call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="largest container ports" limit=5 and pick the top 2 results as PORT_TITLEs, then perform the same two calls above for each.

7) Timeline synthesis and standardization cross-check:
   - Using content from ANCHOR_TITLE, INTERMODAL_TITLE (if pivoted), TEU_TITLE, and figures/ports:
     - Identify 7–10 discrete events: call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on ANCHOR_TITLE with query="Key chronological milestones in containerization (innovations, standards adoption, infrastructure expansion)" max_length=250.
     - Where a specific ISO standard is mentioned (ISO 668 or ISO 1496-1), call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on INTERMODAL_TITLE (or ANCHOR_TITLE if INTERMODAL_TITLE unavailable) with query="Timeline and scope of ISO 668 and ISO 1496-1" max_length=200 to cross-check.
     - Decision: If ISO standards are not mentioned in either ANCHOR_TITLE or INTERMODAL_TITLE, call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="ISO 668" limit=5, set ISO668_TITLE to the top result, and call Wikipedia:get_summary with title=ISO668_TITLE plus Wikipedia:extract_key_facts (title=ISO668_TITLE, topic_within_article="Container dimensions and categories", count=5).

task_description:
Objective: Produce an evidence-backed research briefing on safety risks, thermal runaway causes, notable incidents, and mitigation strategies for lithium-ion batteries in consumer electronics, synthesizing and cross-validating information across multiple Wikipedia articles. Deliver a structured JSON report with the following keys: executive_summary (3–5 bullet points), cause_effect_map (causes, triggers, outcomes, mitigations), incidents (Samsung Galaxy Note 7 and Boeing 787 battery incidents with 3–5 key facts each), mitigations (role of Battery Management Systems and other engineering controls with 5–7 bullets), cross_article_consistency (agreements/contradictions with citations by article title), and methodology (tools used and decision branches taken).

Strict execution plan, queries, limits, and decision logic:

1) Seed discovery via search (use Wikipedia:search_wikipedia):
   - Perform six searches with limit=10 each:
     a) query="lithium-ion battery"
     b) query="thermal runaway"
     c) query="Samsung Galaxy Note 7"
     d) query="Boeing 787 battery"
     e) query="Battery management system"
     f) query="Environmental impact of lithium-ion batteries"
   - Selection rules (case-insensitive):
     • For (a): pick the first result whose title contains "lithium-ion battery" (accept pluralization). Use this exact title as title_LiIon.
     • For (b): pick the first result whose title contains "thermal runaway". Use this as title_TR.
     • For (c): pick the first result whose title contains "Samsung Galaxy Note 7". Use this as title_Note7.
     • For (d): pick the first result whose title contains both "Boeing 787" and "battery" (order irrelevant). Use this as title_B787.
     • For (e): pick the first result whose title contains "Battery management system". Use this as title_BMS.
     • For (f): pick the first result whose title contains BOTH "Environmental" and "lithium" (or BOTH "Recycling" and "lithium-ion" if no environmental title found). Use this as title_Env. If no such title in (f), perform an additional search query="Lithium-ion battery recycling" with limit=10 and pick the first title containing both "recycling" and "lithium"; if still none found, set title_Env = title_LiIon and later extract environmental content from sections.

2) Canonical article triage and section targeting (use Wikipedia:get_sections and Wikipedia:get_summary):
   - For title_LiIon, call get_sections.
     • If any section title contains one of ["Safety", "Risks", "Failure modes", "Thermal runaway", "Hazards"], record the best match as LiIon_section_safety (prefer exact "Safety" > "Failure modes" > "Thermal runaway" > others).
     • Always call get_summary(title=title_LiIon) and save as sum_LiIon.
   - For title_TR, call get_summary and save as sum_TR.
   - For title_BMS, call get_summary and save as sum_BMS.
   - For title_Note7 and title_B787, call get_sections for each to detect incident-related sections (see Step 5).

3) Deep extraction on thermal runaway within Li-ion (use Wikipedia:extract_key_facts and conditional Wikipedia:summarize_article_section or Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query):
   - Call extract_key_facts(title=title_LiIon, topic_within_article="thermal runaway", count=7) → facts_LiIon_TR.
   - If LiIon_section_safety exists, call summarize_article_section(title=title_LiIon, section_title=LiIon_section_safety, max_length=180) → section_sum_LiIon_safety.
     • Else, call summarize_article_for_query(title=title_LiIon, query="safety risks thermal runaway consumer electronics", max_length=250) → targ_sum_LiIon_safety.
   - Call Wikipedia:get_article(title=title_LiIon) and count literal occurrences of the phrase "thermal runaway" (case-insensitive). If occurrences < 3, mark LiIon_TR_coverage="sparse"; else "adequate". If "sparse", plan to rely more on title_TR for causes and mechanisms (affects Step 6 comparisons).

4) Related topic expansion (use Wikipedia:get_related_topics with fallback to Wikipedia:get_links):
   - Call get_related_topics(title=title_LiIon, limit=15) → rel_LiIon.
   - Define keyword filters: K = ["thermal runaway", "battery management", "separator", "electrolyte", "safety", "recall", "explosion", "fire", "Samsung Galaxy Note 7", "Boeing 787"].
   - From rel_LiIon, select up to 5 titles whose title string contains any keyword from K (case-insensitive). Name this set S_rel (distinct from the five canonical titles captured in Step 1; duplicates allowed but handle once).
   - Decision/fallback: If neither a title containing "Samsung Galaxy Note 7" nor one containing both "Boeing 787" and "battery" appears in rel_LiIon, then also call get_links(title=title_LiIon) → links_LiIon and scan for such titles to add into S_rel (up to 2 additions). Ensure S_rel contains at least 3 items total by filling with other K-matches from rel_LiIon or links_LiIon as available.

5) Incident-focused drill-down (use Wikipedia:get_sections, Wikipedia:summarize_article_section, and Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query):
   - For title_Note7:
     • From previously fetched sections or call get_sections if not already done, check for a section including one of ["Recall", "Incidents", "Battery", "Safety"]. Prefer exact "Recall"; otherwise best match by order listed.
     • If a matching section exists, call summarize_article_section(title=title_Note7, section_title=<matched>, max_length=180) → inc_Note7.
     • Else, call summarize_article_for_query(title=title_Note7, query="battery fires recall incidents", max_length=250) → inc_Note7.
   - For title_B787:
     • Similarly, detect and summarize a section including one of ["Battery", "Incidents", "Grounding", "Safety"]. Prefer exact match order as above (Battery > Incidents > Grounding > Safety). Summarize with max_length=180; else use summarize_article_for_query(title=title_B787, query="lithium-ion battery incidents fires grounding", max_length=250) → inc_B787.

6) Cross-article causal mechanism validation (use Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query and Wikipedia:get_links):
   - From title_TR: call summarize_article_for_query(title=title_TR, query="lithium-ion batteries causes separator failure overcharging thermal runaway mechanisms", max_length=250) → causes_TR.
   - From title_BMS: call summarize_article_for_query(title=title_BMS, query="safety protections overcharge prevention thermal management cell balancing cutoff", max_length=250) → safety_BMS.
   - Call get_links(title=title_TR) → links_TR. From links_TR, select up to 3 titles containing any of ["separator", "electrolyte", "overcharge", "short circuit", "lithium-ion battery"]. For each selected title, call get_summary and retain summaries as cross_evidence[]. Use these to check for consistent causal pathways (e.g., separator failure, overcharge, internal short) across title_LiIon, title_TR, and the linked articles.

7) Environmental/recycling angle (conditional on title_Env) (use Wikipedia:get_sections, Wikipedia:summarize_article_section, Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query, Wikipedia:extract_key_facts):
   - If title_Env != title_LiIon:
     • Call get_sections(title_Env). If a section contains one of ["Environmental impact", "Recycling", "Toxicity", "End of life"], summarize the best match (prefer Environmental impact > Recycling > Toxicity > End of life) with max_length=150 → env_sum.
     • Call extract_key_facts(title=title_Env, topic_within_article="environmental impact recycling", count=5) → env_facts.
   - Else (title_Env == title_LiIon):
     • Use get_sections(title_LiIon) (already fetched). If a section contains one of ["Environmental impact", "Recycling"], summarize it with max_length=150 → env_sum. Also call extract_key_facts(title=title_LiIon, topic_within_article="recycling environmental impact", count=5) → env_facts.

8) Process selected related topics S_rel (parallelizable loop) (use Wikipedia:get_summary, Wikipedia:get_sections, Wikipedia:summarize_article_section, Wikipedia:extract_key_facts):
   - For each title in S_rel not equal to title_LiIon, title_TR, title_BMS, title_Note7, or title_B787:
     • Call get_summary → rel_sum[title].
     • Call get_sections → rel_secs[title]. If any section matches ["Safety", "Incidents", "Controversy", "Criticism"], summarize best match (prefer Safety > Incidents > Controversy > Criticism) with max_length=150 → rel_section_summaries[title].
     • Call extract_key_facts(title=title, topic_within_article="safety risk", count=3) → rel_facts[title].

9) Synthesis and cross-consistency assessment (agent-logic on tool outputs):
   - Build a cause_effect_map by collating: causes from causes_TR, facts_LiIon_TR, and cross_evidence[]; mitigations from safety_BMS and section_sum_LiIon_safety/targ_sum_LiIon_safety; outcomes from inc_Note7 and inc_B787.
   - Compare mentions of primary causes (e.g., separator failure, overcharge, internal short, manufacturing defect) across sum_LiIon, causes_TR, and cross_evidence[]:
     • If LiIon_TR_coverage=="sparse", weight causes_TR and cross_evidence[] more heavily; note this in cross_article_consistency.
     • Identify at least 3 points of agreement and up to 2 apparent contradictions or gaps (e.g., if one article emphasizes manufacturing defects while another emphasizes design or charging misuse). Cite article titles where each point was observed.
   - Incorporate env_sum and env_facts into mitigations or considerations section.

10) Output format (return as JSON, no external links):
   - executive_summary: 3–5 bullet points highlighting key safety risks, two notable incidents, and top mitigation.
   - cause_effect_map: object with keys causes (bulleted), triggers (bulleted), outcomes (bulleted), mitigations (bulleted with specific BMS protections).
   - incidents: object with keys note7 and b787, each containing title, section_used (or query if fallback used), and 3–5 key facts.
   - mitigations: 5–7 bullets on BMS and other engineering controls with article-title attributions.
   - cross_article_consistency: object with agreements (3+ bullets), contradictions_or_gaps (1–2 bullets), and weighting_note based on LiIon_TR_coverage.
   - methodology: ordered list of tool calls performed, noting decision points taken (e.g., which sections existed, whether fallback queries were used, whether links were used to augment related topics).

Notes and constraints:
- Use only the specified Wikipedia tools. Do not use external resources.
- Enforce all stated limits and selection rules.
- Titles must come from the search results or link/related-topic lists as specified.
- All comparisons and synthesis must be grounded in the fetched content.
- Where multiple candidate section titles exist, apply the stated preference order exactly.
- Ensure at least these tools are used at least once: search_wikipedia, get_article, get_summary, summarize_article_for_query, summarize_article_section, extract_key_facts, get_related_topics, get_sections, get_links.
dependency_analysis:
INHERENT DEPENDENCIES (Wikipedia-only server):
- Discovery → Content → Analysis workflow: search_wikipedia identifies canonical article titles; those titles feed get_summary/get_article/get_sections for deeper content; identified sections enable summarize_article_section; focused extraction/condensed views use summarize_article_for_query and extract_key_facts.
- Graph expansion: get_related_topics provides semantically related articles; get_links provides a raw link set for fallback or cross-validation targets.

KEY TOOL CHAINS AND DATA FLOW:
1) Seed chain: search_wikipedia → (title selection) → get_sections + get_summary for title_LiIon, title_TR, title_BMS; sets context for all downstream steps.
2) Section-dependent summarization: get_sections (title_LiIon) → conditional summarize_article_section or summarize_article_for_query for safety content.
3) Deep extraction: extract_key_facts (title_LiIon, topic="thermal runaway") complements section summaries; get_article (title_LiIon) quantifies coverage (occurrence count) to guide weighting in cross-validation.
4) Topic expansion and fallback: get_related_topics (title_LiIon) → select S_rel by keyword rules; if missing critical incident topics, then fallback to get_links (title_LiIon) to supplement S_rel.
5) Incident drill-down: get_sections (title_Note7/title_B787) → summarize_article_section if a targeted incident section exists; otherwise summarize_article_for_query to extract incident details.
6) Causal mechanism cross-check: summarize_article_for_query (title_TR for mechanisms, title_BMS for protections) → get_links (title_TR) to discover mechanism-relevant linked articles → get_summary for those links → cross-evidence array for validation against LiIon/TR content.
7) Environmental angle (conditional title_Env): get_sections + summarize_article_section + extract_key_facts on either a distinct environmental article or fallback to the Li-ion article’s relevant sections.
8) Parallel topic processing: For each title in S_rel (excluding already handled canonical articles), run get_summary → get_sections → summarize_article_section → extract_key_facts; outputs are later merged during synthesis.

CRITICAL DECISION POINTS:
- Title selection filters after search_wikipedia determine canonical titles; downstream calls strictly depend on these chosen titles.
- Safety content path: if LiIon has a Safety-like section (per ordered preferences), use summarize_article_section; else fall back to summarize_article_for_query with a targeted prompt.
- Coverage weighting: if the phrase "thermal runaway" occurs fewer than 3 times in the full Li-ion article (via get_article), weight the Thermal Runaway article and linked mechanism pages more heavily in the synthesis.
- Related topics robustness: if get_related_topics does not include high-priority incident topics (Samsung Galaxy Note 7 and Boeing 787 battery), then use get_links to find them; ensures mandatory incident coverage.
- Incident sections: if precise incident-related sections exist, summarize those; otherwise use targeted query summarization.
- Environmental content: if a dedicated environmental/recycling article cannot be found, extract from Li-ion’s own environmental/recycling sections.

PARALLEL VS SEQUENTIAL REQUIREMENTS:
- Sequential: All search_wikipedia calls and title selection must precede any summaries/sections operations. Section-dependent summarization must follow get_sections. Causal cross-check requires completing TR and BMS targeted summaries before link-based cross-evidence summaries.
- Parallelizable: Processing of S_rel topics (summaries, sections, facts) can run in parallel after S_rel is determined. Note7 and B787 incident extraction can run in parallel once their titles are set.

CROSS-SERVER DEPENDENCIES:
- Single server (Wikipedia) only; cross-server dependencies are not applicable. Cross-validation is achieved within the Wikipedia server by triangulating across multiple articles (main topic, mechanism, incidents, and linked mechanism pages).

COMBINATIONS AND VALIDATION LOOPS:
- Iterative/fallback loop between get_related_topics and get_links ensures inclusion of critical incident topics.
- Section-existence checks create conditional branches for whether to use summarize_article_section or summarize_article_for_query.
- Coverage assessment using get_article triggers a reweighting decision in the synthesis step.

Overall, the task enforces a deep dependency chain where later steps (incident summaries, causal validation, and synthesis) are contingent on earlier discovery and section-detection results, and it mandates use of all provided Wikipedia tools with both sequential and parallel execution phases.

task_description:
Research the history and global spread of the game of Chess, then compare it with the game of Go, investigating how each game influenced culture and strategy in different civilizations. Follow these steps:

1. Search Wikipedia for 'Chess' and 'Go (game)' to find the correct article titles.
2. Retrieve the full sections list for both the Chess and Go articles.
3. For the Chess article, summarize the 'History' section (max 250 words). Then, extract 5 key facts focused on 'origins and spread to Europe'.
4. For the Go article, summarize the 'History' section (max 250 words). Then, extract 5 key facts focused on 'origins and cultural significance in East Asia'.
5. Get related topics for both Chess and Go (limit 10 each). Identify any overlapping or thematically connected related topics between the two games (e.g., topics about board games, strategy, competitions, or cultural influence).
6. For each overlapping or thematically connected topic found in step 5 (up to 3 topics), get a summary of that Wikipedia article.
7. Using the Chess article, get a tailored summary for the query 'how chess was used in military strategy and education' (max 250 words).
8. Using the Go article, get a tailored summary for the query 'how Go was used in military strategy and philosophy' (max 250 words).
9. Search Wikipedia for 'World Chess Championship' and 'Go competition', retrieve summaries of the top result for each, and extract 3 key facts from each about the competitive history of these games.
10. Compile a final comparative report with the following sections:
    - **Origins**: Compare the geographic and temporal origins of Chess vs Go.
    - **Cultural Spread**: How each game spread across civilizations, citing specific facts from the extracted key facts.
    - **Strategic & Educational Use**: Compare how each game was used in military strategy or education, drawing from the tailored summaries.
    - **Competitive History**: Compare the competitive/championship traditions of both games using the facts from step 9.
    - **Shared Themes**: Discuss the overlapping related topics found in step 5 and what the summaries of those topics reveal about connections between the two games.
    - **Conclusion**: A brief synthesis of which aspects are unique to each game and which are shared cultural phenomena.

All findings must be sourced exclusively from Wikipedia tool calls. The final report should be structured with clear section headers and cite which Wikipedia article each piece of information came from.

**Chain 3 (Tailored Summaries — Parallel):**

**Synthesis Decision Point:**

**Tool Call Estimate:** ~20+ tool calls minimum: 4 searches, 2 get_sections, 2 summarize_article_section, 2 extract_key_facts (Chain 1), 2 get_related_topics, up to 3 get_summary (Chain 2), 2 summarize_article_for_query (Chain 3), 2 get_summary + 2 extract_key_facts (Chain 4).

task_description:
Build a rigorous, cross-validated briefing on carbon capture and storage (CCS) technologies and companies using only Wikipedia tools. Your objective is to: (1) identify exactly 3 CCS technology pages that represent distinct capture approaches; (2) identify exactly 5 companies with verifiable involvement in those technologies; (3) produce mechanism and controversy summaries per technology; (4) extract and cross-validate key facts and relationships; and (5) present a technology–company involvement matrix with evidence citations (Wikipedia article titles). Follow the strict workflow, decision rules, limits, and output format below.

Scope and constraints:
- Topic seed: "Carbon capture and storage" (primary), with fallback seeds "Carbon capture", "Direct air capture", "Post-combustion capture", "Oxy-fuel combustion".
- You must use all of these Wikipedia tools in an interdependent workflow: search_wikipedia, get_summary, get_sections, summarize_article_section, summarize_article_for_query, extract_key_facts, get_links, get_related_topics, get_article.
- Select exactly 3 capture technologies and exactly 5 companies. If you cannot reach those counts via primary paths, use the provided fallbacks.
- All decisions must be justified using article titles returned by the tools; do not use any external resources.

Workflow (strict sequence with decision points and iterations):
1) Find the canonical CCS overview page.
   - Call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query "Carbon capture and storage", limit 5.
   - For each result, call Wikipedia:get_summary.
   - Decision rule 1A (canonical page selection): Choose the result whose summary’s first sentence indicates it is the general concept (look for phrases like "is a process", "is a technology", "is a method" about capturing CO2). If multiple match, prefer the one titled exactly "Carbon capture and storage" or the one with the most general phrasing.
   - Disambiguation guard: If the selected page’s summary contains phrases like "may refer to" or indicates a disambiguation, discard it and pick the next best candidate.

2) Extract candidate technology sections from the canonical page.
   - Call Wikipedia:get_sections on the selected canonical title.
   - Decision rule 2A (section targeting): If a section titled exactly one of ["Technologies", "Methods", "Types", "Approaches"] exists, pick that section. If more than one exists, prioritize in the listed order. If none exist, proceed to Step 2 fallback.
   - If a section is found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section on that section with max_length 300 to understand which capture approaches are enumerated.
   - Also call Wikipedia:get_links on the canonical page to capture linked candidate technology titles.
   - Build a candidate list of technology titles from: (a) links appearing within the targeted section if determinable, else (b) all links whose titles or summaries (use Wikipedia:get_summary for each) suggest capture approaches (look for terms like "capture", "combustion", "adsorption", "absorption", "sequestration", "direct air capture").
   - Step 2 fallback (if no suitable section found): call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts on the canonical page with topic_within_article = "types of capture technologies", count 7; then supplement by calling Wikipedia:search_wikipedia for each of these queries with limit 3: "Direct air capture", "Post-combustion capture", "Pre-combustion capture", "Oxy-fuel combustion". For each search result, call Wikipedia:get_summary and keep those that describe a capture method.

3) Select exactly 3 distinct capture technologies.
   - Decision rule 3A (technology selection): From your candidate list, select 3 titles that are distinct capture approaches (e.g., do not select both a general and a sub-page if they overlap; prefer the page whose summary describes a method/process/technology rather than a general concept). Distinctness test: summaries should indicate different mechanisms (e.g., post-combustion vs direct air capture) using keywords like "post-combustion", "pre-combustion", "oxy-fuel", "direct air".
   - If you have fewer than 3, expand using Step 2 fallback terms and repeat selection.

4) Analyze each chosen technology page (repeat per technology; parallelization allowed but document results per item):
   - For each technology title T:
     a) Call Wikipedia:get_summary(T) for quick classification.
     b) Call Wikipedia:get_sections(T).
     c) Mechanism summary: If there is a section labeled one of ["Process", "Technology", "Mechanism", "Operation"], call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section(T, that section, max_length 200). Else call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query = "How this technology captures CO2 and the core mechanism", max_length 200.
     d) Controversy/environmental impacts: If there is a section labeled one of ["Criticism", "Controversy", "Environmental impact", "Challenges", "Limitations"], call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section(T, that section, max_length 200). Else call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query(T, query = "Criticisms, environmental concerns, and controversies", max_length 200).
     e) Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts(T, topic_within_article = "key performance metrics, capture rate, energy penalty, notable projects", count 5).
     f) Call Wikipedia:get_links(T). Keep up to 10 link titles for candidate companies or projects associated with T.
     g) For each of the up to 10 link titles from (f), call Wikipedia:get_summary on the linked title and classify:
        - Company classifier: summary contains phrases like "is a [country/adjective] company", "is an American company", "is a company", "corporation", "manufacturer", "firm".
        - Project/plant classifier: summary contains "project", "plant", "facility", "pilot", "demonstration".
        Keep a per-technology list of up to 5 companies and up to 3 projects identified from these links (prefer items whose summaries explicitly mention CCS or the specific capture method; if more than the limit, choose those whose summaries most closely mention the technology name or synonyms).

5) Build the global company list and cross-validate involvement.
   - Combine all per-technology company candidates, deduplicate by exact title.
   - If the combined list has more than 5 unique companies, pick the 5 that appear linked from the most technology pages; break ties by alphabetic order.
   - If fewer than 5 companies are identified, run a fallback search: call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query "Carbon capture company" limit 10; for each result, call Wikipedia:get_summary and keep those classified as companies; add these until you have 5 total, preferring those whose summaries mention CCS or any of the selected technologies.
   - For each of the final 5 companies C:
     a) Call Wikipedia:get_summary(C).
     b) Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts(C, topic_within_article = "CCS projects, technology partnerships, and capture methods involved", count 5).
     c) Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics(C, limit 10) to find related technology or project pages. For any related topic that matches one of the 3 technologies or their synonyms, record that as supporting evidence.
     d) Cross-validation loop: For each company–technology pair (C, T), determine involvement status using this precedence of evidence:
        - Confirmed if C appears in T’s get_links list AND C’s related topics or key facts mention T or a direct synonym; OR if both C and T point to the same specific project link.
        - Probable if C’s extract_key_facts or related topics mention the capture method by name (or a clear synonym) but C is not linked from T’s page.
        - Uncertain if neither page provides direct evidence; in this case, call Wikipedia:get_article(T) and Wikipedia:get_article(C) and re-scan their content for occurrence of the other’s title or clear method keywords. If still no evidence is found, keep as Uncertain.

6) Resolve contradictions and finalize facts.
   - Contradiction rule: If key facts from a company imply involvement in a technology X while a technology page T suggests a different or conflicting characterization (e.g., classifies the company under a different method), mark as Contradiction and resolve by re-running Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on both pages with query = "What capture method does [Company or Technology] use or support?" max_length 150. Use the latest tailored summaries to choose the dominant claim; if still ambiguous, keep both claims and label as Unresolved.

Expected output format (plain text, no tables):
- Executive Summary (<= 150 words):
  - Briefly state the 3 selected technologies and 5 selected companies.
- Technologies (3 items): For each technology T:
  - Title
  - Mechanism summary (<= 120 words)
  - Controversies/impacts summary (<= 120 words)
  - Key facts (5 bullet points)
  - Example linked projects/companies (up to 5 bullet points listing Wikipedia titles)
- Companies (5 items): For each company C:
  - Title
  - 1–2 sentence summary
  - Key facts (3–5 bullet points)
  - Related topics used as evidence (bullet list of Wikipedia titles)
- Technology–Company Involvement Matrix (narrative list): For each technology T, list the 5 companies with statuses and evidence, formatted as:
  - T: C1 – Status [Confirmed/Probable/Uncertain], Evidence [list of Wikipedia article titles]; C2 – Status ...; etc.
- Contradictions and Resolutions: Bullet list describing each contradiction encountered and how it was resolved, including which additional summarize_article_for_query calls were used.
- Sources: Bullet list of all Wikipedia article titles you directly used in summaries, key facts, links, or related topics.

Operational limits and parameters:
- All search_wikipedia calls must specify limit as given above for each step.
- In Step 4f, cap candidate link evaluation to 10 per technology.
- Do not include URLs; cite articles by title only.
- Keep all summaries within stated length limits.
- Ensure exactly 3 technologies and exactly 5 companies are presented in the final output.

Deliver the final report per the format above. Do not ask for additional input.
dependency_analysis:
Inherent tool relationships and workflow patterns:
- search_wikipedia → get_summary/get_article: Searching yields candidate titles; summaries are needed to classify whether a title is a canonical concept, a technology, a company, or a disambiguation. Full articles (get_article) act as a last resort to re-scan raw content for cross-validation.
- get_sections → summarize_article_section: Sections must be enumerated before targeted section summaries can be produced.
- get_article/get_sections → summarize_article_for_query: If a relevant section is missing, a query-tailored summary compensates with focused extraction from the whole article.
- extract_key_facts depends on a confirmed title; its output supports selection, ranking, and cross-validation.
- get_links → get_summary: Links from a page seed discovery of related entities (companies/projects); each linked title is summarized to classify the entity type.
- get_related_topics complements get_links by surfacing relationship-based evidence for cross-validation when links do not directly connect two pages.

Scenario-based dependencies (designed for this task):
- Canonical page selection depends on search results and summary analysis (Decision 1A); disambiguation detection triggers fallback to next candidate.
- Technology identification depends on locating a relevant section via get_sections (Decision 2A). If the section is absent, the agent must pivot to extract_key_facts on the overview page and auxiliary searches (fallback path) to seed technology candidates (iterative enrichment).
- Technology selection (Decision 3A) requires reading summaries (get_summary) to ensure distinct mechanisms; if insufficient candidates are available, the fallback queries expand the pool.
- Per-technology analysis chains together: get_summary → get_sections → summarize_article_section (or summarize_article_for_query fallback) → extract_key_facts → get_links → get_summary on each link for classification. Each step consumes the previous step’s outputs: sections inform which section to summarize; missing sections trigger query-based summarization; links generate titles that must be summarized to classify as company or project.
- Company shortlist formation depends on the union of per-technology classified companies and, if needed, a fallback search_wikipedia + get_summary loop. Deduplication and ranking rely on counting which technologies link to each company (derived from get_links classifications).
- Cross-validation requires combining evidence from multiple tools: a company’s involvement is Confirmed if both the technology page links to the company (get_links) and the company’s related topics or facts reference the technology (get_related_topics/extract_key_facts). If evidence is incomplete, the agent escalates to get_article for both pages to re-scan for textual mentions (iterative refinement loop). If contradictions are found between key facts and technology claims, summarize_article_for_query is invoked again to focus on method involvement and resolve or mark as Unresolved.

Critical decision points and fallbacks:
- DP1: Canonical overview selection (summary-based classification; disambiguation fallback).
- DP2: Section targeting for technology enumeration; fallback to extract_key_facts and supplementary searches.
- DP3: Distinct technology selection; fallback to expand candidate pool.
- DP4: Mechanism and controversy section availability; fallback to query-tailored summarization.
- DP5: Company vs project classification via summary keywords; items that do not match are excluded from company candidates.
- DP6: Company selection count; fallback to search for "Carbon capture company" to meet the exact quota.
- DP7: Involvement status (Confirmed/Probable/Uncertain) determined by combined evidence from get_links, get_related_topics, extract_key_facts; if ambiguous, escalate to get_article and additional summarize_article_for_query for contradiction resolution.

Parallel vs sequential execution:
- Sequential phases: Canonical page selection; technology section identification; final selection of exactly 3 technologies; final selection of exactly 5 companies; final cross-validation and contradiction resolution.
- Parallelizable phases: Per-technology deep dives (summaries, section summaries, key facts, link harvesting and link target summaries) can run independently for each chosen technology. Likewise, per-company verification (summary, key facts, related topics) can run in parallel. However, the final involvement matrix requires consolidating evidence from all parallel branches.

Cross-server dependencies:
- Not applicable in this setup because all tools belong to the single Wikipedia server. All cross-validation is intra-Wikipedia, leveraging multiple endpoints (links, related topics, sections, summaries, and full articles) to corroborate facts.

Data flow overview:
- Seed query → candidate overview titles (search_wikipedia) → canonical selection (get_summary)
- Canonical title → sections (get_sections) → targeted section summary (summarize_article_section) OR overview fact extraction (extract_key_facts) + auxiliary searches (search_wikipedia)
- Candidate technology titles → summarization and section analysis (get_summary + get_sections + summarize_article_section/summarize_article_for_query) → technology facts (extract_key_facts)
- Technology titles → outbound links (get_links) → linked title classification (get_summary) → candidate company/project lists
- Aggregated companies → summaries and facts (get_summary + extract_key_facts) → related topics (get_related_topics) → cross-evidence with technology pages
- Ambiguities/contradictions → full article scans (get_article) → focused re-summarization (summarize_article_for_query) → final involvement status determination.

This dependency architecture compels the agent to interleave discovery, classification, validation, and resolution steps across multiple tool outputs. Each downstream tool relies on upstream context (titles, sections, link lists, or fact extracts), and multiple fallback paths ensure the agent must understand and exploit these dependencies to complete the task.

task_description:
Research the history and evolution of the Panama Canal, then conduct a comparative analysis with the Suez Canal. Follow these steps:

1. Search Wikipedia for 'Panama Canal' and 'Suez Canal' to identify the correct article titles.
2. For both canals, retrieve the full article sections list, then summarize the following specific sections: construction history, economic impact, and any sections related to expansions or modifications.
3. Extract 7 key facts from each canal's article, focused on the topic 'engineering and construction challenges'.
4. For the Panama Canal article, get related topics and identify at least 3 related articles about key figures or engineering concepts (e.g., locks, specific engineers, or related treaties). Retrieve summaries of those 3 related articles tailored to the query 'role in Panama Canal construction or operation'.
5. Do the same for the Suez Canal: get related topics, pick 3 related articles about key figures, geopolitics, or engineering, and summarize them tailored to 'role in Suez Canal history'.
6. For both canals, summarize the main article tailored to the query 'economic and geopolitical significance in global trade' with a max length of 300 words each.
7. Search Wikipedia for 'Canal lock' (or the appropriate article about canal lock engineering) and extract 5 key facts focused on 'how locks work in ship canals'. Then get the sections of that article and summarize the section most relevant to the Panama Canal's lock system.
8. Search for 'Panamax' and get a summary of that article, then summarize it tailored to the query 'ship size limitations imposed by the Panama Canal'.
9. Search for 'New Suez Canal' or the Suez Canal expansion and get a summary, comparing it to the Panama Canal expansion (search for 'Panama Canal expansion' and get its summary as well).
10. Finally, compile all findings into a structured comparative report with the following sections:
    - Overview of each canal (from tailored summaries)
    - Engineering challenges comparison (from extracted key facts)
    - Key historical figures and their contributions (from related topic deep-dives)
    - Lock engineering vs sea-level design (from Canal lock article and section summaries)
    - Ship size constraints: Panamax vs Suez constraints (from Panamax and related articles)
    - Modern expansions comparison (from expansion article summaries)
    - Geopolitical and economic significance comparison

The final output should be a well-organized markdown report with clear section headers, citing which Wikipedia articles each piece of information came from.
