task_description:
Produce a cross-validated, comparative research brief on global DC fast-charging standards for electric vehicles using ONLY the provided Wikipedia tools. Focus on four target standards: Combined Charging System (CCS), CHAdeMO, North American Charging Standard (NACS), and GB/T (GB/T 20234 series). Follow the steps and decision rules below exactly; do not assume external knowledge. Execution plan with required tool usage, decision points, and thresholds:

1) Candidate discovery and normalization (sequential; branching fallback):
- Use Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query = "electric vehicle DC fast charging standards CCS CHAdeMO NACS GB/T", limit = 15.
- From results, identify titles likely corresponding to: Combined Charging System, CHAdeMO, North American Charging Standard (NACS), and GB/T 20234 (or GB/T-related charging standard pages). If any are missing:
  - Run additional Wikipedia:search_wikipedia calls with each of these queries (limit = 10 each) until you have one candidate title per standard:
    a) "Combined Charging System"
    b) "CHAdeMO"
    c) "North American Charging Standard"
    d) "GB/T 20234"
  - If a search yields multiple plausible titles for a standard (e.g., disambiguation or variant names), call Wikipedia:get_sections on each candidate and pick the title with the greater number of sections (ties broken by longer section list length when concatenated as text).

2) DC fast-charging relevance filter (sequential per standard; conditional exclusion):
- For each selected title, call Wikipedia:get_summary.
- Check if the summary includes at least one keyword from both of these sets:
  - Set A (current type): ["DC", "direct current"]
  - Set B (speed/power): ["fast", "high-power", "rapid", "quick"]
- If a title fails this check, call Wikipedia:get_sections and look for section titles containing any of: ["DC", "fast", "high-power", "rapid", "quick"]. If none are found, exclude that title from further analysis and document the exclusion reason in the final report.

3) Sections and technical detail extraction (sequential; adaptive selection; fallbacks):
- For each remaining standard title:
  a) Call Wikipedia:get_sections.
  b) Identify the most relevant technical section to extract specs by scanning section titles for these keywords (priority order): ["Specification", "Specifications", "Technical", "Connector", "Charging", "Power", "Technology"]. If multiple candidates exist, pick the one with the greatest number of subsections (or the longest title string if subsections not exposed).
  c) If a relevant section is found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with max_length = 200 on that section.
  d) Independently, call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with topic_within_article = "power levels, voltage, current, connector pins, communication protocol", count = 7.
  e) If the extract_key_facts result does not clearly include a communication protocol reference (look for any of: "CAN", "PLC", "Power Line Communication", "ISO 15118", "HomePlug Green PHY", "CHAdeMO protocol"), call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query = "communication protocol used (e.g., PLC, CAN, ISO 15118) and signaling method", max_length = 200.
  f) If no relevant section was found in step (b), call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query = "technical specifications: max power (kW), voltage (V), current (A), connector type, pin configuration, DC charging capability", max_length = 250. If this still appears too general, call Wikipedia:get_article and scan for the same keywords to manually identify details in subsequent reasoning.

4) Related topics and link-based cross-context (parallel calls per title; scoring and conditional enrichment):
- For each standard title:
  a) Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics with limit = 10.
  b) Call Wikipedia:get_links.
  c) Maintain a whitelist of important related items (match by substring, case-insensitive): ["ISO 15118", "IEC 62196", "IEC 61851", "CharIN", "Tesla Supercharger", "CHAdeMO Association", "GB/T 20234", "SAE J1772", "CCS Combo", "Type 2 connector", "Type 1 connector"].
  d) Compute a connectivity score = (number of whitelist matches in get_related_topics) + (number of whitelist matches in get_links). If connectivity score < 2, mark this standard as low-connectivity.
  e) For each matched whitelist item, call Wikipedia:get_summary and extract any governance, compatibility, or adoption statements.
  f) If two or more standards are marked low-connectivity, run one more Wikipedia:search_wikipedia per low-connectivity standard with a refined query (limit = 10):
     - CCS: "Combined Charging System standard power levels"
     - CHAdeMO: "CHAdeMO specification DC fast charging details"
     - NACS: "North American Charging Standard technical details"
     - GB/T: "GB/T 20234 DC charging specification"
    If these searches reveal a better candidate title (evaluate with get_sections count as in step 1), switch to that title and repeat step 3 for it.

5) Adoption and regional presence extraction (sequential per standard; structured counting for ranking):
- For each standard title, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query = "adoption by regions and countries; notable markets and OEM adoption; regulatory status", max_length = 200.
- Count explicit mentions of any of these regions/countries in the returned summary text (case-insensitive substring match): ["Europe", "United States", "China", "Japan", "India", "South Korea", "Australia", "Canada", "United Kingdom"]. Record the count per standard.

6) Cross-validation of technical claims (sequential; branching verification):
- Power and connector standards check:
  a) Call Wikipedia:get_summary on "IEC 62196" and "IEC 61851".
  b) If any standard's extracted max power (kW) or connector naming appears to rely on IEC references, cross-check phrases against these summaries. If a mismatch or ambiguity is detected (e.g., conflicting kW values or connector type conventions), call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on the relevant IEC article with query = "relationship to [STANDARD NAME] power levels and connector types", max_length = 200, and record discrepancies.
- Communication protocol check:
  a) Call Wikipedia:get_summary on "ISO 15118".
  b) For each standard, compare the communication protocol claim with the ISO 15118 summary. If the standard claims ISO 15118 but the context suggests otherwise (or vice versa), call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on the standard with query = "does this standard use ISO 15118 or CAN/PLC? clarify signaling and versions", max_length = 200, and flag any conflict.

7) Adoption ranking and tie-breaking (deterministic):
- Rank the standards by the adoption mention count from step 5 (highest to lowest). If there is a tie, break it by higher connectivity score from step 4. If still tied, break by the number of sections reported by Wikipedia:get_sections (higher wins).

8) Final deliverable (structured, concise, and cross-validated):
- Produce the following output:
  a) Executive summary (<= 200 words) stating the top adoption-ranked standard, key technical differences, and notable interoperability issues.
  b) For each standard (CCS, CHAdeMO, NACS, GB/T), include a bullet list:
     - Overview (2 sentences).
     - Key technical specs: max power (kW), typical voltage (V) and current (A) ranges, connector type/pin configuration (as available).
     - Communication protocol (e.g., PLC + ISO 15118, CAN-based), and any known versions.
     - Backward compatibility/interoperability notes and adapter availability (as described on Wikipedia).
     - Key regions/countries and OEMs mentioned.
     - Governance bodies/industry groups (e.g., CharIN, CHAdeMO Association) with brief roles.
  c) Comparison and validation notes:
     - Adoption ranking with the counts used.
     - Connectivity scores per standard.
     - Cross-validation outcomes: list any discrepancies found between standard pages and IEC/ISO pages, and the resolution (which source you treated as more authoritative within Wikipedia).
     - Interoperability summary bullets, e.g., "CCS vs CHAdeMO: incompatible; adapters exist? (per article)."
  d) Methodological appendix:
     - List the exact Wikipedia titles used for each standard after normalization.
     - Number of tool calls per standard (approximate counts are acceptable) and any fallbacks invoked.

Constraints and notes:
- Use only the provided Wikipedia tools. Do not reference any external content.
- Use the exact queries and limits specified above. Max lengths for summarization calls: as given in steps 3, 4, 5, and 6.
- Ensure every tool is used at least once in the overall workflow: search_wikipedia, get_summary, get_article (only if needed per fallback in 3f), summarize_article_for_query, summarize_article_section, extract_key_facts, get_related_topics, get_sections, get_links.
- Document all exclusions and fallback switches explicitly in the final deliverable.
- If any standard cannot be validated as DC fast-charging per the rules in step 2, exclude it and proceed with the remaining ones; still deliver the comparison with available standards and include an exclusion note.
dependency_analysis:
Inherent dependencies (Wikipedia tool ecosystem):
- search_wikipedia -> (title candidates) -> get_summary/get_sections/get_article: A standard discovery pipeline begins with search to identify candidate titles, then summary/sections/article calls refine and extract content. Sections inform the use of summarize_article_section; summaries inform filtering decisions and targeted queries via summarize_article_for_query.
- get_sections -> summarize_article_section: Section metadata is required to select the specific section to summarize for technical details.
- get_summary/get_article -> summarize_article_for_query: High-level content informs tailored query summaries (e.g., communication protocols, adoption) and provides context to disambiguate claims.
- extract_key_facts depends on a stable title and can be scoped by topic to yield structured facts that are cross-checked against section summaries and targeted summaries.
- get_related_topics/get_links -> downstream enrichment: Related topics and links feed further get_summary and summarize_article_for_query calls on governance and standards bodies and compute connectivity scores.

Scenario-based dependencies and decision logic:
- Title normalization: search_wikipedia outputs multiple possible titles; get_sections (number of sections) is used as a heuristic to select the canonical title. This is a sequential dependency.
- Relevance filter: get_summary must satisfy keyword conditions (DC + fast/high-power). Failure triggers a branch to get_sections to scan section titles; persistent failure excludes the title from the workflow. This enforces an early decision gate.
- Technical extraction: get_sections first identifies the best section; summarize_article_section then extracts a focused summary. In parallel, extract_key_facts provides structured specs. If key facts miss protocol details, summarize_article_for_query is invoked with a protocol-specific query. If no section matches at all, summarize_article_for_query serves as a fallback, and, if still insufficient, get_article is used to manually inspect content. This creates a tiered dependency chain with fallbacks.
- Connectivity scoring and enrichment: get_related_topics and get_links run in parallel to compute a connectivity score via whitelist matching. Low scores trigger additional search_wikipedia calls with refined queries and a potential title switch validated by get_sections, followed by repeating the technical extraction step. This establishes an iterative loop driven by intermediate metrics (connectivity score < 2).
- Adoption ranking: summarize_article_for_query (adoption-focused) produces text analyzed for mentions of specified regions/countries. These counts feed a ranking algorithm. Ties are broken using connectivity scores (from related/links) and, if needed, number of sections (from get_sections). This shows multi-metric decision dependencies.
- Cross-validation: Claims about power/connectors are checked against IEC pages: get_summary of IEC 62196/61851 and, when needed, summarize_article_for_query tailored to the specific standard relationship. Communication protocol claims are checked against ISO 15118 via get_summary and, if ambiguous, summarize_article_for_query on the standard to clarify. This cross-checking creates bidirectional validation paths across multiple titles.

Parallel vs sequential requirements:
- Sequential phases: discovery/normalization -> relevance filter -> technical extraction -> adoption extraction -> ranking -> reporting. Each depends on outputs of the previous stage.
- Parallel calls within a phase: For each standard, get_related_topics and get_links can run in parallel, as can retrieval of governance summaries for matched whitelist items. Technical extraction combines section summary and key facts in parallel to cross-confirm specs.

Critical decision points:
- Title selection based on sections count (post-search normalization).
- Inclusion decision based on DC fast-charging keyword detection in summaries/sections.
- Low-connectivity detection (score < 2) that triggers refined search and possible title replacement followed by re-extraction.
- Cross-validation discrepancies (IEC/ISO vs standard page) that require additional targeted summarize_article_for_query calls to resolve or flag conflicts.
- Ranking tie-breakers that rely sequentially on connectivity score and section count.

Cross-server dependencies:
- Not applicable: all tools operate on the single Wikipedia server. Cross-validation is achieved by consulting multiple interconnected Wikipedia articles (standards bodies and related standards) rather than external servers. If any article is insufficient, the task specifies in-server fallbacks (targeted summaries, full article retrieval) without using external sources.

Overall, the task enforces deep, multi-step dependencies: initial search determines candidate titles; sections determine which summarization tool to use; missing facts trigger targeted summaries; links/related topics drive enrichment and tie-breaks; and IEC/ISO pages are used to validate or contradict claims from standard pages. Multiple iterative loops and conditional branches ensure the agent must understand and leverage tool interdependencies to complete the brief.

task_description:
Objective: Build a comprehensive, cross-validated research dossier on Electronic waste (e-waste) policies, technologies, and stakeholders for the United States, China, and India using only the provided Wikipedia tools. Deliver a structured output that includes: 1) Executive overview, 2) Country policy profiles (United States, China, India), 3) International frameworks relevant to e-waste, 4) Technology solutions, and 5) Link-network overlaps across the core and country-specific articles. The final deliverable must be a structured summary with clearly labeled sections, each citing the article titles used for each finding. Required tools usage and sequence are specified below.

Output format (produce this at the end):
- Executive Overview: 2–3 paragraphs summarizing global e-waste scale, hazards, and policy landscape. Include 5 key facts with article titles.
- Country Policy Profiles (United States, China, India): For each country, include:
  - Selected Primary Article Title
  - Section Summaries: Summaries of up to 3 relevant sections (Legislation, Policy, Regulation, Recycling, Management). If sections differ, list the actual section titles used.
  - Policy Instruments: At least 3 instruments (e.g., extended producer responsibility, right to repair, import/export controls). For each instrument, include a 1–2 sentence relevance summary and the source article title.
  - 5 Key Facts extracted from the primary article (policy focus).
  - Related Topics Consulted: List at least 3 related topics and provide a 1–2 sentence summary of their relevance to the country’s e-waste context.
- International Frameworks: Summarize at least 4 frameworks/treaties/standards (e.g., Basel Convention, RoHS, WEEE Directive, Right to repair) with a 2–3 sentence description tied to e-waste policy relevance.
- Technology Solutions: Summarize at least 3 recycling/processing technologies with focus on processes, efficiency, and hazards (e.g., hydrometallurgy, pyrometallurgy, urban mining). Include 5 key facts.
- Link-Network Overlaps: Provide a list of entities (NGOs, treaties, companies, directives) that appear as links in multiple core/country articles. Indicate overlaps (entity name, articles where it appears).
- Source Articles Used: Enumerate all Wikipedia article titles that were fetched and used.

Step-by-step required workflow and parameters (strictly follow tool usage and decision logic):
1) Establish the core domain article(s):
   - Use Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with queries (limit=10 each):
     - "Electronic waste"
     - "E-waste"
   - Select the most relevant general overview article (prefer title "Electronic waste" if present). Record the chosen title.
   - Fetch full content using Wikipedia:get_article for the chosen core article.
   - Retrieve sections using Wikipedia:get_sections.
   - Create the Executive Overview:
     - If a section matching any of ["Environmental impact", "Hazards", "Health effects", "Global statistics"] exists (exact title match required), use Wikipedia:summarize_article_section for up to two such sections (max_length=150 each).
     - Additionally use Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on the core article with query: "global scale of e-waste and policy landscape" (max_length=250).
     - Extract 5 key global facts using Wikipedia:extract_key_facts on the core article (topic_within_article="global overview", count=5).

2) Country Policy Profiles (repeat the following for each country: United States, China, India):
   - Initial search phase (parallel searches, then sequential selection):
     - Use Wikipedia:search_wikipedia (limit=10) with the following queries per country:
       - For United States: "Electronic waste in the United States", "E-waste in the United States", "Waste management in the United States", "Recycling in the United States"
       - For China: "Electronic waste in China", "E-waste in China", "Waste management in China", "Recycling in China"
       - For India: "Electronic waste in India", "E-waste in India", "Waste management in India", "Recycling in India"
   - Selection decision rule:
     - Prefer an article whose title contains "Electronic waste" or "E-waste" and the country name. If none found, choose the most relevant alternative: first "Waste management in <Country>", else "Recycling in <Country>". Record the selected title.
   - Fetch and analyze:
     - Use Wikipedia:get_article on the selected country article.
     - Use Wikipedia:get_sections to list available sections.
     - Section summarization (sequential with fallbacks):
       - Attempt to summarize up to three of the following sections via Wikipedia:summarize_article_section (max_length=150 each), in priority order: "Legislation", "Policy", "Regulation", "Recycling", "Management". Only summarize sections that exist with exact title match.
       - If fewer than two relevant sections exist, use Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on the selected article with queries:
         - Query A: "e-waste legislation and regulation" (max_length=250)
         - Query B: "policy instruments and implementation" (max_length=250)
     - Key facts:
       - Use Wikipedia:extract_key_facts (topic_within_article="policy instruments", count=5) on the selected country article.
     - Related topics expansion (iterative with threshold):
       - Use Wikipedia:get_related_topics (limit=15) on the selected country article.
       - From the related topics, identify at least three policy-relevant topics (examples: "Extended producer responsibility", "Right to repair", "Basel Convention", "RoHS", "WEEE Directive", "Circular economy"). If fewer than three policy-relevant topics are found, expand by calling Wikipedia:get_related_topics on the core "Electronic waste" article (limit=20) and select additional topics that have relevance to the country context.
       - For each selected related topic (minimum 3 per country):
         - Use Wikipedia:get_summary to obtain a concise overview.
         - Use Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query: "relevance to <Country> e-waste policy" (max_length=200) to tailor the summary.

3) International frameworks (cross-validation and synthesis):
   - Use Wikipedia:get_related_topics (limit=20) on the core "Electronic waste" article to discover frameworks and standards.
   - Target at least four of the following if present: "Basel Convention", "Restriction of Hazardous Substances Directive" (RoHS), "Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Directive" (WEEE), "Right to repair", "Extended producer responsibility", "Planned obsolescence".
   - For each chosen framework/standard:
     - Use Wikipedia:get_article to ensure full access to content.
     - Use Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query: "e-waste policy relevance and mechanisms" (max_length=250).
     - Use Wikipedia:extract_key_facts (topic_within_article="policy mechanisms", count=3).

4) Technology solutions (process-focused analysis):
   - Use Wikipedia:search_wikipedia (limit=10 each) with queries:
     - "E-waste recycling technology"
     - "Urban mining"
     - "Hydrometallurgy e-waste"
     - "Pyrometallurgy e-waste"
   - Select at least three distinct technology/process articles relevant to e-waste processing.
   - For each selected technology article:
     - Use Wikipedia:get_article.
     - Use Wikipedia:get_sections.
     - If a section titled "Process" or "Technology" exists, use Wikipedia:summarize_article_section (max_length=150).
     - Else use Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query: "process steps, efficiency, and hazards" (max_length=250).
   - Use Wikipedia:extract_key_facts (topic_within_article="process efficiency and hazards", count=5) across these articles (perform once per article and aggregate).

5) Link-network overlaps (entity mapping across articles):
   - Use Wikipedia:get_links on the core "Electronic waste" article.

6) Source tracking:
   - For every article title used in steps 1–5, list it under "Source Articles Used" in the final output.

Constraints and decision points to enforce:

- For country policy topics, ensure at least three policy instruments per country using related topics from the country article; if insufficient, supplement from related topics on the core "Electronic waste" article.

dependency_analysis:

Scenario-based dependencies and decision logic:
- Core setup: The task begins by searching for the global anchor article (Electronic waste). The article content and sections (via get_article and get_sections) determine whether section-specific summaries can be extracted or whether query-tailored summarization is necessary.
- Country profiles: Multiple search queries per country (parallel calls) feed a selection decision. The selected article becomes the source for sections and section summarization. If section titles like "Legislation" or "Policy" are present, summarize those; otherwise, fallback to query-based summarization (summarize_article_for_query) focused on policy and regulation.

- Related topic expansion (get_related_topics) on country pages may not always yield sufficient policy instruments; if fewer than three are found, the process iteratively calls get_related_topics on the core article to supplement, ensuring a minimum threshold of policy-relevant topics per country.
- For each related topic selected, cross-validation occurs via parallel use of get_summary (concise overview) and summarize_article_for_query (country-specific relevance), combining general information and tailored interpretation.
- International frameworks: get_related_topics from the core article identifies frameworks (e.g., Basel Convention, RoHS, WEEE). Each framework is then validated through get_article and summarized via summarize_article_for_query, with extract_key_facts capturing mechanisms and relevance.
- Technology solutions: search_wikipedia locates process-focused articles (urban mining, hydrometallurgy, pyrometallurgy). get_sections informs whether a "Process" or "Technology" section exists; if not, summarize_article_for_query is used with a precise process-oriented query. extract_key_facts consolidates efficiency and hazard facts.
- Link-network overlaps: get_links is run on the core and country articles. The overlap detection step requires combining link sets and identifying intersecting entities across at least two articles, which adds cross-validation of shared stakeholders and frameworks.

Parallel vs. sequential requirements:
- Parallel: Initial searches per country and technology topics; related topic summaries for multiple items; link retrieval from multiple articles.
- Sequential: Section retrieval precedes section summarization; fallback summarization requires prior determination of missing sections; related topic identification precedes get_summary and summarize_article_for_query; frameworks selection precedes their article fetching and summarization.

Critical decision points:

- Section-based summarization vs. query-based summarization depending on availability of exact section titles.
- Related topics sufficiency threshold (≥3 policy-relevant topics per country) leading to iterative expansion from the core article’s related topics.
- Technology section presence determining whether to use summarize_article_section or fallback to summarize_article_for_query.

Cross-server dependencies:
- Not applicable. All tools are provided on a single server (Wikipedia). Cross-validation is performed across articles within the same server using complementary tools (sections, summaries, related topics, links).

task_description:
Research brief: Analyze the Eurovision Song Contest voting system and benchmark three high-performing countries using only the provided Wikipedia tools. Follow the exact multi-step procedure below and produce the specified structured output. Do not use any external resources. Use only the exact queries and titles provided, with the stated selection and fallback logic.

Goal: Produce a structured brief that includes (a) a concise overview of the current/recent voting system and key reforms, (b) a benchmark comparison for three selected countries, (c) cross-validation of wins against the winners list, and (d) brief profiles of up to two influential winning artists/groups.

Use the tools in this sequence with the given parameters and decision rules:

1) Identify the primary article and voting system details
- 1.1 Search for the main contest article:
  - Use Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with {"query": "Eurovision Song Contest", "limit": 5}.
  - Selection rule: Choose the result whose title exactly matches "Eurovision Song Contest" if present; otherwise choose the first search result whose title contains "Eurovision Song Contest".
  - Let MAIN_TITLE be the chosen title.
- 1.2 Inspect sections of MAIN_TITLE:
  - Use Wikipedia:get_sections with {"title": MAIN_TITLE}.
  - Decision: If any section title includes "Voting system" or "Voting" (case-insensitive), select the most specific one. Preference order: a section containing "Voting system" over a generic "Voting". Let VOTING_SECTION be the chosen section title.
  - If VOTING_SECTION exists, use Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with {"title": MAIN_TITLE, "section_title": VOTING_SECTION, "max_length": 200} to obtain a voting overview summary.
  - If no such section exists, fallback:
    - Use Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with {"query": "Voting at the Eurovision Song Contest", "limit": 3}.
    - Choose exact title match if present; else use the first search result. Let VOTING_PAGE be that title.
    - Use Wikipedia:get_summary with {"title": VOTING_PAGE} for the voting overview summary.
- 1.3 Extract key reforms from MAIN_TITLE:
  - Use Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with {"title": MAIN_TITLE, "topic_within_article": "Voting system changes and scoring reforms", "count": 7}. These will serve as the key reform bullets.
- 1.4 Find key linked pages from MAIN_TITLE:
  - Use Wikipedia:get_links with {"title": MAIN_TITLE}.
  - From the returned links, try to locate titles exactly equal to "Voting at the Eurovision Song Contest" and "List of Eurovision Song Contest winners". Record whether each is found.
  - If "List of Eurovision Song Contest winners" is not found via links, plan to locate it via search in step 3.1.

2) Country benchmarking (selection via related topics, then deep-dive)
- 2.1 Preferred country pages: "Sweden in the Eurovision Song Contest", "Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest", "Ukraine in the Eurovision Song Contest".
- 2.2 Use Wikipedia:get_related_topics with {"title": MAIN_TITLE, "limit": 30}.
  - Selection logic:
    - From related topics, identify which of the three preferred titles appear. Use them.
    - If any preferred titles are missing, fill remaining slots in this exact priority order by availability from related topics or otherwise via search in 2.3: "United Kingdom in the Eurovision Song Contest", "Ireland in the Eurovision Song Contest", "Spain in the Eurovision Song Contest", "France in the Eurovision Song Contest", "Netherlands in the Eurovision Song Contest".
    - You must end with exactly 3 distinct country articles. Let the final set be COUNTRY_TITLES[3].
- 2.3 If a needed country article is not present in related topics, search for it explicitly using Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with {"query": COUNTRY_NAME + " in the Eurovision Song Contest", "limit": 5}. Choose exact match if present; otherwise select the first result. Add it to COUNTRY_TITLES.
- 2.4 For each country in COUNTRY_TITLES, perform all of the following:
  - 2.4.1 Use Wikipedia:get_summary with {"title": COUNTRY_TITLE} for a high-level overview.
  - 2.4.2 Use Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with {"title": COUNTRY_TITLE, "topic_within_article": "wins, runner-up finishes, best results, debut year", "count": 7}. This should provide structured facts.
  - 2.4.3 Use Wikipedia:get_sections with {"title": COUNTRY_TITLE}. Then attempt to summarize a detailed performance section using Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with {"title": COUNTRY_TITLE, "section_title": SELECTED_SECTION, "max_length": 180}. Section selection priority order: "Participation and results" first; if not present then "History"; if not present then "Performances"; if not present then "Results".
  - 2.4.4 If none of the above sections exist, use Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with {"title": COUNTRY_TITLE, "query": "summary of performance and contest history", "max_length": 180}.
  - 2.4.5 Wins mention detection: If the output of 2.4.2 does not contain the word "win" or "winner" (case-insensitive), then run Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with {"title": COUNTRY_TITLE, "query": "number of wins and winning years", "max_length": 160} to capture wins info.

3) Winners list acquisition and cross-validation
- 3.1 Determine the winners list article:
  - If earlier in 1.4 you found a link exactly titled "List of Eurovision Song Contest winners", use that title. Otherwise, run Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with {"query": "List of Eurovision Song Contest winners", "limit": 5} and select the exact match if present; else the first result. Let WINNERS_TITLE be the chosen title.
- 3.2 Use Wikipedia:get_article with {"title": WINNERS_TITLE} to fetch the full content.
- 3.3 Use Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with {"title": WINNERS_TITLE, "query": "top winning countries and their total wins", "max_length": 200} to obtain a concise summary of top winning countries and counts.
- 3.4 Cross-validate country wins:
  - For each country in COUNTRY_TITLES, compare the wins information obtained in step 2.4 (facts and, if needed, the wins-focused summary) with the result of 3.3. If wins counts appear consistent, mark status = "consistent". If they differ or are ambiguous, mark status = "discrepancy" and include a details string citing both figures or noting ambiguity.

4) Influential winners context
- 4.1 Use Wikipedia:get_related_topics with {"title": WINNERS_TITLE, "limit": 20}.
- 4.2 From the returned topics, select up to two titles that are individual artists or groups using this priority order if present: "ABBA", "Loreen", "Johnny Logan", "Celine Dion". If fewer than two of these appear, select the first remaining related topic(s) that are persons or musical groups clearly tied to Eurovision wins.
- 4.3 For each selected artist/group (up to two):
  - Use Wikipedia:get_summary with {"title": ARTIST_TITLE}.
  - Use Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with {"title": ARTIST_TITLE, "topic_within_article": "Eurovision win(s) and impact", "count": 5}.

5) Final synthesis and output
- 5.1 Construct a structured brief based solely on data gathered via the above tool calls.
- 5.2 Output format (return a single JSON object with exactly these fields):
  - voting_system_overview: string summarizing the current or recent voting system and how jury and televote are combined, including any mention of notable changes.
  - key_reforms: array of up to 7 strings, each a key change or reform (include years when available from the extracted facts).
  - country_benchmarks: object keyed by each COUNTRY_TITLE. Each value is an object containing: wins_count (string or number as available), best_results (string), debut_year (string), notable_years (string), participation_trajectory (2-4 sentence summary synthesized from section summaries and facts).
  - cross_validation: array of objects, each with {country: COUNTRY_TITLE, status: "consistent" | "discrepancy", details: string explaining the comparison and any differences}.
  - influential_winners: array of up to 2 objects, each with {artist: ARTIST_TITLE, summary: 2-3 sentence narrative on Eurovision win(s) and impact, key_facts: array of up to 5 short bullet strings from extract_key_facts}.
  - sources_used: array of strings listing all Wikipedia article titles actually used during the process (deduplicate titles).

Constraints and fixed parameters
- Only use the specified Wikipedia tools and the exact search queries and titles given above. Do not invent new queries.
- Selection rules must be followed exactly: prefer exact title matches; otherwise choose the first search result. Section selection must follow the explicit priority orders stated.
- Mention detection: treat "wins" as present if the word "win" or "winner" appears in extract_key_facts for that country (case-insensitive). If not mentioned, perform the wins-focused summarize step.
- The final brief must be derived only from tool outputs obtained in this workflow. Do not include any external knowledge or assumptions.
- All steps are immediately executable with the provided tools; no additional inputs are required.
dependency_analysis:
Inherent tool dependencies and data flow
- Search → Fetch → Analyze: The workflow begins with Wikipedia:search_wikipedia to identify the correct page titles. Those titles are then consumed by Wikipedia:get_sections, Wikipedia:get_summary, Wikipedia:get_article, and analysis tools like Wikipedia:summarize_article_section, Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query, Wikipedia:extract_key_facts, Wikipedia:get_related_topics, and Wikipedia:get_links. Thus, search results drive all subsequent tool calls.
- Section-driven summarization: Wikipedia:get_sections feeds directly into Wikipedia:summarize_article_section, which cannot be used without an appropriate section title obtained from the sections list.
- Link discovery: Wikipedia:get_links on the main article is used to discover the winners and voting system subpages; if links are missing, the workflow falls back to Wikipedia:search_wikipedia to recover needed titles.
- Related topic exploration: Wikipedia:get_related_topics provides a pool of candidate country pages. The presence or absence of preferred country titles dictates whether to proceed with those titles or use a fallback via additional searches.

Scenario-based dependencies and decision points
- Primary article selection: The exact or best-match title from search determines the MAIN_TITLE used by all subsequent steps. Incorrect selection would break downstream calls.
- Voting section presence check: If a suitable voting section exists on MAIN_TITLE, the agent uses summarize_article_section; otherwise, the agent must branch to the separate voting-dedicated page via search and get_summary. This ensures robustness despite article structural variability.
- Country selection decision: The presence of preferred country articles in related topics influences whether to use them directly or to supplement with fallback countries via search. This creates a dynamic selection process based on available relationships.
- Section prioritization within country pages: The agent uses get_sections and then applies an ordered list of preferred section titles. If no preferred sections exist, it must branch to summarize_article_for_query. This dependency ensures the agent adapts to article-specific structures.
- Wins mention detection: The content of Wikipedia:extract_key_facts (country-level) determines whether an additional summarize_article_for_query call is needed to extract explicit wins and winning years.
- Winners list discovery: The workflow prioritizes discovering the winners list via get_links on MAIN_TITLE; if absent, it branches to a search-based retrieval. This decision affects which title is passed to get_article and summarize_article_for_query for top winners extraction.
- Cross-validation: Data from country pages (extract_key_facts and possibly summarize_article_for_query) must be compared with winners list summaries. Discrepancies trigger a specific reporting path in the final output, ensuring cross-source validation within Wikipedia.
- Influential winners selection: Related topics from the winners list page drive the choice of notable artists/groups. A priority list governs selection, and if priority names are absent, the agent must choose the first relevant individual/group from related topics.

Parallel vs. sequential requirements
- Sequential phases:
  - Phase 1 (MAIN_TITLE identification and voting system extraction) must precede discovering links and related topics, which inform downstream steps.
  - Phase 3 (winners list acquisition) depends on Phase 1 link discovery or fallback search; it must occur before cross-validation.
  - Phase 4 (influential winners context) depends on the winners list title from Phase 3.
- Parallelizable work:
  - Phase 2 country deep-dives (summary, key facts, sections, and conditional wins query) can be performed in parallel for each selected country once COUNTRY_TITLES is finalized. However, cross-validation in Phase 3.4 cannot be completed until Phase 3.3 is done.

Cross-server considerations
- Single-server environment (Wikipedia). All dependencies are intra-server. Cross-server validation is not applicable here.

Overall, the task enforces deep tool interdependence: initial search results determine titles for section inspection and summarization; link and related-topic discovery influence which additional articles to fetch; extracted facts trigger conditional summarization; and winners list data is used to cross-validate country-level results. The final synthesis mandates combining outputs from multiple tools and branches into a structured, verifiable brief.

task_description: Perform a comprehensive biological and historical research task on extreme survival mechanisms focusing on 'Tardigrades'. You must follow this strict chain of tool executions: 1. Use `search_wikipedia` to find the exact article title for 'Tardigrade'. 2. Use `get_sections` on the Tardigrade article to identify the exact title of the section discussing their survival abilities (look for terms like 'Survival', 'Physiology', or 'Cryptobiosis'). 3. Use `summarize_article_section` to get a summary of that specific section. 4. Use `extract_key_facts` to extract exactly 5 key facts from the Tardigrade article specifically focused on the topic 'extreme survival mechanisms and protective molecules'. 5. Analyze the section summary and key facts to identify exactly two specific biological states or protective molecules involved in their survival (e.g., Cryptobiosis, Anhydrobiosis, Trehalose, or Damage suppressor protein/Dsup). Use `search_wikipedia` if necessary to find their exact Wikipedia article titles. 6. For the FIRST identified state/molecule, use `get_related_topics` to find related concepts. Select one relevant broad biological concept from the results (e.g., Extremophile) and use `summarize_article_for_query` to summarize it tailored to the query: 'adaptation to extreme radiation and dehydration'. 7. For the SECOND identified state/molecule, use `get_summary` to retrieve its general overview. 8. Use `get_links` on the main Tardigrade article. Filter the retrieved links to find one closely related to space exposure or astrobiology (look for keywords like 'Space', 'Astrobiology', or specific spaceflight missions). 9. Use `get_article` to retrieve the full text of that space-related article. Analyze the full text to identify the specific year and spacecraft/mission name that first exposed them to the vacuum of space. 10. Compile your findings into a final JSON output with the following exact keys: 'survival_section_summary' (output from step 3), 'survival_key_facts' (output from step 4), 'first_mechanism_context' (output from step 6), 'second_mechanism_summary' (output from step 7), and 'space_exposure_details' (brief text explaining the specific space mission and year extracted in step 9).
dependency_analysis:
The task requires a deep, branching dependency tree utilizing every available Wikipedia tool. 
1. Sequential Root Initialization: `search_wikipedia` provides the foundational exact title ('Tardigrade') required by subsequent tools.
2. Parameter Extraction (Dependency): `get_sections` provides a list of headings; the agent must logically evaluate these to select the correct `section_title` argument for `summarize_article_section`.
3. Entity Generation (Decision Point): The combined outputs of `summarize_article_section` and `extract_key_facts` serve as unstructured input from which the agent must extract two distinct biological entities (e.g., Cryptobiosis, Trehalose). This dictates the arguments for parallel sub-chains.
4. Chain A (Contextual Branch): Entity 1's title is passed to `get_related_topics`. The output list requires a decision point to select a relevant target for `summarize_article_for_query`.
5. Chain B (Fact Retrieval Branch): Entity 2's title is passed directly to `get_summary`.
6. Data Transformation & Filtering (Dependency): `get_links` is called on the root article, generating a massive array. The agent must filter this array using semantic conditions (e.g., 'Space') to isolate a specific article title.
7. Deep Parsing (Dependency): The isolated space-related link dictates the input for `get_article`. The agent must parse the unstructured full text to extract precise historical data points (mission name and year).
8. Final Synthesis: All parallel and sequential data streams converge into a rigidly formatted JSON output, validating the successful traversal of the entire tool graph.

task_description:
Comparative research task: Reconstruct and compare city-level public health measures during the 1918 influenza pandemic in Philadelphia, St. Louis, and San Francisco, then contextualize them against national-level guidance and related epidemiological concepts. Use only the provided Wikipedia tools and follow the exact workflow and decision rules below. The output must be a structured report with the sections specified at the end.

Target cities and national context:
- Cities: Philadelphia, St. Louis, San Francisco
- National/global anchor article: the main Wikipedia article on the 1918 influenza pandemic (often titled "1918 influenza pandemic" or "Spanish flu").

Overall workflow (sequential with decision branches and iterative refinement):
1) Identify the national/global anchor article:
   a. Call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="1918 influenza pandemic" and limit=3.
   b. From results, pick the title that most directly represents the global event (prefer a title exactly matching "1918 influenza pandemic"; if not present, prefer "Spanish flu").
   c. Call Wikipedia:get_summary on the chosen title to verify it’s the general article. If the summary clearly describes the global pandemic, proceed; otherwise, choose the next best candidate and re-verify.

2) For each city (Philadelphia, St. Louis, San Francisco), locate a city-specific article or the best available proxy:
   a. Attempt the following queries in order until you find a result whose title contains both the city name and either "influenza" or "Spanish flu":
      - "1918 influenza pandemic Philadelphia" (or city name substituted)
      - "Spanish flu Philadelphia"
      - "1918 flu Philadelphia"
      Use Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with limit=5 for each query.
   b. Selection rule: Choose the first result containing the city name AND either "influenza" or "Spanish flu" in the title. If none across all three queries:
      - Fallback A: Use the city’s main article (its exact city name) if present in the search results; proceed with that as the proxy.
      - Fallback B: If you didn’t find the city main article via the above queries, perform a direct search with the city name only (e.g., query="Philadelphia" limit=3) and select the city’s main article title.

3) Validate and analyze the chosen city article (or proxy):
   a. Call Wikipedia:get_sections on the city article title to list sections.
   b. If any of the following section titles (case-insensitive substring match) are present, collect summaries for each using Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with max_length=250:
      - "Public health"
      - "Response"
      - "Measures"
      - "Impact"
      - "Non-pharmaceutical"
      - "Mortality"
      - "Second wave"
      - "Masks"
   c. If none of the above sections are found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query twice on the same article with:
      - query="public health measures, closures, mask mandates, mortality, second wave"
      - query="dates of school closures, event bans, business closures, reopening, enforcement"
   d. Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts on the city article with topic_within_article="public health" and count=7. If fewer than 5 usable facts are extracted, immediately re-call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts on the same article with topic_within_article="" (empty) and count=7 to broaden coverage.

4) Augment city context from linked and related pages:
   a. Call Wikipedia:get_links on the city article to retrieve linked titles. From that list, choose up to 2 links that appear to represent officials or institutions relevant to policy (e.g., pages containing terms like "commissioner", "department of health", "mayor"). For each of the selected links (up to 2 per city), call Wikipedia:get_summary and extract 1–2 sentences describing their role.
   b. Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics on the city article with limit=10. From the returned topics, pick up to 2 topics that are epidemiology/policy relevant (e.g., terms likely to be "Non-pharmaceutical intervention (epidemiology)", "Quarantine", "Social distancing"). For each selected related topic, call Wikipedia:get_summary.

5) National/global context extraction (cross-validation anchor):
   a. Using the national/global anchor title from step 1, call Wikipedia:get_sections to enumerate sections.
   b. If a section with a title containing one of the following appears, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section (max_length=250) to obtain it:
      - "Responses"
      - "Public health"
      - "Non-pharmaceutical"
      - "By country" or "United States"
   c. If none of these sections are found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="United States public health measures, closures, masks, mortality, second wave" on the anchor article.
   d. Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts on the anchor article with topic_within_article="United States" and count=7. If fewer than 5 facts appear relevant to the U.S., re-call with topic_within_article="public health" and count=7.

6) Iterative decision branches for missing city-specific detail:
   - If a city lacks mortality figures after steps 3 and 4, perform a targeted call to Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on the city article with query="mortality rate per 100,000; total deaths; excess mortality". If still not found, consult the national anchor article by calling Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="[City Name] mortality"; if the city is not addressed there, explicitly note the gap.
   - If no interventions are described for a city after steps 3 and 4, re-run Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on the city article with query="school closures; public gatherings; theaters; churches; mask ordinance; enforcement".

7) Synthesis and cross-check:
   a. For each city, distill:
      - First observed cases (date description if given) and initial actions
      - Major closures/bans (schools, theaters, gatherings)
      - Mask mandates or recommendations (presence/absence and enforcement)
      - Reopening decisions and any subsequent re-closures (second wave response)
      - Mortality figures (total and/or per 100,000 if available)
      - Named officials/agencies and their roles (from step 4a summaries)
   b. Compare the city-level measures to the national/global anchor insights:
      - Identify 2–3 convergences (e.g., early closure pattern) and 1–2 divergences for each city.
      - If any numerical mortality values are found for all three cities, compare them and highlight city-to-city differences.

8) Cross-topic contextualization:
   a. From the union of related topics selected in step 4b across all three cities, pick the top 5 unique topics.
   b. For each of the 5 topics, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on that topic with query="How this concept shaped city-level measures in 1918 (closures, masks, enforcement)" using max_length=250, to produce a short applied-context rationale.

Expected output format (use plain text with bullet lists, no tables or heavy formatting):
- Title: Comparative Public Health Measures During the 1918 Influenza in Three U.S. Cities
- Methods and tool usage summary: Briefly list which Wikipedia tools were used at each step.
- City analyses (one section per city):
  - Article used: [title]
  - Dedicated city-pandemic article found: Yes/No (if No, specify proxy used)
  - Sequence of key dates and actions (4–6 bullets)
  - Public health measures (at least 5 bullets)
  - Mask policy and enforcement (bullets)
  - Mortality data (include units if per 100,000, or totals)
  - Notable officials/agencies and roles (2 bullets from linked page summaries)
  - Key extracted facts (5–7 bullets)
- National/global anchor comparison:
  - Anchor article title: [title]
  - Summarized U.S.-focused measures (3–5 bullets)
  - Cross-check findings: convergences/divergences for each city (2–3 bullets per city)
- Cross-topic context (5 topics): For each topic, provide a 2–3 sentence rationale connecting the topic to the city measures.
- Decision log: Document which fallbacks were used for each city (e.g., missing section -> summarize_article_for_query used; missing mortality -> targeted query used).
- Sources used (titles only): List every Wikipedia article title consulted across all calls.

Tool usage constraints and concrete parameters:
- Always use the exact queries provided above for search and summarize_article_for_query.
- For all summarize_article_section calls, use max_length=250.
- For extract_key_facts, use count=7 as specified and apply the fallback rule if <5 facts are relevant.
- For get_related_topics, use limit=10.

Wikipedia:get_related_topics identifies conceptual neighbors (e.g., non-pharmaceutical interventions) that are then summarized and query-tailored with Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query to explain relevance.

Scenario-based dependencies and decision points:
- Anchor selection: The output of Wikipedia:search_wikipedia determines which title is passed to Wikipedia:get_summary. If the summary does not indicate global relevance, a different search result is selected. This upstream validation affects all downstream cross-validation steps.
- City article resolution: If the initial city-focused searches do not yield a city-pandemic-specific title, the workflow conditionally falls back to selecting the city’s main article (via fallback A/B), ensuring continuity. The chosen title directly feeds into get_sections, section-based summaries, and all subsequent extraction/expansion steps.
- Section vs. query summarization: Wikipedia:get_sections output determines whether Wikipedia:summarize_article_section is used (if relevant sections exist) or whether Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query is used as a fallback to retrieve targeted content when sections are absent.
- Insufficient facts loop: If Wikipedia:extract_key_facts (topic-scoped) returns fewer than 5 relevant facts, a controlled loop broadens the scope by calling extract_key_facts again without a topic filter (same article, count=7). The result of the first extraction dictates whether this iterative step runs.
- Missing data contingency: If mortality or intervention details remain absent after section and query summarization, an additional query-focused summarize call is performed on the city article; failing that for mortality, the national anchor is queried for city-specific mentions. The presence or absence of data after these calls controls whether a gap note is produced.
- Contextual link and topic selection: The outputs of Wikipedia:get_links and Wikipedia:get_related_topics drive which titles are passed to Wikipedia:get_summary and Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query for contextual explanations. Selection criteria (policy/officials for links; epidemiology/policy relevance for related topics) create a conditional branching in which only targeted subsets are further processed.

Parallel vs. sequential requirements:
- Sequential: Anchor identification and validation must occur before cross-validation extraction, as it guides national-level comparisons. Within each city, section discovery must precede section summarization; if sections fail, query summarization is the fallback. Fact extraction depends on article choice.
- Parallel: After the anchor is set, the three city workflows can run in parallel following the same dependency logic. Within each city, link-based official/agency summaries and related-topic summaries can also proceed in parallel after the base article is established.

Cross-server considerations:
- All tools are hosted on the Wikipedia server; there are no additional servers available. Consequently, cross-server dependencies are not applicable in this task. However, multi-article cross-validation within the same server is enforced: city-level findings are checked against the national/global anchor article.
