task_description:
Research brief: Compare three historical trade networks—the Hanseatic League, the Republic of Venice’s maritime trade system, and the Trans-Saharan trade network—focusing on governance, key commodities, and key cities, then identify cross-network overlaps and validate them. Use only the provided Wikipedia tools. Follow this exact workflow and decision logic to ensure deep dependency use and cross-validation:

Inputs (fixed):
- Target networks (canonical search queries):
  1) "Hanseatic League"
  2) "Republic of Venice"
  3) "Trans-Saharan trade"
- Commodity keyword set for standardization and frequency counting: ["grain", "timber", "furs", "salt", "spices", "silk", "gold", "slaves", "ivory", "amber", "fish", "wine"]
- Section title detection keywords:
  - Governance: ["Government", "Governance", "Organisation", "Organization", "Administration", "Political"]
  - Economy/Trade: ["Economy", "Trade", "Commerce", "Economics"]
  - Members/Cities: ["Members", "Cities", "Towns", "Membership", "Participants"]
- City validation criteria: An article summary must contain the substring "city" or "town" or "port" (case-insensitive) in the first sentence to count as a city.
- Overlap threshold: If overlapping city hubs across at least two networks < 2, trigger fallback expansion.
- Top counts:
  - Extract up to 5 key commodities per network after standardization.
  - Extract up to 10 validated city hubs per network.
  - Select top 3 cross-network commodities by frequency across networks (ties alphabetically).
  - Summaries: governance (<= 100 words), origins (<= 60 words), commodity deep dives (<= 120 words per commodity).

Step-by-step procedure:
1) Article discovery (sequential, then parallel per network):
   - For each query (Hanseatic League, Republic of Venice, Trans-Saharan trade), call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with limit=5.
   - Choose the article title that exactly matches the query if present; otherwise choose the top result whose title contains the full query phrase (case-insensitive). If none contain the full phrase, pick the first result.
   - For each selected title, call Wikipedia:get_article and Wikipedia:get_sections.

2) Section targeting and tailored summaries (per network):
   - From the section list, find the first section whose title contains any governance keywords. If found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with max_length=180. If not found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="governance and administration" and max_length=180.
   - Similarly, find the first Economy/Trade section using economy keywords; if found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with max_length=180. If not found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="commodities traded and key goods" and max_length=180.
   - For origins, search for a "History" or similar section containing "History" in the title; if found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with max_length=120. If not found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="origins and early development" and max_length=120.

3) Extract key facts (per network):
   - Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with topic_within_article="governance" and count=5.
   - Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with topic_within_article="commodities" and count=7.
   - Combine the economy/trade section summary and the extracted commodity facts; standardize to the commodity keyword set by matching case-insensitively and normalizing plurals (e.g., "spice" -> "spices"). Keep up to 5 unique matching commodities. If fewer than 3 are found, supplement by scanning link titles from Step 4 for matches to the commodity keyword set.

4) Candidate city extraction and validation (per network):
   - Call Wikipedia:get_links on the network article. From returned link titles, select candidates as those starting with an uppercase letter and not containing disambiguation parentheses. Limit to the first 40 candidates after filtering.
   - For each candidate title, call Wikipedia:get_summary. If the first sentence contains "city" or "town" or "port" (case-insensitive), keep it as a validated city. Stop when you have up to 10 validated cities per network; if fewer than 10, keep all validated.

5) Cross-network city overlap (global synthesis):
   - Compute the set of validated cities per network from Step 4. Identify overlapping cities that appear in at least two of the three network sets.
   - Decision point A (fallback): If overlapping cities < 2, for each network call Wikipedia:get_related_topics with limit=15. From these related topics, take any titles containing the substring "city" or "cities" or specific city names implied by network context; validate each candidate by calling Wikipedia:get_summary with the same criteria as above and union them into the network's city set. Recompute overlaps.
   - Decision point B (second fallback): If overlapping cities still < 2, run Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with the following queries and limit=5:
     • "List of Hanseatic cities"
     • "List of cities of the Republic of Venice" OR "Venetian cities"
     • "Trans-Saharan trade cities"
     For each top result selected, call Wikipedia:get_article and Wikipedia:get_links; validate link titles as cities using Wikipedia:get_summary; augment each network's city set and recompute overlaps.

6) Cross-network commodity synthesis and deep dives:
   - Combine the standardized commodities from Step 3 across all networks; compute per-network presence and total frequency across networks.
   - Select the top 3 commodities by how many networks include them (ties alphabetically). For each selected commodity:
     a) Call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with the commodity name and limit=5; pick the best-matching canonical article as in Step 1.
     b) Call Wikipedia:get_article and then Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="historical trade regions" and max_length=120.
     c) Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics with limit=8 to capture any geographic-region-related topics; keep those containing regional or geographic terms (e.g., names of regions, seas, or continents) to annotate the deep dive.

7) Hub confirmation via related topics:
   - For each overlapping city identified in Step 5, call Wikipedia:get_related_topics on the city article with limit=10. If any related topic title contains "Hanseatic", "Venice", "Venetian", or "Trans-Saharan", tag the city as a "confirmed hub"; otherwise tag as "candidate hub".

8) Output format (produce these sections):
   - Executive summary:
     • Count of validated cities per network
     • Number of overlapping cities and their names with hub tags
     • Top 3 cross-network commodities
   - Network profiles (one per network):
     • Governance summary (<= 100 words)
     • Origins snapshot (<= 60 words)
     • Key commodities (up to 5 standardized items)
     • Key cities (up to 10 validated city names)
   - Cross-network synthesis:
     • Overlapping cities with hub tags and a single-sentence rationale for each (cite related topic keyword that triggered confirmation if applicable)
     • Commodity deep dives: for each of the top 3 commodities, a 1–2 sentence summary of historical trade regions and a short mapping stating which networks traded it
   - Methodology notes:
     • Mention which tools were used at which steps and which fallback branches were triggered (Decision A and/or B)
   - References:
     • List all Wikipedia article titles consulted during the workflow, grouped by step

Strict tool-use requirements:
- You must use all of these tools at least once: Wikipedia:search_wikipedia, Wikipedia:get_article, Wikipedia:get_summary, Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query, Wikipedia:summarize_article_section, Wikipedia:extract_key_facts, Wikipedia:get_related_topics, Wikipedia:get_sections, Wikipedia:get_links.
- Tool outputs must inform subsequent tool inputs exactly as specified (e.g., section titles from get_sections must feed summarize_article_section; link titles must feed get_summary for validation; commodity names must feed search_wikipedia in Step 6).
- Do not use any external resources or assumptions beyond what the tools return and the fixed inputs in this task description.
dependency_analysis:
Inherent chains and data flow:
- Discovery chain: search_wikipedia → get_article provides canonical pages; get_sections enumerates structure, enabling targeted summarization via summarize_article_section. If sections are missing, summarize_article_for_query fills gaps with tailored content. This is a standard search → fetch → analyze pipeline.
- Extraction and validation chain: get_links produces candidate linked titles; get_summary validates which candidates are cities using content semantics from the first sentence. This transforms raw link graphs into typed entities (cities) using cross-tool inference.
- Fact extraction chain: extract_key_facts (topic-specific) and summarize_article_section (Economy/Trade) are combined to build a standardized commodity set via a provided keyword list; missing commodities trigger fallback to scan link titles, creating a multi-tool fusion of structured (facts) and unstructured (links) signals.

Scenario-based dependencies and decision points:
- Section presence decision: get_sections determines whether to call summarize_article_section (if a matching section exists) or summarize_article_for_query (fallback). Governance, economy, and history each use this gate, forcing branching based on structural availability.
- Overlap sufficiency decision: After building per-network validated city sets (via get_links → get_summary), the intersection size determines whether to invoke expansion fallbacks. Decision A expands via get_related_topics; Decision B escalates to search_wikipedia for list-type pages, then get_article → get_links → get_summary to enrich city sets. Each fallback reuses prior outputs (network titles) and adds new validated cities before recomputation.
- Commodity relevance decision: If fewer than 3 standardized commodities emerge from extract_key_facts + section summary, the workflow conditionally consults get_links to scrape additional candidates, ensuring sufficient breadth for cross-network frequency computation.
- Commodity deep dive selection: The union and frequency of standardized commodities across networks determine which items become input queries for search_wikipedia → get_article → summarize_article_for_query and get_related_topics to extract region-specific context.
- Hub confirmation decision: For overlapping cities, get_related_topics is used to cross-validate their association with the networks by matching topic titles against network names (e.g., "Hanseatic", "Venetian", "Trans-Saharan"). This step may reclassify a city as confirmed or candidate based on related-topic evidence.

Parallel vs sequential:
- Per-network profiling (Steps 2–4) runs in parallel for each of the three target articles once selected. Cross-network synthesis (Steps 5–7) is sequential, depending on completion of per-network sets and overlaps.

Cross-server considerations:
- All tools reside on the single Wikipedia server in this scenario; hence, no cross-server dependency applies. Nevertheless, cross-tool dependencies emulate cross-data-source validation by using different Wikipedia endpoints: structure (get_sections), content summaries (get_summary, summarize_article_for_query), link graphs (get_links), and related-topic graphs (get_related_topics).

Critical dependency highlights:
- Titles from search_wikipedia strictly gate all subsequent calls (get_article, get_sections, get_links, extract_key_facts), ensuring that incorrect selection cascades would be caught by fallback and validation steps.
- Section titles from get_sections directly parameterize summarize_article_section; absent sections force a logical pivot to summarize_article_for_query, preventing dead ends.
- Link titles from get_links become parameters to get_summary and get_related_topics for validation and hub confirmation; their intersections drive conditional expansions.
- Commodity names extracted and standardized feed new search_wikipedia calls for deep-dive articles, creating a deep dependency chain from section/summary extraction to new content discovery and regional context aggregation.

task_description:
Objective: Build a research-grade comparative report on five international auxiliary languages (Esperanto, Interlingua, Volapük, Ido, and Lojban), with conditional expansion to Novial and Lingua Franca Nova if related-topic evidence warrants it. Your report must compare design goals, grammar, vocabulary sources, phonology/orthography, history, organizations/community, and criticism/reception, and include cross-validation of founders via separate Wikipedia pages.

Scope and items:
- Base languages to analyze: ["Esperanto", "Interlingua", "Volapük", "Ido", "Lojban"].
- Candidate expansion languages: ["Novial", "Lingua Franca Nova"].
- Central concept article for initial linkage check: "International auxiliary language".

Required tool sequence and logic (execute exactly in this order with specified decisions/fallbacks):
1) Seed discovery and validation using links:
   a) Call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="International auxiliary language", limit=5. Select the article titled exactly "International auxiliary language" (if multiple results, choose the one with that exact title; if not found, choose the top result and proceed, noting divergence).
   b) Call Wikipedia:get_links on the selected central article. From the returned links, check if at least 5 of the following are present: "Esperanto", "Interlingua", "Volapük", "Ido", "Lojban". Decision point:
      - If at least 5 are present, proceed with the base set as defined.
      - Else, for each of the base language names, call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia (limit=3) and select the title that explicitly refers to the language (prefer titles with "(language)" suffix or the unambiguous language article). Record the resolved titles for subsequent steps.

2) For EACH base language (sequentially process to honor dependencies):
   Title resolution:
   - If not already resolved in 1b fallback, resolve now by calling Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with the language name (limit=3) and select the correct language article as above. Use the final resolved article title for all further calls on that language.

   Section discovery:
   - Call Wikipedia:get_sections for the language article.
   - Target section families (case-insensitive match; accept closest synonyms):
     • Grammar family: ["Grammar", "Morphology", "Syntax"].
     • Phonology family: ["Phonology", "Phonetics"].
     • Vocabulary family: ["Vocabulary", "Lexicon", "Word formation"].
     • History family: ["History"].
     • Organizations/community family: ["Organizations", "Community", "Movement"].
     • Criticism/reception family: ["Criticism", "Reception", "Controversy"].

   Section summarization (branch per family):
   - For EACH family above:
     • If a matching section title exists from get_sections, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section(title=<resolved>, section_title=<best match>, max_length=180 for all families except History where max_length=250).
     • Else, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query(title=<resolved>, query=<family keyword such as "grammar", "phonology", "vocabulary", "history", "organizations", "criticism">, max_length=220).

   Key facts extraction:
   - Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts(title=<resolved>, topic_within_article="founder, creation year, vocabulary sources, design goals, number of speakers, orthography", count=7). Parse out:
     • Founder name(s)
     • Year of creation (if provided)
     • Design goal(s)
     • Vocabulary source(s)
     • Any speaker count claim (if present)
     • Orthography/phonology notes (if present)
   - If any of these items are absent in extracted facts, mark them as "not stated" for that language.

   Related topics scan for expansion:
   - Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics(title=<resolved>, limit=10). If any of the candidate expansion languages ["Novial", "Lingua Franca Nova"] appear, record which ones and increment a global tally counter for each occurrence.

   Founder cross-validation (per language):
   - For EACH founder name obtained from extract_key_facts (if multiple, process each one):
     • Call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia(query=<founder name>, limit=2). Select the most plausible biography article.
     • Call Wikipedia:get_summary(title=<selected founder article>).
     • Check whether the summary string contains the language name (case-insensitive substring check). Decision and retry logic:
       - If it contains the language name, mark founder cross-validation as "confirmed" for that founder.
       - Else, if a second search result exists, repeat get_summary for the second result and re-check.
       - If neither summary mentions the language, mark as "discrepancy" for that founder and flag in the final report.

3) Conditional expansion:
   - After processing all base languages, evaluate the global tallies for ["Novial", "Lingua Franca Nova"] from get_related_topics:
     • If the combined tally across base languages is ≥ 3 for a candidate language, add that language to the analysis set.
   - For EACH newly added language (up to two):
     • Resolve the correct article title via Wikipedia:search_wikipedia(query=<language name>, limit=3) and select the language article.
     • Call Wikipedia:get_sections.
     • Summarize only "History" and "Grammar" families using the same section/fallback rules as in Step 2 (History max_length=250; Grammar max_length=180).
     • Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts(title=<resolved>, topic_within_article="founder, creation year, design goals, vocabulary sources", count=6).
     • Skip founder cross-validation for expansion languages.

4) Final synthesis requirements (output format):
- Produce a structured narrative with bullet lists only (no tables). For EACH analyzed language, include bullets with the following headings and concise content from your tool-gathered summaries/facts:
  • Founder(s) and creation year (plus founder cross-validation status: confirmed or discrepancy)
  • Design goal(s)
  • Grammar highlights
  • Vocabulary sources
  • Phonology/Orthography notes
  • History overview (2–3 lines max)
  • Organizations/Community (if any)
  • Criticism/Reception (if any)
  • Related languages flagged (from get_related_topics)
- Then add a "Comparative highlights" section with 7–10 bullets contrasting the languages on: agglutination vs isolation, regularity of grammar, extent of Romance/Germanic vocabulary mix, presence/role of governing bodies, orthographic simplicity, degree of logical/engineered design, and any noted criticisms.
- Explicitly list any founder cross-validation discrepancies found.

Concrete parameters and thresholds:
- search_wikipedia limits: as specified above (mostly 3 or 5).
- summarize_article_section max_length: 180 (except History 250).
- summarize_article_for_query max_length: 220.
- extract_key_facts count: 7 for base languages; 6 for expansion languages.
- Related-topic expansion threshold: add a candidate language if its related-topic tally ≥ 3 across the base languages.
- Founder cross-validation retry: up to 2 search results per founder.

Deliverables:
- A single consolidated report following the specified bullet structure, covering all base languages and any expansion languages qualified by the threshold.
- A short note at the end describing any decision branches taken (e.g., missing sections replaced by tailored summaries, expansion triggered/not triggered).
dependency_analysis:
Available server: Wikipedia. All tools belong to this server, so cross-server dependencies are not applicable. The task creates deep, multi-step dependencies among Wikipedia tools with several decision points and iterative checks.

Inherent tool chains:
- search_wikipedia → (title resolution) → get_sections → (branch) → summarize_article_section OR summarize_article_for_query.
- Article content → extract_key_facts → (names/years pulled) → search_wikipedia (founders) → get_summary (founder bio) → cross-validation result.
- Core topic article → get_links → validates presence of base language pages (seed validation) and affects title resolution.
- Per-language get_related_topics → contributes to global tallies → triggers conditional expansion workflow → (same summarize/extract chain for added languages).

Scenario-based dependencies and decision points:
1) Seed linkage validation: get_links on "International auxiliary language" determines whether base set titles are likely present; if insufficient linkage is found, the workflow falls back to per-language search_wikipedia to resolve correct titles. This ensures accurate titles before data extraction.
2) Section presence branching: get_sections dictates whether to use summarize_article_section (if a target section or synonym exists) or summarize_article_for_query (if not). This conditional preserves topical relevance even when articles differ structurally.
3) Key facts to identity cross-check: extract_key_facts outputs founder name(s) and creation year, which then drive a secondary search_wikipedia for the founder biography. get_summary of the founder page is string-checked for the language name to confirm or flag discrepancies. A retry on the second search result adds robustness.
4) Related-topic driven expansion: get_related_topics on each base language yields related language names. A global tally (frequency across base languages) determines if Novial or Lingua Franca Nova meet the threshold (≥3). Meeting this threshold triggers an additional mini-pipeline (title resolution → sections → summarize/extract) for expansion languages.
5) Fallbacks and retries: Multiple points have controlled fallbacks—e.g., title disambiguation via search_wikipedia if central links are insufficient; alternate summarization via summarize_article_for_query when sections are absent; retrying founder validation with the second search result if the first fails.

Parallel vs. sequential requirements:
- Within each language’s processing, calls are sequential due to dependencies: title resolution → sections → summarization → key facts → related topics → founder cross-validation.
- Across languages, processing could be parallelized logically, but the task requires sequential processing to accumulate and evaluate the global related-topic tallies before conditional expansion.

Data flow summary:
- Initial search determines the core article (International auxiliary language). get_links informs whether to rely on in-article links or perform per-language search for title resolution. Resolved titles feed into get_sections and summarization calls. Summaries and extract_key_facts provide substantive content for report sections. extract_key_facts outputs feed founder names into a secondary validation loop (search_wikipedia + get_summary). Per-language get_related_topics contribute to global counters that control expansion into Novial and/or Lingua Franca Nova. Expansion languages follow a reduced summarization/extraction path without founder validation. All outputs are synthesized into a final structured comparative report, with an explicit log of decision branches taken.

task_description:
Conduct a comprehensive comparative research analysis of the scientific contributions and legacy of three pioneering women in STEM: Marie Curie, Ada Lovelace, and Rosalind Franklin. Follow this exact research methodology:

1. **Discovery Phase**: Search Wikipedia for each of the three scientists using their names as queries (limit results to 5 each). From the search results, identify the exact Wikipedia article title for each person.

2. **Structural Analysis**: For each of the three identified articles, retrieve the full section structure. Identify which sections relate to (a) their scientific contributions/work, (b) their legacy/impact, and (c) their personal life. Record the exact section titles.

3. **Deep Dive - Scientific Contributions**: For each scientist, summarize the section most closely related to their scientific work/contributions (use max_length of 200 words). Also extract 5 key facts from each article focused on the topic 'scientific discoveries'.

4. **Deep Dive - Legacy and Impact**: For each scientist, summarize the section most closely related to their legacy or impact on science (use max_length of 200 words). Additionally, use the query-tailored summary tool to get a summary of each article tailored to the query 'influence on modern science and technology' (max_length 300 words).

5. **Cross-Referencing and Connection Mapping**: For each of the three articles, retrieve related topics (limit 10). Then, get the links from each article. Analyze the overlaps: identify any related topics or links that appear in common across two or more of the three scientists' articles. For any shared linked article that appears in at least two of the three scientists' link lists, get its summary to understand the connection point.

6. **Deep Investigation of Shared Themes**: Based on the shared links/topics discovered in step 5, pick up to 3 of the most interesting shared linked articles. For each, extract 3 key facts and retrieve their sections to understand the thematic bridge between the scientists.

7. **Final Comparative Report**: Compile a structured report with the following sections:
   - **Individual Profiles**: For each scientist, present their key facts, scientific contribution summary, and legacy summary.
   - **Interconnections**: List all shared topics/links found across the three scientists, with brief explanations from the shared article summaries.
   - **Thematic Bridges**: Describe the common themes that connect these three women in STEM based on the deep investigation of shared articles.
   - **Comparative Impact Assessment**: Based on all gathered data, provide a comparative assessment of how each scientist's work influenced subsequent fields, noting any chain of influence (e.g., did Lovelace's computational thinking influence fields that later used Curie's or Franklin's discoveries?).

Present the final report in a well-organized format with clear headings and citations to the specific Wikipedia articles consulted.

task_description:
Conduct a comprehensive comparative research analysis of the Space Race between the United States and the Soviet Union, focusing on how their respective rocket programs evolved and influenced each other. Follow this exact research workflow:

1. **Initial Search Phase**: Search Wikipedia for 'Space Race' to identify the main article. Also search for 'Soviet space program' and 'NASA' to find related core articles.

2. **Structural Analysis**: For each of the three main articles found (Space Race, Soviet space program, and NASA), retrieve their section listings to understand how they are organized and identify sections related to key milestones, rocket technology, and historical timeline.

3. **Deep Dive into Key Sections**: From the Space Race article, summarize the sections that cover the origins/background of the competition and the major milestones (e.g., sections about Sputnik, Moon landing, or similar milestone sections identified from the section listing). From the Soviet space program article, summarize the section covering early rocketry or origins. From the NASA article, summarize the section covering its formation or history.

4. **Key Facts Extraction**: Extract 7 key facts from the Space Race article focused on the topic 'rocket technology milestones'. Extract 5 key facts from the Soviet space program article focused on 'Sputnik and early achievements'. Extract 5 key facts from the NASA article focused on 'Apollo program'.

5. **Cross-Reference Investigation**: From the Space Race article, retrieve all links to identify pivotal figures and programs mentioned. Then, pick the following three linked topics and investigate them further: 'Wernher von Braun', 'Sergei Korolev', and 'Apollo 11'. For each of these three articles:
   a. Get a summary of the article.
   b. Get a query-tailored summary focused on 'contribution to the Space Race'.
   c. Extract 3 key facts.

6. **Related Topics Exploration**: Get related topics for both 'Wernher von Braun' and 'Sergei Korolev' (limit 5 each). Identify if there are any overlapping or connecting topics between the two lists that reveal shared influences or connections between the US and Soviet programs.

7. **Synthesis Query-Focused Summaries**: Using the Space Race article, generate a query-tailored summary (max 300 words) for the query 'How did Cold War politics drive technological innovation in space exploration?'. Also generate a query-tailored summary from the NASA article for the query 'international cooperation after the Space Race' (max 250 words).

**Final Output Requirements**: Compile all findings into a structured research brief with the following sections:
- Executive Summary (synthesize the query-focused summaries)
- Timeline of Key Milestones (drawn from key facts across all articles)
- Comparative Profiles of Key Figures (von Braun vs Korolev, using their summaries and key facts)
- Technology Transfer and Cross-Pollination (using related topics overlap analysis and link analysis)
- Legacy and International Cooperation (from the NASA international cooperation summary)
- List of all Wikipedia articles consulted during the research

task_description:
Research the history of optical telegraphy networks in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, with a focus on the French semaphore telegraph system developed by Claude Chappe. Create a comprehensive report that:

1. First, establish the historical context by searching for 'Semaphore telegraph' to understand the general concept
2. Investigate Claude Chappe's biography and the development of his telegraph system
3. Examine the technical specifications of the Chappe semaphore system (arm angles, code books)
4. Research the expansion of the French telegraph network (particularly the Paris-Lille and Paris-Toulouse lines)
5. Explore how other nations responded by building their own optical telegraph systems
6. Analyze the role of optical telegraphy in military communications during the Napoleonic Wars
7. Investigate why optical telegraphy was eventually superseded by electric telegraphy

For each investigation step, use appropriate Wikipedia tools to gather, verify, and synthesize information. Cross-reference key facts about system range, transmission speeds, and network size across multiple articles to ensure accuracy.

task_description:
Comparative evidence synthesis of urban congestion pricing schemes in five cities (London, Stockholm, Singapore, Milan, New York City) using only Wikipedia tools, with iterative refinement, cross-validation, and decision branches. Your goal is to build a structured, cross-city comparison of policy designs and measured outcomes by chaining multiple Wikipedia tools in a controlled workflow. Do not use any external sources.

Scope and cities:
- Target cities: London, Stockholm, Singapore, Milan, New York City.
- Target policy pages (discover programmatically; do not hardcode): seek each city’s congestion pricing/charge/tax scheme.

Key outputs (deliver in the final answer as bullet lists; one block per city, followed by a cross-city comparison block):
For each city, extract and report:
- Canonical article title used and a 2–3 sentence overview (from get_summary).
- Alternate related article(s) used for cross-checking (titles only).
- Start date and current status (operational/suspended/planned), citing the page titles in-line.
- Charging zone description and hours of operation.
- Charge structure: amounts (peak/off-peak if any), vehicle categories, dynamic pricing if applicable.
- Exemptions/discounts (notable categories such as residents, low-income, disabled, EVs, taxis, etc.).
- Reported impacts with figures and units where available:
  - Traffic volume changes (initial year and longer-term if both exist).
  - Average speed changes.
  - Public transport ridership changes.
  - Air quality metrics (e.g., NO2, PM, CO2 changes).
  - Road safety metrics (e.g., collision/fatality changes).
  - Revenue (annual or total) and stated allocation/use of funds.
- Noted criticisms, legal challenges, and political outcomes (e.g., referenda) with a 2–4 sentence summary.
- Data confidence: list any conflicting figures found (min–max or multiple values) and identify which article titles provided which figures.
After per-city sections, produce a cross-city comparison:
- Rank cities by reported traffic reduction (largest to smallest) and by reported air pollutant reduction (choose one pollutant with the most comparable data, e.g., NO2). If city lacks that pollutant, skip it and note missing data.
- Identify 3–5 common design elements shared by at least three cities (e.g., charge coverage, technology, exemptions) and 3–5 key divergences.
- Synthesize 5 practical, evidence-grounded takeaways for policymakers, strictly derived from the gathered Wikipedia data.

Tool-driven workflow and required queries (execute for each city independently, then aggregate):
1) Discover the canonical page via search_wikipedia (limit: 10). Run the following city-specific queries in this order until you find the most relevant candidate by title relevance and snippet context:
   - London: ["London congestion charge", "Congestion charge London", "Congestion pricing London"].
   - Stockholm: ["Stockholm congestion tax", "Stockholm congestion charge", "Congestion tax Stockholm"].
   - Singapore: ["Electronic Road Pricing", "Congestion pricing Singapore", "Road pricing Singapore"].
   - Milan: ["Area C Milan", "Milan congestion charge", "Congestion charge Milan"].
   - New York City: ["Congestion pricing in New York City", "New York congestion pricing", "NYC congestion pricing"].
   Decision rule A: Prefer a page whose title explicitly matches the scheme name (e.g., "London congestion charge", "Electronic Road Pricing"). If multiple plausible results exist, pick the one with sections likely to cover operation/effects (validated in step 3). If none look suitable, broaden to generic-but-city-specific topics (e.g., "Transport in [City]"), then narrow via step 4.

2) Fetch the candidate page with get_article and get_summary. Record the title and the summary as the city’s initial overview.

3) Inspect structure with get_sections. Target sections to extract if available: History, Background, Implementation, Operation, Charging/Charges/Tariffs/Pricing, Results/Effects/Impact, Criticism/Controversy/Opposition, Revenue/Finance/Funding, Exemptions/Discounts/Exclusions. Use summarize_article_section with max_length: 180 for each present target section.
   Decision rule B: If a target section is missing, immediately call summarize_article_for_query on the same page with a focused query string specific to that topic (max_length: 260). Use these exact query strings when sections are absent:
   - For charge structure: "charge amount, pricing, tariffs, peak, off-peak, vehicle categories".
   - For zone/hours: "charging zone boundaries, hours of operation".
   - For impacts: "effects on traffic, average speed, public transport ridership".
   - For air quality: "air pollution, NO2, PM, CO2 changes after congestion charge".
   - For revenue: "revenue amount, annual revenue, allocation, use of funds".
   - For exemptions: "exemptions, discounts, residents, taxis, low-income".

4) Broaden/validate context using get_related_topics (limit: 10) on the candidate page. Identify up to two related titles that are either:
   - An alternative canonical program page (e.g., Singapore’s "Electronic Road Pricing" vs a generic congestion pricing page), or
   - A closely linked topic likely to include performance metrics (e.g., “Air quality in [City]”, "Road pricing", or a specific zone name such as "Area C").
   For each selected related title, get_summary and then summarize_article_for_query with:
   - Query 1: "impacts on traffic, average speed, public transport ridership" (max_length: 220).
   - Query 2: "air pollution, NO2, PM, CO2 changes" (max_length: 220).
   Decision rule C: If a related topic appears to be the more specific or authoritative scheme page (e.g., contains a dedicated Operation/Effects section in its get_sections output), switch your primary canonical page to that title and re-run step 3 on it. Keep the former page as an alternate source in your notes.

5) Extract quantitative highlights using extract_key_facts twice on the canonical page:
   - Call 1: topic_within_article: "effects on traffic, speed, ridership, revenue, air pollution, equity"; count: 7.
   - Call 2: topic_within_article: "history, implementation timeline, political process, referendum"; count: 7.
   Use these to fill gaps and to cross-check figures found in step 3 and 4.

6) Mine additional linked evidence with get_links on the canonical page. From the returned links, select up to two that contain any of these substrings (case-insensitive): "air", "pollution", "emission", "NO2", "PM", "CO2", "safety", "crash", "collision". For each selected link title, run summarize_article_for_query with query: "effects attributable to the [city] congestion charge or pricing scheme" (max_length: 220). Use these snippets to cross-validate environmental/safety outcomes. If none match, skip this step for that city and note missing linked evidence.

7) Conflict detection and resolution loop: For any critical metric (traffic change, average speed change, ridership change, notable air pollutant change, and revenue amount) where multiple values are found across the canonical page, related topics, or linked pages:
   - Record all distinct figures found and their associated article titles.
   - If values clearly refer to different timeframes (e.g., initial year vs later period) based on the summaries, keep both and annotate timeframe context if the text indicates it.
   - If timeframe is unclear, present the range (min–max) and list the article titles. Do not guess.

dependency_analysis:
Inherent tool-chain dependencies:
- search_wikipedia -> get_article/get_summary: Search yields candidate titles; these titles are the only valid inputs for subsequent content retrieval tools.
- get_article/get_sections -> summarize_article_section: Section summarization requires knowledge of existing section titles; thus sections must be fetched first.
- get_article/get_summary -> summarize_article_for_query: The tailored summarization requires a known title to target extraction relevant to specific themes when sections are absent or insufficient.
- get_article -> extract_key_facts: Key facts extraction requires a resolved title; used to enrich and cross-check quantitative details.
- get_article -> get_related_topics/get_links: Related topics and links depend on an established article title to broaden and validate the evidence base.

Scenario-based dependencies designed for this task:
- Title resolution decision (Decision rule A): Multiple search queries per city are executed sequentially until a high-fidelity candidate is found; the chosen title controls all downstream calls for that city.
- Structure-driven branching (Decision rule B): After get_sections, the presence or absence of critical sections determines whether to use summarize_article_section (preferred) or summarize_article_for_query (fallback). Missing sections trigger targeted queries to fill specific thematic gaps (charge structure, zone/hours, impacts, air quality, revenue, exemptions).
- Canonical page switching (Decision rule C): get_related_topics is used to detect a more specific or authoritative page (e.g., Singapore’s Electronic Road Pricing). If found, the pipeline rebinds the canonical title and re-executes structural analysis (get_sections -> summarize_article_section) and fact extraction, ensuring the most relevant source underpins the dataset.
- Cross-validation loop: For each city, results from the canonical page are cross-checked against (a) selected related topics via summarize_article_for_query and (b) targeted linked pages identified by get_links (filtered by environmental/safety substrings). Conflicting values are reconciled by recording ranges and attributing each figure to its source title, avoiding unsupported synthesis.
- Iterative completeness fallback: If any required field remains missing after the main and related/linked-page passes, a secondary search_wikipedia call is issued with a composite query (city + missing theme). The best match’s article is retrieved and summarized for the specific missing dimension, ensuring maximal coverage using only Wikipedia data.

Parallel vs. sequential execution:
- Per-city workflows can be run in parallel conceptually, but each city’s internal pipeline is strictly sequential: search -> title selection -> article/summary -> sections -> section summaries or query-based summaries -> related topics discovery and validation -> key facts extraction -> link mining -> conflict resolution -> completeness fallback.
- Aggregation (cross-city ranking and synthesis) occurs only after all per-city pipelines complete.

Critical decision points:
- Title selection from search results (quality and specificity) controls all downstream steps.
- Section availability dictates whether to use section-based or query-based summarization.
- Related topics may supersede the initial canonical article; if so, the pipeline must repeat structural analysis on the new title.
- Link-based evidence is conditionally included only if link titles match environment/safety substrings, ensuring relevance.
- Conflicting metrics trigger a data reconciliation process (record ranges and attribute sources) rather than forced selection.

Cross-server considerations:
- Only one server (Wikipedia) is available in this task; therefore, no cross-server data flow is applicable. All cross-validation is intra-server, conducted via related topics and linked pages within Wikipedia.

Data flow summary:
- Inputs: Fixed city names and explicit search query lists (per-city) with specified limits and max_length parameters.
- Transformations: Section-first extraction when possible; targeted thematic summarization when not; key fact extraction for quantitative enrichment; related/linked page summarization for validation; conflict resolution to handle discrepancies; fallback searches for missing fields.
- Outputs: Structured, attributed city profiles and a synthesized cross-city comparison, strictly derived from the chained Wikipedia tool calls.

1. **Initial Discovery Phase**: Search Wikipedia for each of these three writing systems: 'Cuneiform', 'Oracle bone script', and 'Egyptian hieroglyphs'. For each search, identify the most relevant primary article title from the results.

2. **Structural Analysis Phase**: For each of the three primary articles identified, retrieve the full section listings. Compare the structural organization of these articles and identify which sections deal with (a) origins/history, (b) characteristics/structure of the script, and (c) decline or replacement by later scripts.

3. **Deep Dive Phase**: For each of the three writing systems, summarize the section that covers the origins or earliest history of the script (use the section titles discovered in Step 2). Also summarize the section covering the structural characteristics or how the script works. Use a max_length of 200 for each summary.

4. **Key Facts Extraction**: Extract exactly 7 key facts from each of the three writing system articles, focused on the topic 'historical significance and cultural impact'. This gives 21 facts total.

5. **Cross-Reference Investigation**: From each of the three primary articles, retrieve the related topics (limit 15 each). Identify any topics that appear as related to MORE than one of the three writing systems — these represent shared cultural or historical connections. For each such shared topic found (up to 3), get a summary of that shared topic's Wikipedia article.

6. **Material and Medium Analysis**: For each writing system, use the summarize_article_for_query tool to extract information specifically about the physical materials and tools used for writing (e.g., clay tablets for cuneiform, papyrus for hieroglyphs, turtle shells for oracle bones). Use the query 'writing materials tools medium surface' with max_length 300 for each.

7. **Chronological Comparison**: Use the summarize_article_for_query tool on each of the three articles with the query 'dates chronology when first appeared earliest examples timeline period century BCE' (max_length 250) to establish precise dating for each system.

8. **Synthesis and Final Output**: Compile all findings into a structured comparative report with these sections:
   - **Timeline Table**: Which writing system appeared first, second, and third, with approximate dates
   - **Origins Comparison**: How each system originated (independently invented vs. influenced by others)
   - **Structural Comparison**: Key differences in how each script encodes language (logographic, syllabic, etc.)
   - **Material Culture**: What physical media each used and how that shaped their preservation
   - **Shared Connections**: What related topics or themes link these writing systems together
   - **Legacy Assessment**: A ranked assessment of which system had the most far-reaching impact on subsequent writing systems, supported by the extracted facts

task_description:

Analyze the overlap — identify any related topics that appear in the related topics lists of two or more of the three games. These shared connections represent cross-cultural intersections in board game history.

5. DEEP DIVE ON SHARED TOPICS: For any related topic that appears in at least two of the three games' related topic lists, get the summary of that shared topic's Wikipedia article. If no topics overlap, instead search for 'abstract strategy game' and 'mind sport', get summaries of both, and use the summarize_article_for_query tool to extract information specifically about how these concepts connect Go, Mancala, and Chess.

task_description:

STEP 3: Get the links from the Copernicus article to identify scientists he influenced. From those links, identify at least THREE key figures who further developed heliocentric theory (such as Galileo, Kepler, or similar). 

STEP 4: For each identified successor scientist, obtain their Wikipedia articles and extract key facts about their contributions to astronomy or the heliocentric model. Cross-reference by getting related topics from each of these articles.

task_description:

Objective:

Required workflow (execute in the exact sequence, including all branches where conditions are met):

1) Discovery (verification via search):
- Use Wikipedia:search_wikipedia for each query below (limit = 5) to confirm article existence and surface alternatives; record top match per query:
  - "Containerization"
  - "Intermodal container"
  - "Malcolm McLean"
  - "Twenty-foot equivalent unit"
  - "Port of Singapore"
  - "Port of Rotterdam"

2) Section mapping for targeted themes (per selected article):

- Use only the specified queries and articles; all decisions must be based on tool outputs.
- Ensure every conditional branch is evaluated; perform fallbacks where specified.

The agent must map theme labels (History, Impact, Logistics, Environmental, Urban, Economy) to actual section titles. Only then can summarize_article_section be called correctly. If the desired theme sections are missing in port articles, the agent must branch to get_related_topics and then apply summarize_article_for_query on those related titles, injecting the appropriate query string based on topic relevance.
3) Fact extraction enables parameterized analysis: extract_key_facts requires a title and topic_within_article; the chosen topic key (e.g., "supply chain efficiency" or "urban development and capacity (TEU)") depends on which article is being processed. These facts are later combined with section summaries.
4) Links-driven branching: get_links on "Containerization" and port articles determines whether we directly summarize related concepts (Just-in-time manufacturing, Lean manufacturing, Free trade zone, Transshipment). If the link is present, we call get_summary directly; if absent, we must fall back to search_wikipedia before summarizing. Thus, link presence/absence controls the subsequent tool usage and parameters.
5) Cross-validation loop for TEU: The agent must run summarize_article_for_query on both "Twenty-foot equivalent unit" and "Intermodal container" with targeted queries. If the resulting summaries show inconsistency (as assessed by the agent), an iterative refinement is triggered: extract_key_facts on both articles focusing on "TEU standard" to resolve discrepancies. This is an explicit dependency where one tool’s outputs (summaries) determine whether further tool calls (extract_key_facts) are necessary.

Parallel vs sequential:
- Discovery (search_wikipedia) for all queries can be parallel. However, selection of titles must be performed per query before get_article.
- Section mapping and summarization are sequential per article: get_sections must precede summarize_article_section, and missing-section detection must precede get_related_topics and summarize_article_for_query.
- Links-driven exploration per article follows get_links; the branch (direct summary vs search fallback) is sequentially dependent on link presence.
- Cross-validation requires sequential calls: two summarize_article_for_query calls precede the decision to run extract_key_facts for clarification.

Cross-server dependencies:
- Not applicable: all tools operate on the Wikipedia server. Cross-validation and fallbacks are implemented within the single server through inter-tool dependencies (search, sections, related topics, links, summaries, facts).

Data flow overview:
- Inputs: Concrete query strings and target article themes specified in the task.
- Flow: search_wikipedia → get_article → get_sections → summarize_article_section; missing-section branch: get_related_topics → summarize_article_for_query; topic-focused facts: extract_key_facts; link-driven branch: get_links → (get_summary or search_wikipedia → get_summary); TEU cross-validation: summarize_article_for_query (two articles) → (optional) extract_key_facts.
- Outputs: The agent synthesizes all tool-derived content into a structured briefing, clearly attributing insights to titles and sections, and documenting branch decisions and consistency checks.

task_description:
Goal: Produce a cross-validated synthesis on human health effects and policy responses related to microplastics by mining and triangulating multiple Wikipedia articles. Deliverable: A structured report with (1) a list of canonical articles selected, (2) section-level summaries tailored to health and policy, (3) verification of policy linkages across pages, (4) intersection of related topics between two core articles, and (5) two triangulated lists: top 5 human health effects and top 5 regulatory measures that appear in at least two distinct articles. All findings must be derived exclusively via the provided Wikipedia tools.

Scope and fixed inputs:
- Initial search queries (use exactly these terms):
  1) "Microplastics"
  2) "Plastic pollution"
  3) "Microbeads"
  4) "Microbead-Free Waters Act"
  5) "Great Pacific garbage patch"
  6) "Nanoplastic"
- Selection thresholds and counts:
  - search_wikipedia limit per query: 5
  - section summarization max_length: 200
  - tailored summarization max_length: 250
  - extract_key_facts count: 7 for primary articles (Microplastics, Microbeads, Microbead-Free Waters Act), 5 for related topics
  - related topics limit: 10 (for each of two core articles)
  - Intersection sampling: up to 3 topics from the intersection, selected by relevance rules below
  - Triangulation requirement: Include an item in a final list only if it is supported by at least 2 different articles’ summaries or key facts collected in this workflow
  - Keywords for section discovery: for health: ["Health", "Human", "Toxicology", "Exposure"]; for policy: ["Policy", "Legislation", "Regulation", "Ban", "Law"]

Step-by-step procedure (tools and decisions are mandatory):
1) Identify canonical articles via search and summary triage:
   - For each of the 6 queries above, call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with limit=5.
   - Selection rule: Choose the top result whose title contains the query term (case-insensitive). If none, choose the first result.
   - For each selected title, call Wikipedia:get_summary.
   - Relevance triage: Mark a title as primary to this study if its summary mentions any of: "health", "human", "toxic", "exposure", "policy", "regulation", "ban", "legislation". Record all selected titles regardless of triage outcome, but indicate which are primary.

2) Deep-dive on three focal articles (expected: Microplastics, Microbeads, Microbead-Free Waters Act):
   - For each focal title, call Wikipedia:get_sections.
   - For each focal title, attempt to call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section on up to two sections:
     a) One health-related section: pick the first section whose title contains any of the health keywords.
     b) One policy-related section: pick the first section whose title contains any of the policy keywords.
     - If a relevant section is not found for a given topic (health or policy), fall back to Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query respectively set to "human health effects of [TITLE]" or "policy and regulation of [TITLE]" (replace [TITLE] with the article’s title). Use max_length per spec.
   - For Microplastics and Microbeads, call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with count=7 and topic_within_article = "human health effects".
   - For Microbead-Free Waters Act (or its closest matching legislative article), call Wikipedia:get_article once to obtain full content, then call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with count=7 and topic_within_article = "provisions, scope, enforcement, exemptions".

3) Validate policy linkages across pages (cross-verification):
   - For "Microplastics" and for "Microbeads", call Wikipedia:get_links. Check if any link title contains the substring "Microbead-Free Waters Act" (case-insensitive). If yes, record that a direct policy linkage exists in links.
   - If not found via get_links, call Wikipedia:get_related_topics on the same article. Check if any related topic title contains "Microbead-Free Waters Act". If found, record that an indirect policy linkage exists via related topics.
   - If neither links nor related topics contain the Act, then call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="Microbead-Free Waters Act" and limit=5 and select the top matching title per the rule in Step 1. Record that a policy page linkage required search fallback.

4) Related topics intersection (context expansion):
   - Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics for "Microplastics" with limit=10.
   - Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics for "Plastic pollution" with limit=10.
   - Compute the intersection of titles (case-insensitive match). If the intersection is empty, expand the second set by calling Wikipedia:get_links on "Plastic pollution" and union those titles with its related topics, then recompute intersection with "Microplastics" related topics.
   - From the final intersection, select up to 3 topics with this priority: titles containing any of ["Nanoplastic", "Marine debris", "Marine life", "Human exposure", "Toxicology"]. If fewer than 3 match, fill remaining slots with any available intersecting titles.
   - For each selected intersecting topic: call Wikipedia:get_summary and Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with count=5 and topic_within_article = "health or ecological impacts".

5) Environmental comparison context (macro vs micro):
   - For the title selected for "Great Pacific garbage patch", call Wikipedia:get_sections.
   - Attempt Wikipedia:summarize_article_section for a section whose title contains any of ["Environmental", "Impact", "Ecology"]. If none, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="environmental impacts and ecological consequences".
   - Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with count=5 and topic_within_article = "environmental impacts" for this article.

6) Triangulate top 5 health effects and top 5 regulatory measures across articles:
   - Candidate pool for health effects: combine all health-focused summaries and key facts from: Microplastics, Microbeads, and the selected intersecting topics.
   - Candidate pool for regulatory measures: combine policy-focused summaries and key facts from: Microplastics, Microbeads, Microbead-Free Waters Act, and any intersecting topics that include policy content.
   - Deduplicate items by concept label (string match ignoring case; the agent must normalize similar phrases, e.g., "endocrine disruption" vs "hormone disruption").
   - Include an item in the final health list only if it appears (explicitly or via clear synonym) in at least 2 distinct articles among the pool above. Select the top 5 by frequency of occurrence; if ties, prefer items present in Microplastics and Microbeads.
   - Include an item in the final regulatory list only if it appears in at least 2 distinct articles among the policy pool; prefer items corroborated by the legislative article. Select the top 5 by frequency; if ties, prefer items that are bans or restrictions.
   - If fewer than 5 health items meet the threshold, add items from the "Nanoplastic" summary/key facts (if present in the intersecting topics). If still fewer than 5, call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="Human exposure to microplastics" (limit=5), select per Step 1, then call Wikipedia:get_summary and Wikipedia:extract_key_facts (count=5, topic_within_article="human health effects") and retry triangulation.
   - If fewer than 5 regulatory items meet the threshold, include additional policy measures from Microbeads and Microplastics policy-focused summaries even if present in only 1 article, but clearly label them as "single-source" in the final output.

7) Final report structure (expected output format):
   - Provide a structured text report with these sections:
     a) Canonical titles selected: list all 6 queries with the final chosen titles; mark which were primary (per Step 1 triage).
     b) Section summaries: for each focal article (Microplastics, Microbeads, Microbead-Free Waters Act), present the health and policy summaries used, indicating whether they came from summarize_article_section or summarize_article_for_query and naming the section when applicable.
     c) Policy linkage validation: for Microplastics and Microbeads, state whether the Act was found via get_links, get_related_topics, or via search fallback.
     d) Related topics intersection: list the two related-topics sets, the computed intersection, the 3 selected topics, and include each of their summaries and 3–5 key facts.
     e) Macro vs micro context: provide the Great Pacific garbage patch impact summary and 3–5 key facts, noting contrasts with microplastics health-focused content.
     f) Triangulated lists: two lists each with up to 5 items. For each item, cite the supporting article titles (minimum 2 for inclusion, unless marked single-source per the fallback), and include one-sentence rationale.
   - Ensure all claims in the final lists point back to specific article titles included in this workflow.
dependency_analysis:
Inherent tool chains and data flow:
- search_wikipedia → get_summary: Use search results to select canonical article titles; summaries support quick relevance triage and prevent fetching irrelevant full content.
- get_sections → summarize_article_section vs summarize_article_for_query: The presence of a relevant section title determines whether to summarize a specific section or to request a tailored article-wide summary. This creates a branching dependency based on section availability.
- get_article → extract_key_facts: For legislative content (e.g., Microbead-Free Waters Act), full article content improves fact extraction fidelity; extract_key_facts then distills provisions/scope/enforcement details.
- get_links/get_related_topics: Validate inter-article policy linkages discovered in focal pages; if neither confirms linkage, trigger a fallback search_wikipedia call to explicitly locate the legislative article.
- get_related_topics (two cores) → intersection → get_summary/extract_key_facts: Related topic sets from Microplastics and Plastic pollution are intersected to identify shared context; the intersecting topics are then summarized and mined for key facts.

Scenario-based dependencies and decision points:
- Decision 1 (Title selection): For each query, pick a canonical title based on the search result title containing the query term; downstream calls (get_summary, get_sections, etc.) depend on this selection. If titles deviate (e.g., Microbead-Free Waters Act variants), summaries help confirm the fit.
- Decision 2 (Section availability): After get_sections, if a health or policy section exists, use summarize_article_section; else, use summarize_article_for_query with tailored queries. This enforces adaptive summarization paths.
- Decision 3 (Policy linkage validation): get_links is attempted first for direct linkage; if absent, get_related_topics checks indirect linkage. If still absent, a search_wikipedia fallback locates the legislative article, ensuring coverage despite missing links.
- Decision 4 (Related topics intersection): If the intersection of related topics between Microplastics and Plastic pollution is empty, the workflow expands context by unioning Plastic pollution links with its related topics, then recomputes the intersection, ensuring adequate topic selection for context expansion.
- Decision 5 (Triangulation thresholds): The inclusion of health effects and regulatory measures requires support from at least two distinct articles. If health items are insufficient, the workflow conditionally brings in Nanoplastic or searches for a human exposure-focused page to meet the threshold. If policy items are insufficient, single-source items are allowed but must be labeled, enforcing transparent evidence standards.

Parallel vs sequential execution:
- Parallel: Initial searches for the six queries and their get_summary calls can run in parallel. Related topics retrieval for the two core articles can run in parallel before intersection. Summaries and key facts extraction for the selected intersecting topics can also proceed in parallel.
- Sequential: Title selection must precede section discovery and summarization. The policy linkage validation must follow selection of Microplastics and Microbeads titles. The related topics intersection requires completion of both cores’ related topics retrieval. Triangulation occurs after all summaries/key facts are collected.

Cross-server considerations:
- All tools are on the Wikipedia server; there are no cross-server dependencies. However, cross-tool validation within the same server is used extensively: summaries are validated against section-based summaries; policy linkages are cross-checked via links, related topics, and fallback searches to ensure robustness.

Critical data flows that enforce tool dependency understanding:
- Section-aware summarization requires get_sections outputs to route to either summarize_article_section or summarize_article_for_query.
- Legislative detail extraction requires get_article prior to extract_key_facts to ensure sufficient content for accurate fact distillation.
- Intersection-based topic selection depends on the outputs of get_related_topics from two distinct titles; subsequent summarization and fact extraction are conditioned on that set.
- Triangulation logic depends on aggregating outputs from multiple tools (summaries, section summaries, extracted facts) to enforce multi-article corroboration before inclusion, demonstrating iterative and conditional reasoning across tool outputs.

task_description:
Research the history and global spread of coffee cultivation, then compare it with the history of tea cultivation, to produce a detailed comparative report on how these two beverages shaped global trade networks.

Step-by-step requirements:

1. **Initial Search Phase**: Search Wikipedia for 'history of coffee' and 'history of tea' to identify the most relevant article titles for each beverage.

2. **Article Structure Analysis**: For the top article found for each beverage (coffee and tea), retrieve the full section listings. Identify sections related to: (a) origins/discovery, (b) spread/global cultivation, (c) economic/trade impact, and (d) cultural significance.

3. **Deep Dive - Coffee**: From the coffee history article, extract:
   - A summary of the section on coffee's origins (likely Ethiopia/Yemen)
   - A summary of the section on coffee's spread to Europe and the Americas
   - Key facts (at least 5) focused on 'trade and economics'
   - Related topics from the coffee article (limit 10) to identify any linked articles about specific coffee trade routes, the East India Company, or colonial trade

4. **Deep Dive - Tea**: From the tea history article, extract:
   - A summary of the section on tea's origins (likely China)
   - A summary of the section on tea's spread to Britain and other regions
   - Key facts (at least 5) focused on 'trade and economics'
   - Related topics from the tea article (limit 10) to identify linked articles about the tea trade, Opium Wars, or Boston Tea Party

5. **Cross-Reference Investigation**: From the related topics discovered in steps 3 and 4, identify at least TWO articles that appear connected to BOTH coffee and tea trade history (e.g., East India Company, colonialism, global trade). For each such cross-cutting article:
   - Get a query-tailored summary focused on 'role in coffee and tea trade'
   - Extract 3 key facts about how this entity/event connected coffee and tea commerce

6. **Parallel Comparison - Cultural Dimensions**: Search Wikipedia for 'coffee culture' and 'tea culture'. For each:
   - Get the article summary
   - Get links from each article
   - Identify if there are any overlapping linked articles between coffee culture and tea culture (shared cultural phenomena)

7. **Final Synthesis**: Using all gathered information, produce a structured comparative report with the following sections:
   - **Origins**: Where and when each beverage was first cultivated/consumed
   - **Global Spread Timeline**: Key milestones in how each beverage spread globally
   - **Trade Impact**: How each beverage influenced colonial trade, economic systems, and global commerce (with specific facts from the key facts extraction)
   - **Cultural Significance**: How coffee and tea cultures differ and overlap
   - **Interconnections**: Historical events or entities that linked both beverages' trade histories
   - **Key Differences & Similarities**: A bullet-point summary of at least 5 major differences and 3 major similarities

The final report should cite specific facts gathered from Wikipedia articles and clearly distinguish between information sourced from different articles.
dependency_analysis:
This task creates a rich dependency graph across multiple tool chains:

**Primary Tool Chains:**
1. search_wikipedia → get_sections → summarize_article_section (repeated for both coffee and tea - sequential dependency where search results determine article titles, which determine available sections, which determine summarization targets)
2. search_wikipedia → extract_key_facts (search determines titles for fact extraction)
3. search_wikipedia → get_related_topics → get_article/summarize_article_for_query (related topics from one article feed into new article retrievals - iterative discovery)
4. search_wikipedia → get_summary + get_links (parallel operations on culture articles)

**Critical Decision Points:**
- After initial search: agent must select the BEST article title from search results (not just the first)
- After get_sections: agent must MAP section titles to the four categories (origins, spread, economics, culture) - sections won't have exact names, requiring interpretation
- After get_related_topics for BOTH beverages: agent must perform SET INTERSECTION to find cross-cutting articles that relate to both coffee AND tea trade - this is a data transformation step
- After get_links on culture articles: another set intersection to find overlapping cultural links

**Parallel vs Sequential:**
- Coffee and tea deep dives (steps 3-4) can run in parallel but both must complete before step 5 (cross-reference) can begin
- Within each deep dive, get_sections must precede summarize_article_section, but extract_key_facts and get_related_topics can run in parallel
- Step 6 (cultural comparison) is independent of steps 3-5 and can run in parallel

**Data Flow Complexity:**
- search results → article titles (string extraction)
- article titles → section lists (structural analysis)
- section lists → section titles for summarization (semantic matching)
- related topics from TWO articles → intersection analysis → new article titles → tailored summaries (multi-hop reasoning)
- All accumulated data → final synthesis (aggregation across 15+ tool calls)

**Estimated minimum tool calls: ~25-30** including: 4 searches, 4 get_sections, 8+ summarize_article_section, 2 extract_key_facts (coffee + tea), 2 get_related_topics, 2+ summarize_article_for_query (cross-cutting), 2+ extract_key_facts (cross-cutting), 2 get_summary (culture), 2 get_links (culture)

task_description:
Goal: Produce a rigorous, tool-driven decision brief comparing three tobacco control measures for adoption in the upcoming 12 months. Measures to analyze: (1) Plain packaging of tobacco products, (2) Tobacco advertising bans, (3) Tobacco excise taxation. Use only the provided Wikipedia tools and follow the exact workflow and decision rules below. Deliver a structured output and a methodology log.

Context and Output Requirements:
- Audience: Public health policy steering committee preparing a 12‑month rollout plan.
- Deliverable: A structured policy brief with the following top-level sections per measure and overall summary:
  1) For each measure (three measures total):
     - measure_name
     - article_title (the exact Wikipedia title used)
     - effectiveness_summary (≤ 180 words from section-based or query-based summaries)
     - criticisms_summary (≤ 180 words)
     - implementation_notes (≤ 180 words)
     - key_facts (exactly 7 concise bullet points from extract_key_facts)
     - related_topics (up to 5 items, each as {title, one-sentence summary})
     - country_case_notes (2 items where available, each as {country_title, 1–2 sentence note})
     - unintended_consequences (optional; include if Electronic cigarette is detected, ≤ 120 words)
     - scoring: {effectiveness_score, implementation_challenge_score, public_acceptance_score, legal_risk_score, composite_score, consistency_flag}
  2) Overall recommendations:
     - priority_rank (listing the three measures from highest to lowest composite_score)
     - recommended_package (top 2 measures with justification in ≤ 200 words)
     - 12_month_rollout_plan for the recommended_package with three phases:
       • months_1_3: legislative_preparation actions (3 bullets)
       • months_4_6: adoption_and_regulations actions (3 bullets)
       • months_7_12: enforcement_and_monitoring actions (3 bullets)
  3) methodology_log: Chronological list of tool calls with parameters and decision points taken (inputs and the reason for each branch/fallback), including counts (e.g., how many sections matched, how many related topics selected, country links found).

Fixed Inputs and Targets (do not change):
- Measures and search queries:
  • Plain packaging of tobacco products → search query: "Plain packaging of tobacco products"
  • Tobacco advertising bans → search query: "Tobacco advertising"
  • Tobacco excise taxation → search query: "Tobacco tax"
- search_wikipedia parameters: limit = 5 for each query. Selection rule: choose the result whose title exactly matches the query (case-insensitive). If no exact match, choose the top result returned.
- Section targeting rules (case-insensitive substring match on section titles from get_sections):
  • For effectiveness_summary, acceptable section title keywords: ["Effect", "Impact", "Effectiveness"]
  • For criticisms_summary: ["Critic", "Opposition", "Controversy"]
  • For implementation_notes: ["Implementation", "Policy", "Enforcement"]
  When multiple sections match, choose the one with the most specific match (longest title containing the keyword). If no section matches for a category, use summarize_article_for_query with the following query strings:
  • effectiveness_summary fallback query: "evidence of effectiveness"
  • criticisms_summary fallback query: "criticisms and controversies"
  • implementation_notes fallback query: "implementation and enforcement challenges"
  Use max_length = 180 for all summarize calls used to populate these three summaries.
- Key facts extraction: extract_key_facts with count = 7 and topic_within_article = "effectiveness and health outcomes". If fewer than 7 facts are returned, note in methodology_log and proceed with returned facts (do not re-try).
- Related topics enrichment:
  • Preferred whitelist titles to include if present in get_related_topics (limit = 10): ["Framework Convention on Tobacco Control", "Smoking ban", "Health effects of tobacco", "Nicotine", "Electronic cigarette", "Secondhand smoke"].
  • Select up to 5 items from the whitelist that appear in get_related_topics results (order by the order provided in the whitelist). For each selected title, call get_summary and store as related_topics.
  • If fewer than 3 whitelist items are found in get_related_topics, call get_links on the measure’s main article and attempt to find remaining whitelist titles in the link list; for each found, call get_summary. Stop once you have up to 5 related topics total.
- Country case notes (per measure):
  • From get_links on the main article, select titles that contain any of the following country names (case-insensitive substring): ["Australia", "United Kingdom", "France", "Uruguay", "Thailand", "Philippines", "South Africa", "New Zealand", "Canada", "Ireland"].
  • If at least 2 country titles are found, pick the first 2 alphabetically and for each call summarize_article_for_query with query = "tobacco control and policy" and max_length = 120. Save as {country_title, note}.
  • If fewer than 2 country titles are found, call summarize_article_for_query on title = "Tobacco control" with query = "country case studies on [MEASURE TITLE]" and max_length = 150. Use up to 2 distinct bullet notes drawn from that summary (split into two concise points). Document the fallback in methodology_log.
- Unintended consequences trigger:
  • If either get_related_topics or get_links includes a title matching "Electronic cigarette", call get_summary on title = "Electronic cigarette" and include an unintended_consequences section (≤ 120 words) tailored to the measure (e.g., potential shift to vaping). If not present, omit this section.
- Scoring rules (exact text mining rules against the concatenated effectiveness_summary + criticisms_summary):
  • effectiveness_score (0–100):
    - If text contains any of ["significant reduction", "strong evidence", "effective"], set 85.
    - Else if contains any of ["mixed evidence", "limited evidence"], set 60.
    - Else if contains any of ["no evidence", "ineffective"], set 35.
    - Else set 70.
  • implementation_challenge_score (0–100; higher = harder):
    - If text contains any of ["legal challenge", "lawsuit", "trade dispute"], set 80.
    - Else if contains any of ["industry opposition", "lobbying", "enforcement difficulty"], set 65.
    - Else set 40.
  • public_acceptance_score (0–100; higher = more resistance):
    - If text contains any of ["controversy", "public backlash"], set 60.
    - Else set 30.
  • legal_risk_score (0–100; higher = riskier):
    - If text contains any of ["court", "WTO", "ISDS", "intellectual property"], set 75.
    - Else set 35.
  • composite_score = 0.5*effectiveness_score - 0.2*implementation_challenge_score - 0.1*public_acceptance_score - 0.2*legal_risk_score. Round to nearest integer and clamp to [0, 100].
  • consistency_flag: If any key_facts item contains "no evidence" or "insufficient evidence" while effectiveness_summary contains any of ["strong evidence", "significant reduction", "effective"], set to "review"; otherwise "ok".
- Recommendation and rollout:
  • priority_rank: order measures by composite_score (descending). Break ties alphabetically by measure_name.
  • recommended_package: top 2 measures with a ≤ 200-word justification referencing at least one related_topic title and at least one country_case_note per measure.
  • 12_month_rollout_plan: three phases with 3 bullets each; derive actions from implementation_notes (e.g., draft regulations, stakeholder consultation, enforcement training, public communication, monitoring indicators). Use relative time phrasing: months_1_3, months_4_6, months_7_12.

Strict Workflow (execute in this order for each measure):
1) Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with the fixed query and limit=5; select title per rule above.
2) Wikipedia:get_article on the selected title (store raw text for internal analysis).
3) Wikipedia:get_sections on the same title.
4) For each of the three categories (effectiveness, criticisms, implementation):
   - If a matching section exists per keyword rules, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section (max_length=180).
   - Else call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query (max_length=180) with the specified fallback query string.
5) Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with count=7 and topic_within_article="effectiveness and health outcomes".
6) Wikipedia:get_related_topics with limit=10; select from whitelist; call Wikipedia:get_summary for each selected title; if fewer than 3, call Wikipedia:get_links and attempt to find additional whitelist titles; call Wikipedia:get_summary for each new title until you have up to 5.
7) Wikipedia:get_links on the measure article; filter for country titles per list; if ≥2 found, for each of the first 2 alphabetically call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="tobacco control and policy" (max_length=120). If <2 found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on title="Tobacco control" with query="country case studies on [MEASURE TITLE]" (max_length=150) and extract up to 2 concise bullet notes.
8) If "Electronic cigarette" appears in related topics or links, call Wikipedia:get_summary on title="Electronic cigarette" and include unintended_consequences.
9) Compute scores and composite_score using the exact rules above; set consistency_flag per rule.
10) Repeat steps 1–9 for all three measures; then build priority_rank, recommended_package, and 12_month_rollout_plan as specified.

Final Output Format (JSON-like fields; do not include raw article text):
- measures: [
  {measure_name, article_title, effectiveness_summary, criticisms_summary, implementation_notes, key_facts: [7 strings], related_topics: [{title, summary}], country_case_notes: [{country_title, note}], unintended_consequences (optional), scoring: {effectiveness_score, implementation_challenge_score, public_acceptance_score, legal_risk_score, composite_score, consistency_flag}}
]
- priority_rank: [measure_name in order]
- recommended_package: {measures: [top_two_names], justification}
- 12_month_rollout_plan: {months_1_3: [3 bullets], months_4_6: [3 bullets], months_7_12: [3 bullets]}
- methodology_log: [{step_number, tool, params, decision_note} ...]
