task_description:
Build a cross-article evidence matrix and network synthesis on the topic of microplastic pollution pathways and mitigation using only the provided Wikipedia tools. Follow the exact sequence, decisions, thresholds, and fallbacks below to ensure comprehensive coverage and heavy tool usage.

Goal: Identify 8 highly relevant Wikipedia articles (exactly 8), categorize them into 3 groups (overview, pathway/transport, mitigation/policy), extract targeted section summaries and key facts, compute the inter-article link network to identify a hub article, detect at least one quantitative contradiction across articles if present, and propose research gaps based on underrepresented related topics.

Strict tool usage sequence and decisions:
1) Candidate discovery (Wikipedia:search_wikipedia)
   - Execute all of the following queries with limit=10 for each query; aggregate and dedupe titles across queries:
     • "Microplastics"
     • "Plastic pollution"
     • "Marine debris"
     • "Great Pacific Garbage Patch"
     • "Nurdle"
     • "Microbead"
     • "Single-use plastic"
     • "Plastic bag ban"
     • "Wastewater treatment"
     • "Wastewater treatment plant"
     • "Microfiber pollution"
     • "Ocean gyre"
     • "Stormwater"
     • "Extended producer responsibility"
   - From the deduped pool, compute a relevance score per title:
     • +2 points if the title contains any of: microplastic, plastic, debris, nurdle, microbead, gyre, wastewater, stormwater, microfiber, single-use, bag ban, policy, regulation.
     • If tie-breaking is needed later, you will use link-based centrality (see step 6), but continue to step 2 first.

2) Rapid screening and categorization (Wikipedia:get_summary)
   - For the top 15 titles by score (or all titles if fewer than 15 exist), call Wikipedia:get_summary.
   - Categorize each title into exactly one of three buckets using the summary text and these heuristics (case-insensitive):
     • Overview: summary mentions microplastics, plastic pollution, or marine debris in a broad, general sense (terms like "type of pollution", "widespread", "environmental issue").
     • Pathway/Transport: summary mentions transport terms such as wastewater, stormwater, river, runoff, ocean gyre, currents, textile microfibers, or pathways into aquatic systems.
     • Mitigation/Policy: summary mentions ban, policy, regulation, removal, treatment, control measures, recycling, or governance.
   - Select exactly 8 articles total with category quotas: 2 Overview, 3 Pathway/Transport, 3 Mitigation/Policy. Prefer higher relevance scores. If a category lacks enough candidates:
     • Fallback round A: For the best available Overview article (choose the one with the highest relevance score), call Wikipedia:get_related_topics (limit=10). From the returned topics, pick the first two that, by their titles, plausibly match the missing category (based on keyword heuristics above) and then call Wikipedia:get_summary on those to confirm categorization. Add as needed.
     • Fallback round B: If still short, perform Wikipedia:get_related_topics (limit=10) on the best Pathway/Transport article and repeat the above logic.
     • Stop after two fallback rounds. If still short, proceed with fewer in that category but fill the total of 8 by promoting next best titles by relevance score regardless of category.

3) Section targeting (Wikipedia:get_sections -> Wikipedia:summarize_article_section and fallback Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query)
   - For each of the 8 selected articles, call Wikipedia:get_sections to obtain available sections.
   - For each article, you must capture at least 3 targeted section summaries (max_length=180 each). Use the following priority list of section titles (case-insensitive match; use exact titles if they exist):
     • Primary candidates: "Sources", "Pathways", "Transport", "Environmental impact", "Effects", "Mitigation", "Policy", "Case studies", "Regulation", "Remediation", "Health effects".
     • If a primary candidate is present, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section for that section.
     • If fewer than 3 primary sections are present, fill remaining slots using the fallback method: call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with queries chosen from: "sources of microplastics", "pathways and transport", "mitigation and policy" (choose the ones not already covered). Use max_length=200 for these fallback summaries.
   - Record which method you used per section (section summary vs query-based summary) to show the dependency decision.

4) Key fact extraction (Wikipedia:extract_key_facts)
   - For each selected article, call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with count=4 and topic_within_article set according to the category:
     • Overview: topic_within_article="scope and definitions of microplastics and plastic pollution".
     • Pathway/Transport: topic_within_article="sources and transport pathways into aquatic systems".
     • Mitigation/Policy: topic_within_article="removal, mitigation measures, and policy instruments".
   - Store the 4 extracted key facts per article.

5) Link graph and related topics (Wikipedia:get_links and Wikipedia:get_related_topics)
   - For each of the 8 articles:
     • Call Wikipedia:get_links and count: total_links and cross_links_to_selected (links that exactly match any of the other 7 selected article titles). Store both counts.
     • Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics (limit=10) and store the top 5 related topics per article.
   - Determine the network hub article among the 8 as follows:
     • Primary criterion: the article with the maximum cross_links_to_selected.
     • Tie-breaker 1: the article with the greatest total_links.
     • Tie-breaker 2: if still tied, the article with the highest initial relevance score from step 1.

6) Deep dive on the hub (Wikipedia:get_article)
   - For the hub article only, retrieve its full content via Wikipedia:get_article. Use this full content to:
     • Verify whether there are additional numeric claims about quantities relevant to microplastics/plastic pollution (e.g., tonnes per year entering oceans, removal efficiencies, size estimates).
     • If you find new numeric claims that were not captured in prior summaries, include them in the contradiction check in step 7.

7) Quantitative contradiction detection (Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query across multiple titles)
   - Target variable A: annual quantity of plastic entering oceans (often reported in "million tonnes per year").
     • On each of these titles (if present among your 8, otherwise use the closest substitutes you selected): "Plastic pollution", "Marine debris", and either "Microplastics" or the hub article, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="tonnes per year" (max_length=200). Extract any specific numeric values mentioned.
     • If at least two numeric values are found and the relative difference between the minimum and maximum exceeds 20%, record a contradiction (store both values, the titles, and the query context). If the difference is 20% or less, record as consistent.
   - Fallback variable B (if fewer than two numeric values found for A): estimate of the size of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.
     • Call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on "Great Pacific Garbage Patch" (if among your 8; if not, call it anyway for this step) with query="square kilometres OR km^2" (max_length=200), and also on either "Marine debris" or the hub article with query="Great Pacific Garbage Patch estimate". If at least two numeric values are found and they differ by more than 20%, record a contradiction; otherwise record as consistent.

8) Research gaps and opportunities (using related topics)
   - Compute topic frequency: compile all related topics (top 5 per article) and count how many of your 8 articles list each topic. Identify at least 3 topics that:
     • Appear in the related topics of the hub article, and
     • Appear in the related topics of fewer than 2 other selected articles.
   - Output these 3+ topics as research gaps, explaining why expanding coverage/linkage could improve understanding of pathways or mitigation.

Output format: Return a single JSON object with these keys (and only these):
- selected_articles: array of 8 objects, each with:
  • title (string)
  • category (one of: "Overview", "Pathway/Transport", "Mitigation/Policy")
  • sections_summary: array of up to 3 objects, each with: { method: "section"|"query", section_title_or_query: string, summary: string }
  • key_facts: array of 4 strings
  • related_topics: array of 5 strings
  • link_counts: { total_links: integer, cross_links_to_selected: integer }
- hub_article: { title: string, reason: string }
- contradiction_report: { target_variable: "annual tonnes to oceans"|"GPGP size", status: "contradiction"|"consistent"|"insufficient data", details: array of objects each with { article: string, query: string, extracted_text: string, numeric_value_and_units: string } }
- research_gaps: array of at least 3 objects, each with { topic: string, rationale: string }

Important constraints:
- Use every listed Wikipedia tool at least once as specified above.
- Enforce all numeric thresholds and decision rules (8 articles total; section summary count per article >=3 with fallbacks; key facts count=4; related topics top 5; contradiction threshold=20%).
- Deduplicate titles strictly by exact title string.
- Do not introduce any external sources or files; all information must come from the provided tools.
- If a step’s fallback condition is triggered, clearly indicate in the output where fallbacks were used (in method fields and in reasoning strings).
dependency_analysis:
Inherent tool relationships and data flow:
- search_wikipedia → get_summary: Search results produce candidate titles; summaries are required to screen and categorize them. This enforces a sequential dependency where summaries cannot be obtained without titles from search.
- get_summary → selection quotas: Categorization logic relies on content from summaries, which then determines which titles advance. The chosen set of 8 articles is thus dependent on get_summary outputs.
- get_sections → summarize_article_section: Section listing is a prerequisite to summarizing specific sections. If a section exists, summarize_article_section targets it directly.
- get_sections absence → summarize_article_for_query: When required sections are missing, the fallback query-based summarization depends on the lack of desired sections in get_sections, making a branching dependency.
- extract_key_facts depends on prior categorization: topic_within_article is set by the category assigned from get_summary, creating a parameter dependency.
- get_links and get_related_topics depend on the final set of selected titles: link metrics and related topics can only be computed after selection, influencing the network analysis and later expansion decisions.
- get_links outputs cross-reference other selected titles to compute cross_links_to_selected and determine the hub; therefore, link analysis is contingent on the selected set and requires iterating through all link lists.
- get_related_topics outputs feed two ways: (a) earlier, as fallbacks to fill category quotas (rounds A/B), and (b) later, to compute research gaps by topic frequency. This creates iterative and multi-stage dependencies on the same tool.
- get_article (full content) is only invoked for the hub, which is determined post link analysis; thus, the hub deep-dive strictly depends on the results of get_links.
- summarize_article_for_query is reused for contradiction detection, driven by the hub identification and the presence/absence of numbers found in summaries and the full article text.

Critical decision points and branches:
- Candidate shortfalls: If any category lacks enough titles, the workflow branches to get_related_topics on the best Overview (then Pathway) articles, followed by get_summary on those related titles to refill quotas. This is an iterative fallback loop with a bounded number of expansions (two rounds).
- Section presence: If target sections are present (from get_sections), use summarize_article_section; else fallback to summarize_article_for_query. Each article must meet a minimum of three summaries, enforcing iteration until satisfied.
- Hub selection: Computes cross_links_to_selected using get_links across the selected set. In case of ties, break using total_links, then initial relevance score. The hub choice controls whether get_article is called and which articles are used for contradiction checks.
- Contradiction checks: Primary variable is annual tonnes entering oceans. If insufficient numeric values are found, branch to fallback variable (GPGP size). The outcome can be contradiction, consistent, or insufficient data, depending on numeric extraction results.

Parallel vs sequential:
- Search and initial summaries can be run in parallel per query/title, but selection quotas require a sequential aggregation phase to finalize the 8 articles.
- For each selected article, section discovery, section/query summarization, key fact extraction, and related topics retrieval can run in parallel per article; however, hub determination via link cross-count requires all get_links results collected first.
- Contradiction detection is sequentially downstream of hub identification and may also leverage new numeric claims discovered after get_article on the hub.

Cross-server dependencies:
- All tools reside on the single Wikipedia server in this scenario; thus, no cross-server logic applies. However, intra-server cross-validation is implemented by comparing multiple articles’ numeric claims (using summarize_article_for_query) and by using get_links and get_related_topics to validate relevance and centrality.

Data transformations and re-use:
- Title deduplication and relevance scoring transform search outputs into a ranked candidate set.
- Summaries are categorized via keyword heuristics to set parameters for extract_key_facts and to enforce quotas.
- Section lists are filtered by a priority map to drive which sections to summarize, and missing sections trigger query-based summarization.
- Link lists are intersected with the selected title set to compute cross-links, enabling hub selection.
- Numeric values extracted from query-based summaries are compared with a 20% threshold to classify contradictions.

Overall, the task demands a deep, interdependent chain of calls: search → summarize → categorize → (fallback via related topics) → sections → section/query summaries → key facts → links/related topics → hub selection → full article retrieval → quantitative contradiction analysis → research gaps. Each stage constrains the next, ensuring the task cannot be completed without understanding and orchestrating these tool dependencies.

dependency_analysis:
This task requires an extensive sequential and branching dependency chain using only the Wikipedia server tools:

**PRIMARY DEPENDENCY CHAIN (Sequential Flow):**

2. extract_key_facts('Silk Road') → outputs commodities/cities that determine focus areas

- Branch B: Islamic Golden Age

  - Cross-validation: Check if 'House of Wisdom' is related topic → conditional research
  
- Branch C: Spice Trade

**CONVERGENCE POINT:**

task_description:
Build a research-grade comparative briefing on four gene-modification/biotech modalities: CRISPR, Zinc finger nucleases, Transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs), and RNA interference. Produce a structured report that integrates mechanism, applications, history, ethical/regulatory issues, and cross-linked topic context from Wikipedia only. Use only the provided tools and concrete parameters below. Follow these steps precisely and exhaustively, including all decision points and fallbacks:

Core topics and keyword filters:
- Core technology queries: "CRISPR", "Zinc finger nuclease", "Transcription activator-like effector nuclease", "RNA interference"
- Mechanism-related keywords: mechanism, working principle, mode of action
- Application-related keywords: application, use, uses
- History-related keywords: history, background, development
- Ethics/Regulatory keywords for related topics filtering: ethic, controversy, controversies, regulation, patent, moratorium, governance, policy

Section A – Canonical title identification (sequential; per technology):
1) For each core query (limit = 5), call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia.
2) For each returned candidate title, call Wikipedia:get_summary and select the article whose summary indicates the intended technology. Use these selection rules:
   - CRISPR: prefer a summary mentioning gene editing/genome editing. If multiple, prefer the title with "CRISPR" or "CRISPR gene editing" in the title.
   - Zinc finger nuclease: prefer a summary containing "nuclease" and gene/genome editing.
   - Transcription activator-like effector nuclease: prefer a summary mentioning TALEN(s) and gene/genome editing.
   - RNA interference: prefer a summary mentioning gene silencing/post-transcriptional gene regulation.
   If multiple candidates still qualify, choose the one with the most specific technology focus (avoid organism-specific or unrelated uses) by comparing summaries.

Section B – Section discovery and targeted summarization (sequential with branching; per technology):
3) Call Wikipedia:get_sections on the chosen title.
4) For each of the four topical buckets below, try to locate the best-matching section title using case-insensitive substring match with the indicated synonyms:
   - Mechanism bucket: any of ["Mechanism", "Mechanism of action", "Working principle", "Mode of action"]
   - Applications bucket: any of ["Applications", "Uses", "Usage"]
   - History bucket: any of ["History", "Background", "Development"]
   - Ethics/Regulatory bucket: any of ["Ethics", "Ethical", "Controvers", "Regulation", "Regulatory", "Policy", "Governance"]
5) For each bucket where a matching section_title is found, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with max_length = 200. If no matching section is found in a bucket, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with:
   - query = "<bucket name> of <chosen title>" (e.g., "Mechanism of CRISPR")
   - max_length = 220
   Capture which path was used (section vs query) for later source reporting.

Section C – Key facts extraction with topic focus (multiple calls; per technology):
6) Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts on the chosen title to extract focused facts for three subtopics:
   - topic_within_article = "clinical and therapeutic applications"; count = 5
   - topic_within_article = "delivery methods and limitations"; count = 5
   - topic_within_article = "notable controversies and ethical concerns"; count = 5
   Record the facts per subtopic.

Section D – Related topics triangulation and expansion (parallelizable within each technology; structured branching):
7) Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics with limit = 15 for the chosen title.
8) Filter the returned related topics to those whose titles contain any of the ethics/regulatory keywords (case-insensitive). If 3 or more matches exist, keep the top 3 as they appear; if fewer than 3 match, supplement by calling Wikipedia:get_links on the chosen title and selecting up to 3 items from the links whose titles contain ethics/regulatory keywords. If still fewer than 3, fill remaining slots (up to 3) using the first items from get_related_topics not yet chosen.
9) For each of the up to 3 selected related topics, call Wikipedia:get_summary and keep a 2–3 sentence abstract focused on ethics/regulation/controversy.

Section E – Cross-article verification and contradiction check (sequential; per technology):
10) Call Wikipedia:get_article on the chosen title. For each "notable controversies and ethical concerns" fact extracted in step 6, verify that the full article contains language consistent with the claim (e.g., mentions of the controversy pattern, ethics debate, bans, moratoria, regulatory actions). If you cannot locate supporting language in the full article, mark the fact as "unverified in main article" and attempt to corroborate by checking the summaries gathered in step 9. If still unverified, flag as "potentially unsupported" in the final report.

Section F – Cross-technology synthesis (after completing A–E for all four technologies):
11) Build a comparative matrix with rows for CRISPR, Zinc finger nucleases, TALENs, and RNA interference, and columns for:
   - Mechanism (1–2 sentences)
   - Primary applications (3 bullets)
   - First major milestone year mentioned in history (extract the earliest year mentioned in the History bucket summary or, if absent, from the full article text)
   - Notable controversies (2 bullets), each labeled as verified, corroborated via related topic summary, or potentially unsupported as per step 10
12) Identify cross-cutting ethical/regulatory themes that recur in at least 2 technologies (e.g., off-target risk debates, germline-editing concerns, intellectual property disputes, clinical trial governance). Support each theme with at least one short quote or paraphrase from either a section summary or a related-topic summary, and note the source title.

Deliverable and formatting requirements:
- Provide a structured report with the following sections:
  - Executive summary (200–300 words) comparing the four technologies.
  - Technology profiles: one subsection per technology containing: confirmed article title; mechanism summary; applications summary; history summary; ethics/regulatory summary; 3×5 key facts grouped by subtopic with verification tags (verified/corroborated/potentially unsupported).
  - Comparative matrix (as text-based table or bullet grid), listing the four rows and four columns specified in step 11.
  - Ethics/regulatory themes across technologies with supporting citations (title and whether from section summary, related-topic summary, or full article).
  - Sources used: for each technology, list:
    - Selected article title
    - Which sections were summarized (names) or whether query-based summaries were used
    - Up to 3 related topics used with their titles
- Constraints:
  - Use only the provided tools to gather content.
  - Adhere to the decision rules and fallbacks exactly.
  - Do not include any external URLs or references beyond Wikipedia tool outputs.
  - All search queries and parameters are specified above; do not request additional input.
dependency_analysis:
INHERENT DEPENDENCIES AND WORKFLOW:
- Search → Select → Fetch:
  - Wikipedia:search_wikipedia provides candidate titles. Its outputs feed directly into Wikipedia:get_summary to disambiguate and confirm the relevant article per technology. The confirmed title is then fed into downstream tools for section discovery, summarization, and analysis.
- Section-aware summarization:
  - Wikipedia:get_sections enumerates the article’s structure. Its result determines whether Wikipedia:summarize_article_section can be used (if a matching section exists) or whether to fall back to Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with a targeted prompt. This creates a conditional dependency where get_sections’ presence/absence of specific sections controls the next tool choice and parameters.
- Content extraction vs. full-text verification:
  - Wikipedia:extract_key_facts supplies distilled facts, optionally scoped by topic within the article. These facts must be verified against Wikipedia:get_article (full content) in a cross-check step. Thus, extract_key_facts output drives a verification loop that consumes get_article outputs to label each fact as verified/corroborated/potentially unsupported.
- Related topic triangulation:
  - Wikipedia:get_related_topics proposes related pages. These are cross-validated using Wikipedia:get_links (links within the article) to prioritize ethically/regulatorily relevant topics. Selected related topics then feed into Wikipedia:get_summary for short abstracts. Therefore, get_related_topics and get_links run in parallel and are combined through set overlap logic to determine which topics to expand.

SCENARIO-BASED DEPENDENCIES AND DECISION POINTS:
- Title disambiguation decision:
  - After search_wikipedia, multiple candidates may appear. get_summary content governs selection via technology-specific keyword filters. This is a critical early branch: incorrect selection cascades into irrelevant sections and facts.
- Section vs. query summarization branch:
  - get_sections output determines whether summarize_article_section is possible. If a relevant section is missing (e.g., no explicit "Ethics" heading), the agent must use summarize_article_for_query with bucket-specific queries. This ensures coverage despite inconsistent article structures.
- Related-topic selection logic with fallback:
  - If get_related_topics yields fewer than 3 ethics/regulatory items, the agent must use get_links as a fallback source to meet the quota. If still insufficient, the agent uses the remaining top related topics irrespective of keyword match. This introduces a multi-step decision chain driven by tool outputs.
- Verification and contradiction handling:
  - Facts extracted via extract_key_facts (especially controversies) are checked against get_article. If not corroborated in the full article, the agent must attempt corroboration via related-topic summaries (get_summary on chosen related topics). Failing that, the fact is flagged as potentially unsupported. This creates a multi-stage validation pipeline and classification based on tool outputs.
- Cross-technology synthesis dependency:
  - Comparative insights and shared ethical/regulatory themes depend on the successful aggregation of section/targeted summaries (from summarize_article_section or summarize_article_for_query), fact extraction (extract_key_facts), and related-topic summaries (get_summary). The earliest milestone year extraction depends on history summaries and, failing that, scanning the full article text (get_article).

PARALLEL VS SEQUENTIAL REQUIREMENTS:
- Sequential components:
  - For each technology: (search_wikipedia → get_summary selection) → get_sections → (summarize_article_section or summarize_article_for_query) → extract_key_facts → get_related_topics/get_links selection → get_summary of selected related topics → get_article verification.
  - Cross-technology synthesis (comparative matrix, shared themes) is strictly downstream of completing all per-technology pipelines.
- Parallelizable components:
  - For a given confirmed title, get_related_topics and get_links can be run in parallel. The same applies to running the entire A–E pipeline independently for each of the four technologies before the synthesis step.

CROSS-SERVER CONSIDERATIONS:
- All tools are under the Wikipedia server; cross-server dependencies are not applicable. However, cross-tool dependencies within the same server are explicitly orchestrated to simulate multi-source triangulation (get_related_topics vs get_links vs full-article verification and section summaries).

KEY TOOL CHAINS (EXEMPLARS):
- Chain 1 (disambiguation and confirmation): search_wikipedia → get_summary (iterate candidates) → choose title.
- Chain 2 (section-aware summarization): get_sections → [if section exists] summarize_article_section; [else] summarize_article_for_query.
- Chain 3 (fact extraction and verification): extract_key_facts (topic-focused) → get_article (confirm/contradict) → [if unverified] get_summary on related topics for corroboration.
- Chain 4 (topic triangulation): get_related_topics ↔ get_links (filter and intersect) → get_summary (on selected related topics).
- Chain 5 (synthesis): Aggregated outputs from Chains 2–4 feed into a comparative matrix and cross-cutting themes analysis.

CRITICAL DECISIONS AND ITERATIVE LOOPS:
- Iterative candidate evaluation after search_wikipedia using get_summary to pick the correct article per technology.
- Conditional summarization strategy decided by get_sections outcomes.
- Iterative verification loop for controversies: extracted facts → full-article scan → related-topic summaries → tagging of verification status.
- Topic selection loop: filtering get_related_topics with keyword rules, falling back to get_links, and fallback again to non-keyword matched related topics if needed.

These dependencies ensure the task cannot be completed without a deep understanding of how the Wikipedia tools interlock, when to branch between section-based and query-based summarization, how to triangulate related topics, and how to verify extracted facts using full-text and auxiliary summaries.

task_description:
Research synthesis task: Compare Bonsai, Penjing, and Saikei across origin, techniques, styles, species, and cultural philosophy, and construct a cross-link topic map, using only the provided Wikipedia tools in a dependency-driven workflow. Follow all steps and parameters precisely. Do not use any external resources.

Scope and goal:
- Produce a structured comparative report for a cultural education briefing contrasting three miniature tree arts: Bonsai (Japan), Penjing (China), and Saikei (Japan). Include a cross-link analysis to reveal shared and unique conceptual anchors.
- Required dimensions (cover all five): historic origin, styles classification, shaping/wiring techniques, common tree species used, and cultural/aesthetic philosophy.
- Use every Wikipedia tool at least once in the specified chains. Respect decision points and fallbacks.

Canonical targets (determine via search):
- Primary search terms: "Bonsai", "Penjing", "Saikei" (see Step 1 for limits and selection rules).

Exact workflow and parameters:
1) Identify canonical article titles (search_wikipedia):
   - For each search term in ["Bonsai", "Penjing", "Saikei"], call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with limit=5.
   - Selection rule: Choose the top result whose title exactly matches the search term if present; otherwise choose the top result most semantically aligned with the term (e.g., likely the core article for the concept). Record the chosen titles.

2) Fetch core content and summaries for each chosen title (get_article and get_summary):
   - For each of the 3 titles, call Wikipedia:get_article to retrieve full content.
   - Also call Wikipedia:get_summary to capture a high-level synopsis.

3) Discover available sections to drive conditional extraction (get_sections):
   - For each article, call Wikipedia:get_sections.
   - Target sections to look for (case-insensitive match): "History", "Techniques", "Styles", "Aesthetics", "Species".

4) Section-first extraction with fallback to query summarization (summarize_article_section or summarize_article_for_query):
   - For each article and each target dimension:
     - If the corresponding section exists, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with max_length=200 using the exact section title as returned by get_sections.
     - If no matching section exists, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query set to the dimension keyword (exact strings: "history", "techniques", "styles", "aesthetics", "common tree species used") and max_length=250.
   - Record for each dimension which tool was used (section vs. query) for provenance.

5) Extract key facts to ensure coverage (extract_key_facts):
   - For each article, call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts twice with count=7:
     - Once with topic_within_article="origin and philosophy".
     - Once with topic_within_article="techniques and styles".
   - Use these to corroborate or fill gaps in step 4’s dimension summaries.

6) Build topic relationship sets (get_related_topics and get_links):
   - For each article:
     - Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics with limit=15.
     - Call Wikipedia:get_links to list internal links.
   - If get_related_topics returns fewer than 5 items for any article, supplement by extracting additional candidates from get_links (choose the first 10 links that appear to be concept/topic pages rather than disambiguations based on title cues; document your selection rationale).

7) Cross-link analysis and overlap computation:
   - Compute the intersection of the three related-topic sets (after supplementation if applicable). Identify the top 5 overlapping topics by frequency and centrality (use counts across articles as primary metric; if tied, use presence in get_sections summaries or key facts as a tiebreaker).
   - Compute the top 3 unique topics for each article not appearing in the other two articles’ related-topic sets (use frequency within that article’s links as a tiebreaker if needed).
   - Decision point for Saikei classification: If the Saikei article’s related-topic set includes both "Bonsai" and "Penjing" (exact title match or redirect-equivalent in the results), classify Saikei as a hybrid tradition; otherwise classify it as a distinct tradition.

8) Species coverage validation and enrichment (summarize_article_for_query + get_links):
   - For each article, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="common tree species used" and max_length=250 if not already done in step 4.

     - If fewer than 3 are found, use the article’s get_links output to identify botanical pages (heuristic cues: Latin binomials or genus names with initial capitalized Latin; e.g., "Juniperus", "Acer palmatum"). Extract up to 5 likely species/genera and incorporate them as a supplemental species list. Document the selection and rationale.

9) Targeted contextual expansion for shared anchors (search_wikipedia + get_summary):
   - From the top 5 overlapping topics found in step 7, select exactly 2 that are not purely geographic labels. If fewer than 2 non-geographic topics exist, choose as many as available and supplement with the next most frequent non-geographic links from any one article’s get_links.
   - For each selected topic, call Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with limit=3 to confirm the canonical page, then call Wikipedia:get_summary on the chosen top result. These will become "Context Boxes" in the final report.

10) Final consistency check and gap fill (extract_key_facts fallback):
   - For any article and dimension where both section and query-based summaries are thin or inconclusive (e.g., fewer than 2 concrete claims), call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with count=10 and topic_within_article set to the related dimension (e.g., "history", "styles", "techniques", "aesthetics", or "species"). Use these to strengthen that dimension.

Expected output format (structured text):

- Comparative Analysis by Dimension (for each of the five dimensions, present bullet lists for Bonsai, Penjing, Saikei):

  - Common Tree Species Used (include at least 3 per tradition; indicate any species obtained via link-based enrichment)
  - Cultural/Aesthetic Philosophy
  - For each bullet list, annotate the provenance tool used (e.g., "section summary", "query summary", "key facts").
- Cross-Link Topic Map Summary:
  - Top 5 overlapping topics across all three (with brief one-line relevance each).
  - Top 3 unique topics per tradition with one-line relevance.
- Context Boxes (two):
  - For each selected overlapping topic, include a 3–5 sentence summary synthesized from Wikipedia:get_summary and corroborated by any relevant key facts from earlier steps.
- Appendix:
  - Canonical article titles chosen for each tradition.
  - Sections detected per article (from get_sections).
  - Tool call log per dimension (which tools were used and why, including fallbacks and decision outcomes such as Saikei classification).

Hard constraints:
- Use only the specified Wikipedia tools. No browsing or external datasets.
- Execute all decision points and fallbacks exactly as stated.
- Use all nine tools at least once across the workflow.
- Keep all thresholds and limits as specified (search limits, max_length, counts).
- Provide clear documentation of reasoning at each decision point in the Appendix.
dependency_analysis:
Inherent and scenario-driven tool dependencies designed for maximal inter-tool reliance:

Key tool chains and data flow:
- Discovery chain: Wikipedia:search_wikipedia → Wikipedia:get_article + Wikipedia:get_summary. The search step determines canonical titles; those titles are mandatory inputs for all subsequent per-article operations.
- Section-driven extraction: Wikipedia:get_sections → (branch) Wikipedia:summarize_article_section OR Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query. Section availability dictates which summarization tool is used per dimension. The summarization outputs feed the comparative analysis and are cross-validated by key facts.
- Corroboration and gap-fill: Wikipedia:extract_key_facts supplements or replaces information when section/query summaries are missing or too sparse. This tool is explicitly invoked after initial summaries to enhance coverage, establishing a dependency of the analysis quality on multiple tool outputs.
- Topic mapping: Wikipedia:get_related_topics and Wikipedia:get_links run in parallel per article. Related topics are the primary source for overlap and uniqueness computations; get_links provides a fallback/supplementation source when related topics are insufficient and also powers species enrichment.
- Expansion chain: Cross-article intersection computations (based on get_related_topics supplemented by get_links) select exactly two anchors for deeper context. Those anchors trigger a new use of Wikipedia:search_wikipedia (to confirm canonical titles) → Wikipedia:get_summary for contextual boxes, creating a second-level dependency where results of cross-link analysis determine additional tool calls.

Critical decision points:
- Canonical title selection: If exact match is found in search results, use it; otherwise select the top semantically aligned article. All subsequent tool calls depend on this title-choosing decision.
- Section presence per dimension: If get_sections includes a matching section (e.g., History), use summarize_article_section; else use summarize_article_for_query with a dimension-specific query. This conditional branch is the primary content acquisition decision.
- Related topics sufficiency: If get_related_topics results < 5, then supplement from get_links by curating conceptually relevant links. This decision impacts the integrity of the topic map and subsequent overlap computation.
- Saikei classification: If Saikei’s related topics include both Bonsai and Penjing, classify as hybrid; else distinct. This affects the Executive Summary and Comparative Analysis framing.
- Species coverage adequacy: If fewer than 3 species/genera are identified in summaries, use get_links to mine botanical pages (heuristics applied by the agent). This affects the completeness of the species dimension.
- Context anchor selection: From the computed overlaps, choose 2 non-geographic topics to expand; if insufficient, fallback to non-geographic links by frequency. This controls the second-level search and summary chain.
- Final gap check: If any dimension remains thin (e.g., <2 concrete claims), escalate with extract_key_facts count=10 targeted to that dimension to ensure completeness.

Parallel vs sequential requirements:
- Sequential: Title resolution via search must precede all article-specific calls. Section discovery must precede the choice between section summarization and query summarization. Overlap computations must await completion of all related-topics and links fetches for all three articles.
- Parallel: For each of the three core articles, fetching article content, summary, sections, related topics, and links can be performed in parallel once titles are fixed. Extract_key_facts can also be parallelized per article after initial summaries.

Cross-server dependencies:
- All tools belong to the Wikipedia server; there are no cross-server dependencies. Cross-tool dependencies within the single server are maximized by chaining search → article/summary → sections → section/query summaries → key facts → related topics/links → overlap-driven expansions.

Data flow consolidation patterns:
- Multi-source corroboration: Dimension content is synthesized from section summaries, query-based summaries, and key facts, with explicit provenance recorded.
- Set operations: Intersections and differences on related-topic sets (supplemented by links when needed) drive both the classification decision and the selection of expansion topics.
- Iterative enrichment: Insufficient results at several steps trigger controlled fallbacks (e.g., links supplementing related topics; key facts supplementing thin sections; link-mined species supplementing sparse species summaries), forming iterative loops that guarantee coverage while maintaining strict tool usage patterns.

task_description:
Research the history of deep-sea exploration and develop a comprehensive analysis of the technological evolution that enabled humans to explore the ocean's deepest regions. 

Specifically, you must:

1. Begin by searching Wikipedia for articles on "Deep-sea exploration" to identify the key milestones and pioneers
2. Search for and gather information on the three pioneering figures of deep-sea exploration: William Beebe, Otis Barton, and Jacques Piccard - each representing different eras and contributions
3. For each pioneer, extract key facts about their major contributions and the vessels/submersibles they developed or used
4. Identify the submersibles and vessels mentioned (e.g., Bathyscaphe Trieste, Bathysphere) and get detailed information about each
5. Extract technical specifications and depth records for these vessels
6. Find the related topics and links for Bathyscaphe Trieste to understand the technological lineage and subsequent developments
7. Get the sections for key articles to identify the chronological structure of deep-sea exploration history
8. Cross-validate the depth records by comparing information across multiple articles (Beebe's Bathysphere record vs. Trieste's record)
9. Identify and research one unexpected connection you discover through the related topics or links
10. Compile a final comprehensive report with:
    - Chronological timeline of major depth records (first 1000m, 2000m, 3000m, 6000m, 10,000m milestones)
    - Technical specifications comparison table for the key submersibles
    - Key technological innovations that enabled each depth milestone
    - Names and nationalities of all scientists/explorers mentioned
    - Final verification of the deepest human dive record with source validation

This task requires following the data trail carefully: search results inform which articles to fetch, fetched articles reveal vessel names that require further investigation, and cross-references between articles enable validation of critical facts.
dependency_analysis:

1. search_wikipedia('Deep-sea exploration') → identifies key article titles and pioneer names
2. get_article('William Beebe') + get_article('Otis Barton') + get_article('Jacques Piccard') → parallel fetches for three pioneering figures
3. extract_key_facts for each pioneer → extracts vessel names as input for next step
4. get_article for each vessel (Bathysphere, Bathyscaphe Trieste) → fetches technical specifications
5. get_related_topics for Bathyscaphe Trieste → discovers subsequent developments and related technology
6. get_sections for major articles → provides structure for timeline compilation
7. Cross-validation: compare depth records from get_article outputs to verify consistency

**DECISION BRANCHES:**
- The search results will determine which specific submersible articles to fetch next
- Related topics from Trieste will reveal unexpected connections to explore (decision point)
- Depth record discrepancies between articles trigger cross-validation analysis

**PARALLEL REQUIREMENTS:**
- Three pioneer articles can be fetched simultaneously
- Multiple vessel specifications can be gathered in parallel once identified
- Link extraction and related topics can run concurrently for different articles

**DATA FLOW PATTERN:**
Text search results → Named entities → Full articles → Technical specifications → Cross-references → Related topics → Unexpected discovery → Final synthesis

**CROSS-VALIDATION REQUIREMENT:**
The task explicitly requires comparing depth records from multiple sources (Beebe's 1930 record vs. Trieste's 1960 record) to verify accuracy, necessitating parallel tool calls whose outputs must be compared.

task_description:
Goal: Build a rigorously cross-validated comparative profile of three sign languages—American Sign Language (ASL), British Sign Language (BSL), and Auslan—using only Wikipedia tools. Produce structured findings with sources (Wikipedia article titles only), identify gaps, and reconcile classification and intelligibility claims through iterative cross-checks.

Languages and primary pages to target:
- "American Sign Language"
- "British Sign Language"
- "Auslan"

Target metrics to extract for each language (collect all that are available):
- ISO 639-3 code
- Classification/family and historical influences (e.g., French Sign Language family, BANZSL lineage)
- Manual alphabet type (one-handed vs two-handed; note regional variants if stated)
- Estimated number of signers (include the numeric estimate and the year/context if present)
- Official recognition status and key legal acts (summarize statutes and the jurisdiction)
- Notable linguistic features: at least one phonology or grammar feature (e.g., non-manual markers, typical word order)
- Dialects/varieties mentioned

Cross-language analysis requirements:
- Determine likely mutual intelligibility relationships among the trio, with justification:
  - BSL ↔ Auslan
  - ASL ↔ BSL
  - ASL ↔ Auslan
- Identify at least 5 and up to 10 topics that are common links across all three main articles and briefly explain what their overlap suggests about shared concepts (e.g., common mechanisms like fingerspelling, shared historical nodes, or typical linguistic constructs). If common links across all three are fewer than 5, supplement by including intersections that appear in at least two of the three and justify why they matter.
- Cross-validate family classification claims via related topics and additional pages if needed.

Strict tool-driven workflow (follow in sequence, with specified fallbacks and decision points):
1) Primary article discovery (per language):
   - Use Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with the exact language name. From the results, choose the result whose title exactly matches the target or is the most canonical (e.g., "American Sign Language" for ASL). If multiple close matches, prefer the one with the plain language name rather than a subtopic.
   - Use Wikipedia:get_article on the chosen title.
   - Use Wikipedia:get_sections to list section titles for targeted extraction.

2) Section-targeted summaries (per language):
   - For each of these section title candidates (case-insensitive): ["History", "Status", "Recognition", "Manual alphabet", "Fingerspelling", "Phonology", "Grammar", "Dialects", "Varieties", "Vocabulary", "Mutual intelligibility"], check whether the exact or closely matching title exists in the list from get_sections.
   - For every matching section, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_section with max_length=200.
   - If neither "Manual alphabet" nor "Fingerspelling" is present as a section, call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on the main article with query="manual alphabet fingerspelling one-handed two-handed" and max_length=180.

3) Key fact extraction and numeric capture (per language):
   - Call Wikipedia:extract_key_facts with title=<language>, topic_within_article="classification family, origin, manual alphabet, number of signers, recognition status, ISO 639-3 code", count=7.
   - If fewer than 2 distinct numeric facts are observed for signers or recognition years (e.g., you cannot find any explicit number of signers or any date/year tied to recognition) in either the extracted key facts or section summaries, then call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query again with query="speakers signers estimate year recognition official status law act" and max_length=220.

4) Links and related topics capture (per language):
   - Call Wikipedia:get_links on the main article; store the set of link titles.
   - Call Wikipedia:get_related_topics with limit=10 on the main article.

5) Family and origin cross-validation (cross-language, using prior outputs):
   - From related topics (step 4) and links (step 4), look for any of: "BANZSL", "French Sign Language", "Old French Sign Language", "British, Australian and New Zealand Sign Language".
   - For every such topic found for any of the languages, call Wikipedia:get_summary for that topic to capture a concise classification definition.
   - Decision point A (consistency check):
     - If "BANZSL" appears in related topics or links for BSL but not for Auslan (or vice versa), then run Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with queries "BANZSL Auslan" and/or "BANZSL British Sign Language" (limit=10) and open the most relevant result with Wikipedia:get_article, then call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="classification family member languages" max_length=180 to confirm whether both BSL and Auslan are members.
   - Decision point B (ASL origin check):
     - If "French Sign Language" or "Old French Sign Language" is not found in ASL’s links but classification claims indicate French influence, run Wikipedia:search_wikipedia with query="ASL origins French Sign Language" (limit=10). Open the most plausible result (Wikipedia:get_article) and call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query with query="origin influence" max_length=150 to capture origin evidence.

6) Common-link intersection and supplemental topics:
   - Compute the intersection of link title sets from step 4 across ASL, BSL, and Auslan. Select up to the top 10 common titles.
   - If the intersection yields fewer than 5 common titles, augment by finding topics that appear in at least two of the three link sets that are clearly relevant to sign language typology or practice (e.g., "Fingerspelling", "Manual alphabet", "Non-manual feature"). For each chosen supplemental topic, call Wikipedia:get_summary to include a concise definition in the report.

7) Mutual intelligibility determination (reasoned from collected evidence):
   - If both BSL and Auslan show membership in BANZSL via sections, key facts, or cross-validated pages, set their mutual intelligibility to "high/probable" with justification.
   - If ASL shows French Sign Language lineage and BSL/Auslan show BANZSL, set ASL↔BSL and ASL↔Auslan intelligibility to "low" unless direct evidence suggests otherwise.
   - If conflicting statements are discovered (e.g., a summary suggests higher mutual intelligibility where another suggests low), call Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query on the relevant main articles with queries of the form "intelligibility with <other language name>" (e.g., for ASL, query="intelligibility with British Sign Language") with max_length=150 to gather clarifying evidence. Resolve conflicts by preferring more specific statements (e.g., explicit lexical similarity percentages or explicit intelligibility claims) over general remarks.

8) Output assembly and quality flags:
   - Compile a structured JSON result with the following top-level fields:
     - languages: an array of three objects, one per language, each containing:
       - name
       - iso_639_3 (if available)
       - family (text)
       - influences (array of strings)
       - manual_alphabet_type (one-handed, two-handed, mixed/variant, or unknown)
       - number_of_signers_estimate (number as string, plus context/year in parentheses if present)
       - recognition_status_summary (1–3 sentences)
       - notable_features (1–3 bullet-like strings)
       - dialects_or_varieties (array of strings if available)
       - sources (array of Wikipedia page titles used for these data)
     - shared_topics: array of up to 10 common linked titles across all three languages; if fewer than 5, include a supplemental array of up to 5 intersection-in-two titles with one-sentence summaries (from get_summary) and a note that they appear in two of three.
     - mutual_intelligibility: object with keys "BSL_Auslan", "ASL_BSL", "ASL_Auslan"; each value includes a level (e.g., high/probable, low, uncertain) and a one-sentence justification citing page titles.
     - classification_cross_validation: list of checks performed (e.g., BANZSL presence across pages, French Sign Language origin confirmation) with the outcome of each and the titles consulted.
     - data_quality_flags: per-language notes on missing fields and which fallback paths were taken (e.g., "manual alphabet derived via summarize_article_for_query due to missing section").
   - Ensure each data point includes at least one source title from Wikipedia:get_article, Wikipedia:summarize_article_section, Wikipedia:get_summary, or Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query outputs you used.

Operational thresholds and constraints to follow:
- When choosing sections, match case-insensitively and accept close variants (e.g., "Status and recognition" counts for both "Status" and "Recognition").
- Numeric sufficiency rule: if fewer than 2 numeric facts (e.g., a signer estimate and at least one year tied to recognition or a demographic source) are available after extraction and section summaries, trigger the specified summarize_article_for_query fallback.
- Common link threshold: aim for at least 5 truly common linked titles across all three; if not achievable, apply the supplemental strategy described.
- Keep max_length exactly as specified in steps for summarize calls.
- Favor the most explicit/precise statements when reconciling conflicts. If two conflicting claims persist after all fallbacks, report both with their respective source titles and mark the field as "conflicting" in data_quality_flags.

Time-sensitivity and recency:
- If multiple recognition acts or policy changes are listed, prefer the most recent statements (within the past 10–15 years when dates are available in the text). If recency cannot be determined from the text, do not guess; simply report the explicit items you find.

All data must be derived solely from the specified Wikipedia tools. Do not use URLs or any external systems. Do not request additional input. Execute all steps and decision branches as specified.
dependency_analysis:
Inherent tool dependencies and workflow: The task leverages a search→fetch→analyze pattern. Wikipedia:search_wikipedia identifies the canonical article per language. Wikipedia:get_article retrieves full content for downstream analysis. Wikipedia:get_sections enumerates available section titles, enabling targeted calls to Wikipedia:summarize_article_section. When section coverage is incomplete, Wikipedia:summarize_article_for_query is used to extract focused content from the whole article. Wikipedia:extract_key_facts surfaces structured facts (codes, family, counts), complementing section summaries. Wikipedia:get_links provides link sets for network intersections across languages, while Wikipedia:get_related_topics supplies conceptually linked topics for classification validation. Wikipedia:get_summary supplies concise definitions for auxiliary or cross-validated topics (e.g., BANZSL, French Sign Language).

Scenario-based dependencies and decision points:
- Section-driven branching: get_sections dictates which summarize_article_section calls are made; absence of key sections triggers summarize_article_for_query with targeted queries (manual alphabet, recognition status, signers).
- Numeric sufficiency rule: If extract_key_facts and section summaries yield fewer than 2 numeric facts (signer estimates and/or recognition years), the agent must call summarize_article_for_query again with a specific query to hunt for missing quantitative details.
- Classification cross-validation loop: Outputs from get_related_topics and get_links influence whether to call get_summary on BANZSL or French Sign Language and, if inconsistencies appear (e.g., BANZSL linked for BSL but not for Auslan), trigger additional search_wikipedia calls ("BANZSL Auslan", "BANZSL British Sign Language") followed by get_article and summarize_article_for_query on the found pages to confirm membership. Similarly, lack of explicit ASL–French Sign Language linkage in links triggers a search for origin evidence and subsequent summarize_article_for_query.
- Common link intersection: Parallel get_links calls for ASL, BSL, and Auslan create three link sets whose intersection determines shared_topics. If the pure intersection falls below the 5-item threshold, the agent must branch to a supplemental path: select high-relevance topics that intersect in two of the three sets and consult get_summary for concise definitions.
- Mutual intelligibility determination: Cross-validated classification findings (e.g., BANZSL membership) and origin summaries inform conditional logic to label intelligibility levels. Conflicting evidence triggers additional summarize_article_for_query calls framed as intelligibility queries (e.g., "intelligibility with British Sign Language"), after which the agent reconciles by preferring more specific claims, or flags persistent conflicts.

Parallel vs sequential requirements:
- Sequential: For each language, the chain search_wikipedia → get_article → get_sections → summarize_article_section (conditional) → summarize_article_for_query (fallback) → extract_key_facts is sequential, as later steps depend on earlier outputs.
- Parallel: After primary per-language extraction, the agent can run get_links and get_related_topics in parallel for all three languages to build the intersection and related-topic pools; however, the subsequent intersection computation and cross-validation steps require all three link sets.
- Iterative loops: Cross-validation with BANZSL and French Sign Language involves iterative searching and summarizing until consistency is established or conflicts are recorded. Numeric sufficiency checks can trigger additional summarize_article_for_query calls iteratively until thresholds are met or the field is deemed unknown.

Data flow highlights:
- Section availability (get_sections) directly controls which summarize_article_section calls are valid and whether summarize_article_for_query must be invoked.
- extract_key_facts outcomes (presence/absence of numeric facts) control the need for additional summarize_article_for_query passes.
- get_links outputs from all three languages feed into a set-intersection operation; this result then governs whether supplemental get_summary calls on intersect-in-two topics are required.
- get_related_topics and get_links feed into the list of candidate classification pages (BANZSL, French Sign Language), whose summaries and, if needed, additional searched pages (via search_wikipedia → get_article → summarize_article_for_query) finalize the classification cross-check.

Cross-server considerations: All tools operate on the Wikipedia server. No cross-server sources are available; therefore, all cross-validation and fallback strategies are confined to Wikipedia’s toolset. The design still employs cross-article validation and intersection across multiple Wikipedia entries to emulate multi-source corroboration within the single server environment.

task_description:
A historian is preparing a comprehensive academic monograph on the Haitian Revolution (1791-1804) and requires systematic research across multiple dimensions. Your task is to conduct this research and compile a detailed analytical report.

PHASE 1 - FOUNDATIONAL RESEARCH:
1. Search for 'Haitian Revolution' and obtain the main article
2. Retrieve all sections of the article to understand its structure
3. Extract 8 key facts about the revolution's causes, progression, and outcome
4. Summarize the 'Background' section to understand the preconditions

PHASE 2 - KEY FIGURES ANALYSIS:
1. Use get_related_topics to discover major historical figures associated with the revolution
2. For each of the top 5 most significant figures identified, obtain:
   - A summary of their Wikipedia article
   - 5 key facts about their role in the revolution
   - A query-focused summary specifically about their contributions to Haitian independence

PHASE 3 - INTERNATIONAL DIPLOMATIC CONTEXT:
1. Get all links from the Haitian Revolution article
2. Identify articles related to international reactions from: France, Britain, Spain, and the United States
3. For each country's perspective, obtain targeted summaries about their diplomatic and military responses
4. Extract key facts about how each nation's involvement shaped the revolution's outcome

PHASE 4 - COMPARATIVE REVOLUTIONARY ANALYSIS:
1. Use get_related_topics to find connections to the American Revolution and French Revolution
2. Get summaries for both related revolution articles
3. Summarize specific sections comparing revolutionary methods, ideologies, and outcomes
4. Extract key facts about what made the Haitian Revolution unique among 18th-century revolutions

PHASE 5 - SYNTHESIS AND REPORT:
Compile all findings into a structured report containing:
- Timeline of the 10 most significant events (with dates and descriptions)
- Profiles of 5 key figures (name, role, key actions, historical significance)
- International reaction matrix (country, actions taken, impact on revolution)
- Comparative analysis table (Haitian vs American vs French revolutions)
- Assessment of the revolution's long-term impact on:
  a) The transatlantic slave trade
  b) Independence movements in Latin America
  c) Race relations in the Americas

The final report must integrate information from at least 15 different Wikipedia tool calls, demonstrating clear dependencies where later phases build upon discoveries from earlier phases.
dependency_analysis:
This task creates a multi-phase dependency chain that maximizes tool utilization:

SEQUENTIAL DEPENDENCIES:
1. search_wikipedia → get_article → get_sections: The initial search identifies the target article, which is then retrieved and analyzed for structure
2. get_sections → summarize_article_section: Section titles discovered inform which specific sections to summarize (Background, Aftermath, etc.)
3. extract_key_facts → get_related_topics: Facts extracted reveal key themes and figures, guiding related topic discovery
4. get_related_topics → get_summary/get_article: Related topics discovered (Toussaint Louverture, Dessalines, etc.) trigger article retrievals
5. get_links → summarize_article_for_query: Links reveal international actors, enabling targeted query summaries

DECISION POINTS:
- After get_sections: Agent must decide which sections are most relevant for targeted summarization
- After get_related_topics: Agent must prioritize which figures to research in depth
- After get_links: Agent must filter for internationally relevant articles (France, Britain, Spain, USA)

PARALLEL OPPORTUNITIES:
- Multiple figure profiles can be researched simultaneously after related topics are identified
- International reaction summaries for different countries can proceed in parallel
- Comparative revolution research can happen alongside international context research

ITERATIVE REFINEMENT:
- Initial fact extraction may reveal gaps requiring additional get_article calls
- Related topics from one figure article may lead to discovering additional significant figures
- Links from related articles may provide supplementary perspectives

CROSS-VALIDATION:
- Facts extracted from main article vs. summaries from figure articles must be reconciled
- International perspectives from different country articles may present conflicting accounts
- Comparative analysis requires synthesizing facts across multiple revolution articles

DATA TRANSFORMATION:
- Raw article content must be transformed into structured profiles
- Chronological facts must be organized into a timeline
- Comparative data must be normalized across different article structures

task_description:
Conduct a comprehensive architectural and structural analysis of Gothic architecture, focusing on how load-bearing mechanisms enabled unprecedented verticality. Follow this strict research workflow using the Wikipedia tools: 

1. Use `search_wikipedia` to find the main article for 'Gothic architecture'.
2. Use `extract_key_facts` on this article with the topic 'structural innovations and load distribution' (set count to 5) to identify the core engineering breakthroughs.
3. Based on the extracted facts, identify the 3 most critical structural elements (e.g., Flying buttress, Pointed arch, Rib vault). For each of these 3 elements:
   a. Search for a dedicated Wikipedia article.
   b. If a dedicated article exists, use `get_summary` to retrieve its overview.
   c. If a dedicated article does NOT exist, use `summarize_article_for_query` on the main 'Gothic architecture' article with the query being the name of the element and a max_length of 200.
4. Use `get_related_topics` on the main 'Gothic architecture' article to identify exactly 3 famous European Gothic cathedrals (e.g., Chartres, Amiens, Notre-Dame de Paris, or Cologne). 
5. For each of the 3 selected cathedrals, you must analyze its construction:
   a. First, use `get_sections` on the cathedral's article to retrieve its section list.
   b. Look for a section explicitly titled 'Architecture', 'Design', 'Construction', or 'Structural features'.
   c. If such a section exists, use `summarize_article_section` on that exact section title (max_length: 200).
   d. If no such section exists in the list, fallback to using `summarize_article_for_query` on the cathedral's article with the query 'architectural structure and design' (max_length: 200).
6. Finally, compile your findings into a comprehensive report formatted as follows:
   - **Core Innovations:** The 5 key facts extracted in step 2.
   - **Structural Analysis:** Detailed summaries of the 3 structural elements identified in step 3.
   - **Cathedral Implementations:** The summaries of the 3 cathedrals from step 5, explicitly noting whether the summary came from a dedicated section or a query fallback.
   - **Synthesis:** A concluding paragraph detailing exactly how these specific cathedrals implemented the structural elements to achieve extreme height, based solely on the gathered text.
dependency_analysis:
This task requires a deep, multi-tiered dependency chain with dynamic branching based on intermediate tool outputs. 
1. **Sequential Chain 1 (Discovery):** `search_wikipedia` defines the exact article title -> passed to `extract_key_facts`.
2. **Data Transformation & Extraction:** The text output from `extract_key_facts` must be parsed by the LLM to identify exactly 3 distinct structural components.
3. **Conditional Workflow A (Element Analysis):** For each component, a `search_wikipedia` determines the next tool. IF an article exists -> `get_summary`. IF NO article exists -> fallback to `summarize_article_for_query` using the parent article title.
4. **Sequential Chain 2 (Entity Selection):** `get_related_topics` relies on the initial article title and generates a list of links. The LLM must filter this list to identify exactly 3 cathedral entities.
5. **Conditional Workflow B (Cathedral Analysis):** For each cathedral, `get_sections` is called. The output list becomes a critical decision point. IF a matching architectural section title is found -> its exact string is passed to `summarize_article_section`. IF NOT -> the workflow branches to `summarize_article_for_query`.
6. **Synthesis:** The final output requires aggregating disparate data streams (extracted facts, individual element summaries, and conditional cathedral summaries) into a highly structured final format, proving successful traversal of all parallel and conditional tool branches.

task_description:
Research and analyze the interconnected history of typography and movable type printing, tracing the technological and cultural developments from Gutenberg's invention to the modern digital typography era. Your analysis must:

1. Begin by searching Wikipedia for "History of typography" and identify the key historical periods and figures
2. Get the full article on "History of typography" and identify the major inventions and innovations
3. Extract key facts focusing on technological breakthroughs
4. Get the Wikipedia article on "Johannes Gutenberg" specifically and extract biographical and invention details
5. Get sections from the Gutenberg article to understand his specific contributions
6. Search for and retrieve articles on at least 3 other pivotal figures or developments mentioned (e.g., "William Caxton", "Aldus Manutius", "John Baskerville", or "Claude Garamond")
7. For each additional figure retrieved, extract key facts about their contributions to typography
8. Get related topics for the Gutenberg article to identify any connected developments
9. Search for "Movable type" to understand the broader technological context
10. Compare the key facts extracted from multiple sources to identify patterns in how typography evolved

Compile a comprehensive report that includes:
- Timeline of major typography innovations
- Key figures and their specific contributions
- Technological dependencies (how one innovation enabled the next)
- Geographic spread of printing technology across centuries
- Impact assessment: how these developments changed information dissemination

All findings must be cross-validated by comparing information from multiple Wikipedia articles.
dependency_analysis:
This task creates a deep, multi-layered dependency chain for researching the history of typography:

**Sequential Tool Chain:**
1. SEARCH_WIKIPEDIA for 'History of typography' → provides entry point and identifies key search terms
2. GET_ARTICLE on 'History of typography' → provides full context and lists pivotal figures/developments
3. EXTRACT_KEY_FACTS from 'History of typography' (focusing on technological breakthroughs) → extracts specific innovations and dates

7. SUMMARIZE_ARTICLE_SECTION on 'Gutenberg article' for key sections → extracts focused information
8. EXTRACT_KEY_FACTS from 'Gutenberg article' → extracts specific contributions
9. GET_RELATED_TOPICS for 'Gutenberg' → identifies other figures and developments to investigate
10. SEARCH_WIKIPEDIA for additional figures (William Caxton, Aldus Manutius, etc.) → expands research scope
11. GET_ARTICLE/SUMMARY on each additional figure → collects parallel data streams

**Decision Points:**

**Cross-Validation Requirements:**

**Data Flow:**
Search → Article fetch → Fact extraction → Related topic discovery → Parallel figure investigation → Cross-validation → Synthesis

task_description:
You are an architectural historian tasked with generating a comparative study on three major 20th-century design movements: Brutalist architecture, Art Deco, and Bauhaus.

Execute the following workflow strictly using the provided Wikipedia tools:

1. Search Wikipedia to determine the exact, primary article titles for the three movements: 'Brutalist architecture', 'Art Deco', and 'Bauhaus'.
2. For each of the three articles, use the section retrieval tool to get all section titles. Identify the section corresponding to the movement's inception (specifically look for a section named 'Origins', 'History', or 'Early years').
3. Use the section summarization tool to extract a summary of that specific historical section for each movement, setting the max_length to 150 words.
4. Use the key facts extraction tool on each of the three articles to extract exactly 5 key facts specifically focused on the topic: 'Primary materials and structural characteristics'.
5. Investigate the influences on Brutalism by retrieving the links contained within the 'Brutalist architecture' article.
6. Evaluate the links from the Brutalism article. If the exact entity 'Le Corbusier' is present in the links, fetch a specialized summary of the 'Le Corbusier' article tailored exactly to the query: 'Contribution to Brutalist architecture and concrete materials', setting max_length to 250 words.
7. Synthesize all findings into a structured comparative report containing: the historical origin summary for each movement, the bulleted list of 5 material/structural facts for each movement, and the specialized Le Corbusier analysis.
dependency_analysis: 1. Sequential Title Resolution: Tools like `get_sections`, `summarize_article_section`, and `extract_key_facts` strictly require exact Wikipedia article titles, creating a mandatory initial dependency on `search_wikipedia`. 2. Data-Driven Tool Execution (Iterative): The output of `get_sections` dictates the exact `section_title` argument passed into `summarize_article_section` (requiring string matching for 'History' or 'Origins'). 3. Conditional Workflow & Data Discovery: The agent must execute `get_links` on the Brutalism article, parse the resulting array of strings to check for the presence of the entity 'Le Corbusier', and conditionally trigger `summarize_article_for_query` on Le Corbusier's article if the condition is met. 4. Parameterized Extraction: Utilizes `extract_key_facts` with a highly specific `topic_within_article` parameter to filter out broad information and transform raw article text into targeted structured data regarding materials.

task_description:
Investigate the historical transition from alchemy to modern chemistry as a case study in scientific paradigm shift. The task requires tracing the intellectual lineage through multiple interconnected research paths:

1. PRIMARY RESEARCH PATH (Philosopher's Stone Narrative):
   - Start by searching Wikipedia for "Alchemy" and "History of alchemy"
   - Extract key facts about major alchemical traditions (Islamic, European, Chinese, Indian)
   - Identify the 3 most influential alchemists across all traditions
   - For each influential alchemist, get their Wikipedia article and extract their key contributions
   - Determine if their contributions were primarily mystical/philosophical or experimental/practical

2. SECONDARY RESEARCH PATH (Periodic Table Development):
   - Search and analyze "History of the periodic table"
   - Extract key facts about Mendeleev's contributions
   - Identify 3 elements that were discovered through alchemical practices before being scientifically characterized
   - For each element, find its Wikipedia article and document the historical journey from alchemical "discovery" to modern understanding

3. DECISION BRANCH - Compare the two paths:
   - If the alchemy path shows more mystical traditions, investigate "Islamic alchemy" as a bridge
   - If the alchemy path shows more experimental focus, investigate "Emergence of modern chemistry"
   - Use this decision to determine which section to analyze in detail

4. CROSS-VALIDATION REQUIREMENT:
   - Get related topics for both "Alchemy" and "Chemistry"
   - Identify 2 overlapping topics that represent the bridge between mystical and scientific traditions
   - For each overlapping topic, fetch the article and extract key facts that connect the two paradigms

5. SYNTHESIS OUTPUT:
   - Create a timeline analysis showing:
     a) 5 pivotal moments where alchemy contributed to chemical science
     b) 3 pivotal moments where chemistry definitively rejected alchemical principles
     c) 2 concepts that survived the transition from alchemy to chemistry with modified meanings

6. FINAL COMPARISON:
   - Get sections for both "Alchemy" and "Chemistry" articles
   - Compare their structures to determine which historical periods each discipline emphasizes
   - Identify the exact century where the transition became irreversible

All findings must be cross-referenced between at least 2 different Wikipedia sources before being included in the final analysis.

task_description:
Conduct a comprehensive comparative analysis of the development and cultural impact of three major ancient writing systems: Cuneiform, Egyptian hieroglyphs (as a writing system, not their decipherment), and the Chinese oracle bone script. Follow this research workflow:

1. Begin by searching Wikipedia for 'Cuneiform script', 'Egyptian hieroglyphs', and 'Oracle bone script' to identify the correct article titles for each writing system.

2. For each of the three writing systems, retrieve the full article and extract the section structure. Then:
   a. Extract 7 key facts from each article focused on 'origins and historical development'
   b. Extract 5 key facts from each article focused on 'materials and tools used for writing'
   c. Summarize each article tailored to the query 'What was the cultural and administrative significance of this writing system in its civilization?' (max 300 words each)

3. For each writing system article, identify the section that discusses the script's structure or sign inventory (e.g., how many signs, how the writing system works — logographic, syllabic, etc.). Summarize that specific section (max 200 words each).

4. From the Cuneiform article, get related topics. Then search for 'Sumerian language' among those related topics and retrieve its summary. Similarly, from the Egyptian hieroglyphs article, get related topics and find and summarize the article on 'Demotic (Egyptian)' or the closest match. From Oracle bone script, get related topics and find and summarize the article on 'Chinese bronze inscriptions' or the closest match.

5. For each of these three related/successor writing traditions found in step 4, extract 5 key facts focused on 'relationship to the parent writing system'.

6. Finally, search Wikipedia for 'History of writing' and retrieve that article's sections. Summarize the sections that discuss the independent invention of writing systems (max 200 words), and extract 5 key facts from the full article focused on 'independent origins of writing'.

Compile all findings into a structured comparative report with these sections:
- Section A: Origins & Timeline (when and where each system emerged, based on extracted facts)
- Section B: Script Structure Comparison (logographic vs syllabic vs mixed, number of signs, based on section summaries)
- Section C: Cultural & Administrative Role (based on tailored summaries)
- Section D: Writing Materials & Technology (based on extracted facts on materials/tools)
- Section E: Legacy & Successor Scripts (based on related topic investigation)
- Section F: Independent Invention Context (based on History of Writing findings)

For each section, explicitly note points of similarity and difference across the three writing systems.

**Layer 5 - Section Summaries (summarize_article_section x3):** Critically depends on BOTH Layer 1 (article titles) AND Layer 2 (section titles discovered dynamically). The agent must inspect section structures and make a decision about which section discusses script structure — this is a key decision point.

**Layer 6 - Related Topic Exploration (get_related_topics x3 → search/get_summary x3):** For each writing system, get related topics, then search within those results for specific successor scripts (Sumerian language, Demotic Egyptian, Chinese bronze inscriptions).
